text:
This description of the grammar of the Pite Saami language is intended to provide a general linguistics audience with an overview of phonological and morphosyntactic structures found in the language. It is based on a corpus of spoken language data collected over several years, including both free speech and elicited data. It covers the phonology, morphology and phrasal structures, and how these interact with each other, while also providing a sketch of the clausal phenomena.

The present chapter provides background information on. It includes an overview of the language and its speakers in PSbackground, then provides details about the documentation project on which this study is based in lingDoc, and finally presents a typological profile in typologicalProfile.
summary: The grammar aims to give a general linguistics audience an overview of the phonological and morphosyntactic structures of Pite Saami, based on several years of spoken-language corpus data, including both free speech and elicited material. It covers phonology, morphology, phrasal structure, their interaction, and a sketch of clausal phenomena. The chapter then offers background information on the language and its speakers, describes the documentation project, and presents a typological profile.

The Saami languages form a sub-branch of the Uralic language family. \ is classified as the southern-most Western Saami language in the Northern group.
Together, the Saami languages form a dialect continuum; \ is therefore most closely related to Lule Saami and Ume Saami, the two languages spoken directly to its north and south, respectively. Cf. Sammallahti ( Sammallahti1985, Sammallahti1998) and

for more discussion on the linguistic features which motivate the division of the dialect continuum into ten Saami languages.

sub-branch of the Uralic family tree.
summary: The Saami languages are a sub-branch of the Uralic language family, and the language in question is classified as the southern-most Western Saami language in the Northern group. Because the Saami languages form a dialect continuum, it is most closely related to Lule Saami and Ume Saami, the neighboring languages to its north and south.

section: The Pite Saami language and its speakers
text:
While Pite Saami In English, Saami is also spelled Sámi or Sami.
is the term used in the present study to refer to the language spoken by the \ people, the language also has other names. It is also called Arjeplog Saami (cf.

), referring to Arjeplog, the main municipality it is spoken in. The endonym is bidumsáme giella or bisumsáme giella, which literally mean ‘ ’s language’, as shown in example bidumsaamegiella.

Bidumsáme giella\\
bidum+sáme giella\\
Pite+Saami gen.sg language nom.sg\\
the Pite Saami language 08062141m10s

Nonetheless, speakers of \ (as is true for speakers of other Saami languages) generally refer to themselves and the individual language they speak simply as ‘Saami’, without further specification. This is likely the reason why there is no consensus concerning the endonym, which has two forms (see above); indeed, some speakers are quite unsure that an endonym exists at all.

Germanic cultures have often referred to Saami peoples using the exonym Lapps (cf. the place name Lapland), and thus the language has also been referred to as Pite Lappish in the past. This term is no longer considered respectful by many \ individuals; the name Saami is preferred, as it is borrowed from the endonym sábme or sáme. Nonetheless, a number of speakers I have worked with still refer to their own language as lapska when speaking Swedish.
summary: Pite Saami is also known as Arjeplog Saami, and its endonym is given as *bidumsáme giella* or *bisumsáme giella*, literally meaning “Pite Saami language.” However, speakers often simply call themselves and their language “Saami,” which may explain the lack of consensus about the endonym and why some speakers are unsure that one exists. The language was formerly called Pite Lappish, but this term is now often considered disrespectful, although some speakers still use *lapska* in Swedish.

section: The Pite Saami language and its speakers
text:
The Saami languages are spoken in an area traditionally referred to as Sápmi; this covers a territory stretching from south-central Norway and central Sweden, across northern Norway, Sweden and Finland and over most of the Kola Peninsula in the Russian Federation, as illustrated in Figure sabme.

There is no official geographic or political unit defining any \ linguistic or ethnic area, but the individuals (including both speakers and non-speakers) I have met, worked with or heard about who consider themselves to be \ (regardless of language abilities) all come from an area based roughly on the Arjeplog municipality Note that Arjeplog municipality ( kommun in Swedish) refers to the larger administrative district of ca. 15,000 km 2, while the town of Arjeplog is the main village in the municipality.
in Swedish Lapland and bordering areas in Norway. On the Swedish side, this has traditionally been referred to as Pite lappmark ‘ \ territory’.
For instance, Ruong, himself a native speaker of, claims that the “most genuine form” (Ruong Ruong1943; my translation) of the Pite Saami language is spoken by members of the Luokta-Mavas sameby, A sameby (Swedish, literally ‘Saami village’; samebyar in plural) is a group of reindeer herding families who tend their reindeer together in the same territory.
whose summer reindeer grazing lands are located along the headwaters of the Pite River, and by settled Saamis in the same area. However, speakers from Semisjaur-Njarg sameby to the south were also included as sources in, indicating that Ruong was clearly aware of the dialect variationdifficulty of drawing distinct language borders in the Saami dialect continuum. He indicates that some areas on the north side of the Pite River drainage speak Lule Saami, while speakers along the Skellefte River drainage are more under the “influence of Southern Saami” (; my translation).
Manker’s ethnography of the Saami populations in the Swedish mountains outlines the three samebyar Luokta-Mavas, Semisjaur-Njarg and Svaipa as part of Pite lappmark. includes a map of all Swedish samebyar as a fold-out, and a map of these three \ samebyar.
corroborates this, and adds the forest sameby Ståkke to the list. Collinder1960 and Bergsland1962 also help delineate the southern border of \ territory. Collinder writes that the border “goes along the Pite River between the parishes of Jockmock [sic] and Arvidsjaur, and farther west through the parish of Arjeplog” ( Collinder1960), while Bergsland further specifies that Ume Saami is spoken by “the forest Lapps in southern Arjeplog [...] and by the mountain Lapps in Sorsele” ( Bergsland1962).

As for the Norwegian side, some \ reindeer herding families had their summer reindeer grazing lands in the Norwegian territory adjacent to the international border. The Finno-Ugrian scholar Eliel Lagercrantz worked with \ speakers whose families originated in the Arjeplog municipality but had resettled to the Beiarn area in Norway. Ethnic \ individuals still live in Norway, and are, for instance, still active in the local \ association there, Salten Pitesamisk Forening.

As a result, one can say that \ was traditionally spoken in an area spanning both sides of the Norwegian-Swedish border around the municipality of Arjeplog on the Swedish side and across the border into Saltdal and Beiarn municipalities in Norway.
On the Swedish side, the \ area is essentially limited to the Pite River
drainage above the waterfall at Storforsen, and the sections of the Skellefte River
drainage from the town of Arjeplog and farther upriver.
The map in Figure piteTerritory gives a rough idea of the traditional geographic area, which is the light area on the map. It is based on,,, and, as well as on my own knowledge gained by discussing family histories with \ individuals.

My own research indicates that \ is currently still spoken by a few members of the Luokta-Mavas, Semisjaur-Njarg and Ståkke samebyar, as well as by settled Saami families from the same areas. Furthermore there are a few speakers from the Arjeplog municipality who have since moved to other areas outside of Arjeplog municipality,
even as far away as southern Sweden.
Ethnic \ individuals from Norway have indicated to me that the last \ speakers on the Norwegian side died several generations ago.

summary:
The passage describes the traditional territory of Pite Saami as spanning both sides of the Norwegian-Swedish border, centered on the Arjeplog area in Swedish Lapland and extending into adjacent areas of Norway. It emphasizes that the language border is not sharply defined, since older sources and local evidence show dialect continuity and overlap with neighboring Saami varieties, especially Lule and Southern Saami.  

It also notes that Pite Saami is still spoken by a few people from the Luokta-Mavas, Semisjaur-Njarg, and Ståkke samebyar and by some settled families from the same region, while the last speakers on the Norwegian side are said to have died several generations ago.

section: The Pite Saami language and its speakers
subsection: The state of the Pite Saami language
text:
Traditionally, most \ families lived either as semi-nomadic reindeer herders or as sedentary farmers, fishers and hunters. Despite having always been in contact, these two groups lived very different lifestyles, and spoke Saami in relative isolation from one another. While reindeer herding Saami have often been a topic of Saami studies, the settled Saami are neglected or even actively prejudiced against for not being ‘true’ Saami since they do not herd reindeer. The data supporting the present study and gathered as part of the \ (cf. PSDPcorpus ) originated from both groups.

By the eighteenth century, the Saami peoples had, in general, been converted from animistic polytheism to Christianity, marking the beginning of Saami assimilation to North Germanic culture.
Strict policies in the mid-nineteenth century sent \ children to special ‘nomad schools’ where they were not allowed to speak Saami. Attending these schools also kept them away from their families and from regularly participating in \ life, while reinforcing the state’s drive to exclusively promote Swedish language contact culture and social values.

Accompanying this shift, traditional realms of \ experience are slowly being left behind in favor of Swedish ones. With the introduction of modern conveniences, most \ individuals have moved to permanent dwellings in populated communities, particularly Arjeplog, thereby leaving behind traditional ways of life. Along with this demographic shift, they are also losing the need to carry out traditional occupations using the Pite Saami language. As a result, all \ speakers today speak Swedish language contact fluently, and indeed use Swedish significantly more often in everyday life.

A gradual reverse in political and social policies in Sweden over the last decades led initially to the acceptance and then to the active promotion of multiculturalism, particularly concerning the Saami people. This has helped to positively change attitudes towards \ identity. However, concerning the Pite Saami language and many traditional cultural realms, this change seems inadequate for revitalization. For instance, the Swedish government's minority language law from 2010 only applies the blanket term samiska (‘the Saami language’), and, in doing so, completely disregards the reality that there are five different Saami languages in Sweden. Even within Sápmi, \ is threatened by larger Saami languages, in particular by North Saami, which has an active speech community of around 30,000 speakers, regular television, radio, print and internet resources, and first-language instruction in public school. The robust status of North Saami in addition to the lack of an officially recognized \ orthography allow local government agencies to conveniently support North Saami alone in fulfilling the language law's requirements; any positive effects on the Pite Saami language are essentially negated.

According to my own data collected from \ individuals during fieldwork, there are around 30 speakers left, Cf., who claims there are only 10 speakers, while the English abstract in erroneously claims that the Pite Saami language is “now extinct.”
of around 2000 ethnic \ individuals. With one exception, all speakers are older than 50.
Based on my own observations, all speakers are fluent in the Swedish language contact language, even if many of them did not learn Swedish until they began school. Indeed, Swedish dominates everyday life for most speakers today, particularly for those who do not work in reindeer husbandry, and for those not living in the traditional \ area. Only a few households (less than five) use \ on a regular basis at home or in family situations, and these are still involved in reindeer husbandry. In public realms, the language is rarely used today. For a more detailed description and analysis of the situation the language is currently in, see.
summary:
The passage describes how Saami populations historically included both reindeer herders and settled farmers, fishers, and hunters, but the settled Saami have often been neglected in Saami studies. It also outlines long-term assimilation pressures in Sweden, including Christianization, compulsory nomad schools that banned Saami, and the rise of Swedish as the dominant language in daily life.  

For Pite Saami specifically, the text says the language is now highly endangered, with only about 30 speakers left, most of them over 50, and Swedish is used much more frequently in everyday life. Although multicultural policies have improved attitudes toward Saami identity, they have not been sufficient to revitalize Pite Saami, which is also overshadowed by stronger Saami languages such as North Saami.

text:
The Pite Saami language has been the subject of academic research in the past; cf.,, and.
This extant body of research was consulted in coming to terms with \ linguistic structures in creating the present description.
However, in fulfilling the goal of describing the Pite Saami language as it is spoken in the early 21 st century, the \ corpus, collected from 2008 through 2013, is the main source of data. With this in mind, I consider this a corpus-based description, as opposed to a literature-based description, which would have attempted to incorporate these previous works to a much greater extent. Indeed, everything not specifically cited as coming from another source is based on my own analysis of the corpus.
The current description will hopefully be seen as a supplement to previous work on, and together with previous studies, can facilitate exploring language change as exemplified by a severely endangered language.

In the following sections, previous studies on \ are summarized in previousWork. The current corpus and the documentation involved in creating it are described in PSDPcorpus. Then usingThis provides a short guide to using this description.
summary: The passage explains that while Pite Saami has been studied before, the present description relies primarily on a corpus collected from 2008 to 2013 and is therefore intended as a corpus-based, not literature-based, description of the language as spoken in the early 21st century. Earlier research was consulted, but most claims come from the author’s own analysis of the corpus, and the work is meant to supplement previous studies and help investigate language change in this severely endangered language.

text:
In the late 19 th century the Hungarian scholar Ignácz Halász studied, and wrote several studies in Hungarian on the language.
Lule- és Pite-lappmarki nyelvmutatvéanyok és szótár ‘Linguistic samples and a wordlist from Lule and \ territory’. contains the Gospel of Matthew in Lule Saami, and a combined Lule Saami/ \ wordlist with translations in Hungarian and German.
Népköltési gyüjtemény: a Pite Lappmark Arjepluogi egyházkerületéböl ‘Collection of traditional verses from the bishopric of Arjeplog in \ territory’.
consists of a significant text collection of short \ texts, transcribed using the traditional Finno-Ugrian transcription. Each text is translated as a whole into Hungarian. The majority of the texts are traditional narratives,
and a few poems and songs are also transcribed and translated.
Pite lappmarki szótár és nyelvtan ‘Wordlist and grammatical description from \ territory’.
includes morphological paradigms and a \ wordlist with translations into Hungarian and German.

Sprachlehre des Westlappischen nach der Mundart von Arjeplog ‘A grammar of West Saami based on the Arjeplog dialect’.
is a grammar in German. It is based on three months of fieldwork during which Lagercrantz consulted three \ individuals who had settled in the Beiarn district in Norway but who were originally from the Arjeplog municipality. The book covers semantically driven descriptions of clause structures, a limited description of morphology, and an extended analysis of the phonological system, based on phonetic acoustic experiments.

Lappische Verbalableitung dargestellt auf Grundlage des Pitelappischen ‘Saami verbal derivation as illustrated by ’. is the dissertation of Israel Ruong, who later became professor of Saami languages and culture at Uppsala universitet. Ruong’s native language was; his dissertation, an elaborate categorization of \ verb derivations, is his only study specifically dealing with the Pite Saami language.

Arjeploginsaamen äänne- ja taivutusopin pääpiirteet ‘The fundamentals of Arjeplog Saami phonology and inflection’. is a Fin\-nish-language description of \ phonology and inflectional patterns, and is based on recordings, publications and archived materials on \ from 1950 and earlier. Some paradigms can be found at the end of the book, as well as several \ texts with phonetic and orthographic transcriptions, as well as Finnish translations. The phonetic transcriptions are presented in the transcription standard used in Finno-Ugrian studies.

Note that these studies deal with \ as it was spoken before 1950. Finno-Ugristian studies have traditionally dealt with historical-comparative studies, and have not always been concerned with the synchronic state of Saami languages. Indeed, the distance some scholars keep from the synchronic situation is highlighted by the erroneous claim by Lehtiranta
that \ is “now extinct”.
Consequently, the present study is the first extensive description of the Pite Saami language in English and for a general linguistic audience.

Since the present study is intended to be a synchronic description of the Pite Saami language as used in the early 21 st century and reflected by the \ corpus, the previous work mentioned above have played an indirect but important role in its creation. However, these works were referred to in detail particularly when the data from the corpus were not substantial enough to allow relatively certain conclusions to be drawn. Data based at least partly on sources other than the documentation corpus are clearly marked as such in this description. Specifically, the sections in concerning phrasal and sentence-level syntactic phenomena in Part A ‘ Ausdruckslehre’ (pp. 19--99) were informative, while Part B ‘ Formenlehre’ (pp. 103-141), the paradigms throughout as well as the paradigms in the appendix to were consulted regarding morphology. In writing Chapter derivMorph on derivational morphology, Ruong’s thesis (particularly Chapters 6 through 40, which present his data) provided valuable insights into the variety and complexity of \ derivation from both morphological and semantic perspectives.

In addition to the academic linguistic studies mentioned above, a number of other texts exist concerning the Pite Saami language and its people. describe the current state of the Pite Saami language from the point of view of sociology of language. deals with the etymology of a selection of \ place names along the river Piteälven in the Arjeplog municipality.
A large number of \ vuole This is nominative plural; the nominative singular form is vuolle.
(songs in the Saami singing tradition of yoik) were recorded in the first half of the 20 th century. These can be found transcribed in a number of works:
includes 139 transcriptions of \ melodies and lyrics, with German translations;
have 93 songs by Jonas Eriksson Steggo in the form of transcribed melodies and lyrics, with translations in Swedish and German;
provide 73 songs by a variety of \ individuals in the form of transcribed melodies and lyrics, also with translations in Swedish and German.

discusses a short \ text from a recording done in 1939 by Israel Ruong; the text is presented in three transcription standards (Finno-Ugrian close phonetic standard, the author’s own phonemic transcription, and a modified North Saami orthography) and includes an English translation.
Lars Rensund’s books ( Rensund1982, Rensund1986) detail personal recollections by the author, himself a Pite Saami, and are interspersed with sentences and occasionally entire narratives in. provides an in-depth study of the colonization of \ territory by Swedish language contact settlers up to the middle of the 19 th century.
No educational materials, bible translations or other common texts exist in the Pite Saami language. With the exception of the works by Lars Rensund, most \ speakers today are not aware of any of the works mentioned above.
summary:
The passage surveys earlier linguistic work on Pite Saami, especially 19th- and 20th-century studies by scholars such as Ignácz Halász, Lagercrantz, and Israel Ruong, which include wordlists, grammars, text collections, phonological descriptions, and analyses of verbal derivation. It emphasizes that these works primarily document Pite Saami as spoken before 1950 and were often synchronic only indirectly, while the present study is described as the first extensive English-language description of Pite Saami for a general linguistic audience based on early 21st-century corpus data.  

It also notes additional materials on Pite Saami, including yoik transcriptions, short texts, place-name studies, and personal recollections by Lars Rensund, but says that there are no educational materials or Bible translations in the language and that most speakers are now unaware of these works.

text:
The data forming the basis of the present study were collected as a part of the. This description is a direct result of that project, the main goal of which is the linguistic documentation of the Pite Saami language. The project has so far resulted in audio and video recordings documenting current language usage and grammatical structures and includes an archived corpus comprising 29,208 transcribed and translated \ words (as of early March 2014;

cf. the inventoryRefAppendix for a list of recordings).
From June 2008 until July 2011, the project was carried out by Joshua Wilbur at the Nordeuropa-Institut at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, with support from the Endangered Languages Documentation Programme (ELDP; a part of the Hans Rausing Endangered Languages Project, with financial support from the Arcadia foundation and hosted by the School for Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) at the University of London).
A continuation of the project is underway in 2013 and 2014 at Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg thanks to generous continued funding from ELDP.

Current trends in documentary linguistics documentary linguistics were taken into account. Cf.,,,,, the book series Language Documentation and Description, among others.
Himmelmann’s proposal that “a language documentation is a lasting multipurpose record of a language” is a defining motivation behind the project. Accordingly, the resulting documentation consists of a documentation corpus of a variety of linguistic genres, including \ situations potentially of interest to non-linguistic disciplines and to members of the Pite Saami language community themselves, as well as the present description. Initial results have been archived at five archives at international, national, regional and local levels:
itemize
The Endangered Languages Archive (ELAR) at the School for Oriental and African Studies in London;
The Language Archive at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen;
Dialekt-, ortnamns och folkminnesarkivet i Umeå ‘The Department of Dialectology, Onomastics and Folklore Research in Umeå’. (DAUM) in Umeå, Sweden;
Ájtte: Svenskt Fjäll- och Samemuseum ‘Ájtte: the Swedish Mountain and Saami Museum’; ájtte is the Lule Saami word for a traditional Saami storage shed. in Jokkmokk, Sweden;
Silvermuseet ‘The Silver Museum’. in Arjeplog, Sweden.
itemize
Working with multiple archiving sites as well as having all data in a digital format help ensure accessibility to and longevity of the data.

Access to the materials is available via the archives (in some cases, this is possible via the world wide web).
Ideally, an archive should provide interested parties with access to archived materials, while respecting the privacy and the wishes of recording participants as necessary; with this in mind, access rights to the data related to any given session reflect the wishes of speakers involved in a specific session concerning availability to the linguistics and other scientific communities, the \ and greater Saami communities, and other individuals and groups in general.
Furthermore, as part of a scientific endeavor, the claims made in this book about \ linguistic structures should be reproducible; with this in mind, the original data are available to the academic community via the Language Archive at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen, the Netherlands; see archiveAccess for more details on accessing the archive.
summary: The passage explains that the study is based on a larger documentation project on Pite Saami, whose goal is to create a lasting, multipurpose record of the language. This documentation includes audio and video recordings, a transcribed and translated corpus, and a present grammatical description, all archived at multiple institutions to ensure access, preservation, and respect for speaker privacy.

text:
Data were collected and recordings were transcribed during a total of 23 months at the field site in and around Arjeplog, Sweden,
with the invaluable assistance of a number of \ speakers. They were compensated for their time and effort with a modest consultant honorarium.

The documentation corpus consists of more than 55 hours of recordings covering a variety of genres; cf. the Appendix for a list of recordings, including an indication of genre and medium.
As the morphological structure of \ words is quite complex,
it was necessary to rely on elicitation techniques to gather a sufficient number of word forms for a wide variety of lexemes as a basis for morphological analyses.
As a result, the majority of recordings (approximately 45 hours) consist of elicitation sessions intended to gather specific details concerning the structure of the language.
These were often conducted using Swedish as a metalanguage, but \ was used whenever efficient and useful, and more frequently in recordings made later in the project.
A variety of elicitation methods were used. To a large extent, elicitation sessions were conducted as translational interviews (particularly in early recordings to collect initial wordlists) and sentence completion (using both Swedish and \ triggers, mostly to complete morphology paradigms). However, other methods were used as well, such as vocabulary card ordering tasks to test syntactic structures, and tasks using toy blocks to gather data on spatial relations.
Many non-elicitation linguistic situations were also recorded, covering genres such as conversations, explanations, narrations, performances, as well as songs and readings; in the current documentation corpus, such recordings comprise approximately 17,700 transcribed words. A few written texts were also collected to supplement recordings.

Each collection of materials Note that the archive at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, refers to the entire collection of files concerning a single recording as a ‘session’, not a ‘collection’.
in the corpus corresponds to a recorded linguistic event. Each collection has a unique name based on the pattern:
center pitYYMMDDabc center
(pit =, YYMMDD = abbreviated date of recording with a two-digit year, abc = further disambiguation as needed). Recordings done for the project from 2012 onwards use the ISO 639-3 code sje as a prefix for session names instead of pit, and a four-digit year; e.g., sje20121014b.
All digital files related to a certain collection are named based on this pattern.

In almost all cases, the following recording equipment, standards and software were used for documentation. A small number of deviations exist, and are indicated in the archived metadata for the relevant sessions.

Video: a Panasonic NV-GS500EG-S video camera using miniDV cassettes in short play (SP) mode, using a wide-angle lens attachment and a tripod. In most cases, a RØDE SVM stereo video microphone was mounted on the camera for audio in place of using the built-in microphone.

Audio: an Edirol R-09 digital audio recorder set to record 16-bit WAV format at 44.1 kHz. A variety of microphones was used, depending on the specific recording situation; these included a RØDE SVM stereo video microphone, a Sennheiser lapel microphone connected to a Sennheiser EW 112-p G2 wireless set and a Sennheiser MKE 300 shotgun microphone.

Still images: a Canon IXUS 80IS digital photo camera was used to take digital photographs to supplement documentation. Images are in JPEG format.

Editing/Computing: video/audio recordings were transferred to a Macintosh MacBook Pro for further editing, as necessary. Video was edited using Final Cut Express and Final Cut Pro software. Audio was archived in the original quality, while video was compressed to MPEG-2 or MPEG-4 format.

Transcribing/annotating: the multimedia annotation program ELAN ELAN is free software developed by the Technical Group of the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (see www.lat-mpi.eu/tools/elan/ ).
was used to transcribe and annotate recordings. Annotation/transcription files are archived in both ELAN format and in plain text format.

Initial transcriptions of recordings were completed with the help of native speaker assistants. I am particularly indebted to Elsy Rankvist Elsy Rankvist for her invaluable transcription assistance.
Transcriptions in the corpus are written in various versions of the \ orthography under development by the wordlist project Insamling av pitesamiska ord (cf. orthography ),
but have been standardized according to the principles explained in orthography when cited in this book.
All transcribed words are provided with annotations in the form of at least a translation into English or Swedish or as morpheme-by-morpheme glosses. Such glosses can serve as the sole translation of a transcribed word or utterance, particularly for data from transcribed elicitation sessions. Both glosses and free translations into English and/or Swedish may be provided, especially in non-elicited text genres. Relevant notes or commentary may also exist as annotations.

Metadata were collected in a database using the FileMaker Pro program, then exported to XML and plain text formats for archiving. Information collected concerns participants, the recording situation, location, equipment used and a summary of the contents of the recording, among other things.

Any given collection consists minimally of the following set of digital files:

itemize
audio recording in WAV format (16-bit, 44 kHz)
transcription/annotation file in ELAN and in plain text format

metadata concerning the session in XML and plain text formats
metadata concerning the entire collection in XML

itemize
In addition to the above files, collections may also include the following files:
itemize
video recording in MPEG-2 or MPEG-4 format
digital images in JPEG format
other supplementary files
itemize
summary:
Data were collected over 23 months at and around Arjeplog, Sweden, resulting in a documentation corpus of more than 55 hours of recordings. Because the language’s morphology is complex, most of the corpus consists of elicitation sessions, supplemented by non-elicited genres such as conversations, narrations, songs, and readings.  

The passage also describes the corpus’s organization and documentation practices: each recording event has a uniquely named session, and the materials were recorded with standardized video, audio, photo, and transcription software and equipment. Transcriptions were completed with native speaker assistance, annotated in ELAN, standardized in the book’s orthography, and archived together with metadata in multiple digital formats.

text:
The transcription/annotation files are divided into numbered, utterance-based units and include at least a transcription of any Pite Saami language usage.
A specific utterance can be referred to using the collection/session name and the utterance number.
The \ original is translated into Swedish and/or English, and provided with linguistic glosses. Other comments are included as well, whenever deemed relevant or useful.
Finally, in cases with code-switching, the language being used in a certain utterance, or part thereof, is indicated. Tiers in all ELAN files are organized hierarchically based on the template
in Figure ELANhierarchy for each speaking participant in a recording, plus a ‘notes’ tier for general comments.
A list of all recordings in the corpus can be found in the Appendix on page inventory, including brief descriptions of content and an indication of the number of \ words transcribed and translated per recording.

summary: The transcription and annotation files are divided into numbered utterance-based units, and each utterance can be identified by the collection/session name plus its utterance number. They include transcriptions of Pite Saami, translations into Swedish and/or English, linguistic glosses, relevant comments, and, where needed, language labels for code-switching; the ELAN tiers are organized hierarchically for each speaker with an additional notes tier. A list of all recordings, with brief content descriptions and counts of transcribed and translated words, is given in the appendix.

text:
This description of the grammar and the accompanying documentation corpus are together intended to outline the structural features of the Pite Saami language and provide an empirical foundation for claims made in the present work. In addition, the documentation should give interested individuals (linguists, Saami individuals, etc.) the opportunity to explore other aspects of the language as well. Finally, it should also secure a record of the language as spoken by those \ individuals who likely comprise the last generations of speakers for future generations of ethnic \ individuals.

The following sections are meant to assist in utilizing both the description and the accompanying documentation corpus.
The first section ( accountabilityEtc ) deals with accountability and verifiability, while the second section ( archiveAccess ) provides brief instructions on how to access data from the corpus.
Then, examplesExample illustrates how examples from the corpus are presented.
Finally, orthography covers orthographic considerations and includes a list of phonemes and the graphemes used to represent these.
A list of symbols and abbreviations used in the present work is provided starting on page symbolList.
summary:
The grammar description and accompanying documentation corpus are intended to outline the structural features of Pite Saami and provide an empirical basis for the claims made in the work. They also serve to let linguists and Saami people explore other aspects of the language and to preserve a record of the speech of likely the last generations of speakers for future generations.

The following sections explain how to use the description and corpus: one section addresses accountability and verifiability, another gives instructions for accessing the corpus, a third shows how examples are presented, and a final section covers orthography, including the phonemes and graphemes used. A list of symbols and abbreviations is also provided.

The spoken text is presented in italics in the initial line in the orthographic standard, followed by interpretive information in the form of a morpheme-by-morpheme breakdown in the second line and English glosses in the third line. Lars Rensund’s books ( Rensund1982,Rensund1986). and Lule Saami orthographies E.g., at literacy courses for \ individuals held in Arjeplog occasionally during the last decade and sponsored by the Swedish Saami Parliament. have been used to write \ for a non-technical, non-linguistic audience. However, from 2008 through 2011, Arjeplogs sameförening (the local Saami association in Arjeplog) received funding to complete a lexicographic project called Insamling av pitesamiska ord, This translates roughly as “collecting \ words”. A working version of the resulting lexical database is currently available online at: http://saami.uni-freiburg.de/psdp/pite-lex/. The passage explains that Pite Saami does not yet have an officially recognized orthography, though earlier texts used adapted Swedish or Lule Saami spelling systems. A working orthography was developed through a lexicographic project, and the author adopts it while noting that it remains provisional and sometimes inconsistent.  

It then outlines several spelling conventions: Swedish-based letters are used for plosives, affricates are written with digraphs like <ts> and <tj>, geminate consonants are usually doubled, and preaspiration is marked with <h> in some positions but not after sonorants. The passage also notes that the copular/auxiliary lä may be written as the enclitic ’l after a preceding word ending in an open syllable.

typological profile|(
\ is a Western Saami language in the Saamic branch of the Uralic language family. It is currently spoken by around thirty speakers in and around the Arjeplog municipality in Swedish Lapland. (Cf. PSbackground for more details on the current state of the language.)

With the exception of a limited number of grammatical items, \ words consist minimally of one trochaic foot. All non-final odd syllables are stressed, with the initial syllable being most prominent. (Cf. Chapter ProsodicStructure.)

There are 43 consonant phonemes and 9 vowel phonemes. With the exception of the glottal fricative /h/, there is a length distinction for all consonants (singleton and geminate pairs). There are both voiceless and preaspirated plosive and affricate phonemes. Geminates and preaspirated segments are restricted to foot-medial position. Vowel length is only distinctive in open front position ( /a/ and /aː/). (Cf. Chapter csANDvs.)

Linear morphology in \ is exclusively suffixing. However, grammatical categories are often expressed non-linearly as well. This can take the form of foot-internal consonant alternations, umlaut in the first vowel of the initial foot, and regressive vowel harmony between both vowels of a foot.

Nouns inflect for number and nine cases. Verbs inflect for person, number, tense and mood. Adjectives come in sets of attributive and predicative forms that are not regularly derivable from one another; attributive adjectives do not inflect, while predicative adjectives inflect for number. Number distinctions are limited to singular and plural for nouns, non-personal pronouns and predicative adjectives, but also exhibit a dual category in pronouns and in verb agreement morphology. (Cf. morphology for a brief introduction to \ morphology; details on inflectional morphology can be found throughout Chapters nouns through otherWordClasses.)

There are seven word classes (verbs, nominals, adjectivals, adverbs, postpositions, conjunctions and interjections); these can be distinguished by syntactic criteria as well as their behavior concerning inflectional morphology. Nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs can be derived using linear and/or non-linear morphological processes. (Cf. introWordForms for an overview of the various word forms; Chapter nouns on nouns; Chapter pronouns on pronouns; Chapter adjectivesIntro on adjectivals; Chapter verbs on verbs; Chapter otherWordClasses on the other word classes; Chapter derivMorph provides some examples for derivational morphology.)

Nominal, adjectival, adverbial and postpositional phrases and the verb complex constitute the main components of \ clauses, and are covered in Chapter phraseTypesCh.

\ has nominative/accusative argument alignment.
Basic clauses consist minimally of a single finite verb form and potentially further non-finite verb forms,
as well as any arguments, complements and adjuncts. Copular clauses require the fully inflected copular verb. Negation is expressed by the fully inflected verb of negation in combination with a special non-finite form of the negated lexical verb. Polar interrogatives can be identified by a question marker, but this is exceptionally rare in current \ usage. Clause-level possession can be expressed using a transitive verb with the possessor as the subject and the possessum as the object, or using a copular phrase with the possessum as the subject and the possessor in an oblique case. Relativization uses a relative pronoun introducing a relative clause with a fully inflected finite verb; the relative pronoun is not restricted in the syntactic role it has in the relative clause. Constituent order is not determined syntactically, but by information structure. (Chapters overviewSyntax through complexClauses deal with clause-level syntax.)

The Pite Saami language exhibits a number of features which are potentially remarkable from a general typological point of view, even if most of these features are not particularly unusual among the Saami languages. A selection of such features and the sections that deal with these are listed in Table freakyShit.

typological profile|)
summary:
Pite Saami is a Western Saami language of the Uralic family, spoken by about thirty people in and around Arjeplog in Swedish Lapland. It has complex prosody and phonology, including trochaic feet, extensive consonant length contrasts, preaspirated stops and affricates, and limited vowel-length contrast, while its morphology is entirely suffixing but also uses non-linear alternations such as consonant gradation, umlaut, and vowel harmony.

The language has rich inflectional systems: nouns mark number and nine cases, verbs mark person, number, tense, and mood, and adjectives show distinct attributive and predicative forms. Clauses have nominative/accusative alignment, negation and copular constructions use special finite verbs, and constituent order is governed by information structure rather than syntax.

text:
This description of the phonology of \ begins with a discussion of prosodic structures before the segmental phonology is described. This choice of ordering is motivated by the important role that prosodic positions play in the distribution of phonemes (as well as in morphophonology). It is useful to first understand the prosodic structure of \ words before looking at their segmental composition here, and later to better understand morphophonology.

While there are a number of monosyllabic functional words, all \ lexical forms and many functional words are minimally bisyllabic.
The first two sections ( monosyllabicWords and polysyllabicWords ) describe the prosodic structures of these two groups of words.
Then, utterance-level prosodic phenomena are dealt with in utteranceProsody.
summary: The passage explains that the phonology description begins with prosodic structure rather than segmental phonology because prosodic positions strongly affect phoneme distribution and morphophonology. It notes that while there are some monosyllabic functional words, all lexical forms and many functional words are at least bisyllabic, so the first sections describe monosyllabic and polysyllabic word prosody, followed by utterance-level prosody.

text:
While the majority of \ words are polysyllabic, a small set of functional words are monosyllabic. This set includes, for instance, some interjections interjection, conjunctions conjunction and pronouns pronoun. These monosyllabic words consist of at least one vowel All vowel phonemes except /u͡a/ are attested in monosyllabic words.
and one consonant. This consonant can be in either onset or coda position; it is also possible for both consonant positions to be filled. Consonant clusters consonant cluster are licensed in coda position as well. The possible segmental structure templates for monosyllabic words are listed with examples in Table monosyllabicTemplates.
summary: Most words are polysyllabic, but a small set of functional words, such as some interjections, conjunctions, and pronouns, are monosyllabic. These monosyllabic words contain at least one vowel and one consonant, with the consonant appearing in onset, coda, or both positions; consonant clusters are also allowed in coda position. All vowel phonemes except /u͡a/ occur in monosyllabic words.

text:
All lexical forms and a large number of functional words in \ are minimally bisyllabic. The smallest prosodic segmental structure attested for polysyllabic words is centerVCV center but larger words are both possible and common, and expand upon this minimal foundation; examples are provided throughout the following discussion. Due to a number of phenomena, it is sensible to posit a phonological domain, which, in following basic principles of phonology
and the prosodic hierarchy prosodic hierarchy
(cf. e.g.,,,, ), I will refer to as a foot foot. A \ foot is trochaic stress (counting from left to right) and essentially bisyllabic. Multisyllabic words with an odd number of syllables thus have a final (unstressed) syllable which falls outside of the last foot.
Whether such a final syllable should belong to the preceding foot or not is a theoretical question which will not be addressed here, but it should be noted that the segments in such syllables are subject to highly restrictive phonotactics compared to those clearly located within a trochaic foot. Cf. Vallophones on the phonotactics of vowel phonemes.
Evidence for the foot as a domain can be found in prosodic (intonation, cf. wordStress; minimal size restrictions as described here), phonological (segmental restrictions, cf. Chapter csANDvs ) and morphophonological (stem alternations and vowel harmony, cf. morphophonology ) phenomena.
summary: The passage argues that most lexical forms and many functional words are minimally bisyllabic, with larger words building on this basic prosodic structure. It proposes a trochaic, essentially bisyllabic foot as a key phonological domain, noting that in words with an odd number of syllables the final unstressed syllable lies outside the last foot and shows more restricted phonotactics. Evidence for the foot comes from prosodic, phonological, and morphophonological phenomena such as intonation, segmental restrictions, stem alternations, and vowel harmony.

The initial syllable syllable (cf. syllabification on syllabification) of a \ foot always receives main stress stress. All other foot-initial syllables receive secondary stress. If a final syllable is odd, it does not receive any stress. As a result, the patterns of stressed and unstressed syllables presented in Figure trochees are attested in;

It notes that some recent Swedish loanwords diverge by having an initial unstressed syllable, and that the main acoustic correlates of stress are intensity and pitch rather than vowel length. The text also says that more detailed analysis is needed to fully describe the phonetic behavior of primary versus secondary stress.

text:
prosodic domains
Due to systematic restrictions on the distribution of a number of segments and consonant clusters as well as to the prosodic domains of morphophonologymorphophonological processes, it is useful to name and describe various prosodic positions for polysyllabic words. The domains themselves are described below, while the relevant phonological restrictions and morphophonological processes are described in the pertinent sections on consonant phonemes ( consonants ), vowel phonemes ( vowelPhonemes ) and morphophonology ( morphophonology ). Only a very limited number of recent loan words do not adhere to this structure.
The schema in Figure prosodicDomainFigure shows these prosodic positions, and they are described further below. In the schema, only segments represented by bold capital letters are obligatory.

Note that Table domainExamples provides examples of how a word’s segments fill these positions; it may be useful to refer to this to better understand these prosodic domains.
summary: The passage explains that because certain segments, consonant clusters, and morphophonological processes are restricted by position, it is useful to identify prosodic domains for polysyllabic words. It notes that these domains are illustrated in a schema where only the bold capital-letter segments are obligatory, and that only a small number of recent loanwords fail to follow this structure.

text:
foot stress
A foot in \ is a prosodic unit consisting of a stressed syllable and the following unstressed syllable, and is thus trochaic. Every multi-syllabic \ word consists of at least one foot.
summary: A foot in this system is a prosodic unit made up of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable, so it is trochaic. Every multisyllabic word contains at least one foot.

text:
Foot onset position is the first consonant or consonant cluster of a foot. It is not obligatorily filled.
In Saamic linguistics, this has typically been referred to as the ‘initium’.
summary: Foot onset position is the first consonant or consonant cluster of a foot, and it does not have to be filled. In Saamic linguistics, this position is typically called the “initium.”

text:
V1 is the first vowel of a foot, and is the peak of the stress-carrying syllable for the foot. It can be long or short, and can be a monophthong or a diphthongdiphthong. The vowel in the final V1 position Only words of four or more syllables can have more than one V1 position.
of a word is the location for umlaut and ablaut/ j-harmony (cf. umlaut and VH ).
In Saamic linguistics, this has been referred to as the ‘vowel center’.
summary: V1 is the first vowel in a foot and serves as the peak of the stress-carrying syllable. It may be long or short and may be either a monophthong or a diphthong; in word-final V1 position, it is the site of umlaut and ablaut/j-harmony, and only words of four or more syllables can have more than one V1 position. In Saamic linguistics, this position has been called the “vowel center.”

text:
consonant center
The consonant center is the consonant or consonants that follow V1 (the initial vowel) and precede V2 (the second vowel), and essentially form the core
of a foot. Every foot has a consonant center. The final consonant segment of the consonant center is the onset of the second syllable due to syllabification (cf. syllabification ). The final consonant center of a word is the location for consonant gradation. The term ‘consonant center’ is commonly used in Saami linguistics.
summary: The consonant center is the consonant or consonants between V1 and V2, forming the core of a foot, and every foot has one. Its final consonant belongs to the onset of the second syllable through syllabification, and the final consonant center in a word is where consonant gradation occurs. The term is commonly used in Saami linguistics.

text:
V2 is the second vowel of a foot. It never carries stress. Every foot has a vowel in this position. With the exception of the diphthongdiphthong phoneme /u͡a/, all vowel phonemes are attested here.
In Saamic linguistics, this has been referred to as the ‘latus’.
summary: V2 is the second vowel position in a foot and it never bears stress, though every foot contains a vowel in this slot. All vowel phonemes occur in this position except the diphthong phoneme /u͡a/. In Saamic linguistics, this position is called the “latus.”

text:
C2 is the consonant or consonants following V2. It is not obligatorily filled. If it is followed by a V3, then its final segment is resyllabified as the onset of the following syllable.
In Saamic linguistics, this has also been referred to as the ‘consonant margin’.
summary: C2 is the consonant or consonants that follow V2, and it does not have to be filled. If a V3 follows, the final segment of C2 is resyllabified as the onset of the next syllable. In Saamic linguistics, C2 has also been called the “consonant margin.”

text:
V3 is the unstressed vowel of any syllable following the final foot of a polysyllabic word form, and is thus the last syllable nucleus of a word (when present). Only a limited set of vowel phonemes can occur in this position. If the V3 position is filled, then there is always a consonant margin as well.
In Saamic linguistics, this has been referred to as the ‘vowel margin’.
summary: V3 is the unstressed vowel in the syllable following the final foot of a polysyllabic word, making it the last syllable nucleus of a word when present. Only a limited set of vowel phonemes can occur in this position, and if V3 is filled, it is always accompanied by a consonant margin. In Saamic linguistics, this position has been called the “vowel margin.”

text:
C3 is a consonant or one of a limited set of consonant clusters (cf. CCsWordfinal ) following V3 of a polysyllabic word, and is thus always word-final (when present). It is not obligatorily filled. If the C3 position is filled, then there is always a vowel in V3 and a consonant margin as well.
In Saamic linguistics, this has been referred to as the ‘finis’.
summary: C3 is a word-final consonant slot, or a limited set of consonant clusters, occurring after V3 in a polysyllabic word. It is optional, and when it is filled there is always both a vowel in V3 and a consonant margin. In Saamic linguistics, this position is called the “finis.”

text:
Table domainExamples provides several examples for \ polysyllabic words and how their segments fill the prosodic domains described above. Note that there are always segments in V1, the consonant center consonant center and V2, forming a sort of ‘minimal core.’

Only the final foot of a word can be followed by a single, odd syllable with V3 and potentially C3 segments.

Similarly, only the final foot of a word is subject to morphophonological morphophonology phenomena (cf. morphophonology ). For instance, sálbmagirrje ‘book of psalms, hymnal’ is a compound consisting of sálbma ‘psalm’ and girrje ‘book’. It consists of two feet: sálbma- and -girrje.

It is not possible to add another syllable (e.g., via suffixation) between these two feet because they belong to the same compound noun. Furthermore, the inflected form for acc.sg is sálbmagirjev, in which consonant gradation (weakening of rr to r) is only triggered in the second foot, even though the first foot undergoes gradation (weakening of the cluster /lpm/ to /lm/) in non-compound environments, cf. sálmav ‘psalm- acc.sg’. This is illustrated by the word forms in Table hymnalExample.
summary:
The passage explains that polysyllabic words have a consistent prosodic structure with segments in V1, the consonant center, and V2, forming a “minimal core.” Only the final foot may be followed by a single extra syllable with V3 and possibly C3, and only this final foot is affected by morphophonological processes.  

Using the compound *sálbmagirrje* ‘hymnal’ as an example, the text shows that the word consists of two feet, but no additional syllable can be inserted between them because they belong to one compound noun. It also notes that consonant gradation in the accusative singular affects only the second foot, while the first foot undergoes gradation only in non-compound forms.

text:
syllable!syllabification
The distribution of vowel phonemes between consonant phoneme slots patterns clearly, particularly with respect to intonation and the distribution of vowel phonemes.
This, along with the sonority sequencing principle, indicates that vowels are the nuclei of \ syllables.
However, the location of syllable boundaries is not as easy to determine; in fact, syllable boundaries are not highly relevant in \ prosody.

Because the consonant center consonant center has by far the widest variety of consonants and consonant combinations of any of the consonant positions, it is best to consider this position first..5
Although the consonant center spans the preceding and following syllabic nuclei, there is no solid phonotactic or phonological evidence for where the syllable boundary is located inside the consonant center.
Table syllabificationPatternsInCCent lists the possible syllabification patterns for the consonant center.
4pt

Maximizing onsets, the patterns V.CCCV, VC.CCV and V.CCV would create highly unusual onsets (such as /vkŋ/, /pm/ or /vɲ/) unattested in any other onset positions.
Similarly, trying to maximize codas, the patterns VCCC.V and VCC.V would also result in highly unusual codas (such as /vkŋ/ or /vɲ/) unattested in any other coda positions.
While the pattern VCC.CV would also create some otherwise unattested codas (such as /vt/ or /rk/), these are phonologically similar to attested word-final codas such as /st/ or /jk/ (also fricative plosive and oral-sonorant plosive, respectively).
The patterns VC.CV, V.CV and VC.V result in onsets and codas which are not unusual. However, keeping in mind the far greater diversity of single consonant phonemes licensed in word-initial onset position compared to word-final coda position, syllabification favoring singleton onset consonants results in onsets and codas which most resemble word-initial onsets and word-final codas. Note that even then, onsets and codas in positions other than the consonant center form subsets of the possibilities in consonant center position (with the exception of a few non-native word-onset clusters). It is therefore most plausible that syllables are assigned a single consonant segment as an onset in syllabification. The examples in have2SGPRSb through laughINF
show some results of this syllabification for a variety of consonant constellations in the consonant center.

This syllabification preference for a single onset segment can be applied to syllable boundaries outside of the consonant center, as shown in speakINFa and happinessCOMSG.
speakINFa saːkasti-t saː.kas.titʰ ságastit speak- inf 1480

When the consonant center consists of a geminate geminate phoneme (cf. geminateCs ), there is no phonological test which indicates where the syllable boundary is located;
indeed, this syllable boundary is likely not relevant in \ phonology. With this in mind, a symbolic syllable boundary is postulated somewhere within a phonological geminate; this divides the geminate symbolically into two component parts and results in syllables conforming to a syllable template with a singleton in the onset. In the examples in whileNOMSG through fatherNOMSGa, this symbolic boundary is placed in the middle of the geminate.
whileNOMSG pɔtːɔ pɔt̚.tɔ båddå while nom.sg 0231

If a geminate precedes another consonant segment in the consonant cluster, the syllabification border is after the geminate, as in spoonNOMSG:
spoonNOMSG pisːte pisː.te bisste spoon nom.sg 0190

When the final consonant in the consonant center is preaspirated aspiration!preaspiration, there is again no test for the location of a syllable boundary, as with geminates. With this in mind, a symbolic boundary is posited between the realization of preaspiration (cf. preaspiration ) and the rest of the preaspirated segment, which results in syllables conforming to a syllable template with a simgleton in the onset. The examples in houseNOMSGa and endNOMSG show a preaspirated plosive and affricate, respectively, with a syllable boundary indicated between the glottal fricative (preaspiration) and the stop or affricate component.
houseNOMSGa tɔʰpe tɔh.pe dåhpe house nom.sg 0416
endNOMSG keʰʧe keh.ʧe gehtje end nom.sg 0594
The same is the case when a geminate precedes a preaspirated segment, as in the example in churchNOMSG.
churchNOMSG kirːʰko kirr̥.ko girrko church nom.sg 0640

Note, however, as pointed out above, the actual position of syllable boundaries in \ does not seem to be relevant in other areas of prosody.
For this reason, the consonant center is a preferable prosodic domain to consider when describing prosody and phonotactics, and thus is referred to regularly in the following descriptions.
summary: The passage argues that vowels are the nuclei of syllables, but that exact syllable boundaries are often difficult to determine and are not especially important for prosody. In the consonant center, the most plausible syllabification is to assign a single consonant to the onset, since other splits tend to create unusual or unattested onsets and codas, while geminates and preaspirated segments require only symbolic boundary placement because no phonological test locates the boundary.

subsection: A note on syllables and feet
text:
stress
With the above description on stress in polysyllabic word structure in mind, it should become clear that syllables syllable are only relevant for bearing word stress and creating feet foot, while feet form a relevant unit on several levels (prosodic, phonological, morphophonological). As a result, it could be more useful to rephrase the ‘bisyllabic minimal word structure’ as ‘obligatory footedness’ for \ lexical items and many functional words. Furthermore, the choice of the term ‘foot’ to describe this minimal size requirement may not be ideal because the edges of the \ foot are quite irrelevant to morphophonological morphophonology processes. Instead, the V1+Consonant-Center+V2 core is a vital domain for morphophonology, while segments at the edges are not relevant. Perhaps a better descriptive term would be ‘minimal core’.
summary: The passage argues that syllables are mainly relevant for bearing stress and forming feet, while feet themselves function as an important unit across prosodic, phonological, and morphophonological levels. It suggests replacing the idea of a “bisyllabic minimal word structure” with “obligatory footedness” for lexical items and many functional words, but notes that “foot” may be an imperfect label because morphophonological processes focus on the core rather than the edges. A better term, it proposes, would be “minimal core.”

intonation stress
While the following observations are of a preliminary nature, and a more thorough study must be left for future investigation, the relative intensity of stressed syllables in declarative utterances in \ tends to decrease towards the end of the utterance, with the final stressed lexical item, and particularly the final syllable, being realized with noticeably lower intensity than the beginning syllables. As an example, the waveform and intensity trace for the utterance glossed in intonationDropEx are provided in Figure intonationGraphic.

da lä tjakktja ja gillgijmä sarvajd njuovvat\\

Here, the initial syllable nucleus of the first lexical item in the sentence tjakttja has an intensity of 69.7 dB. The other lexical items hover between 63.5 dB and 70.3 dB. An example sentence shows this pattern clearly: the initial stressed syllable has relatively high intensity, while the final lexical item drops sharply in intensity on its last syllable.

text:
devoicing
The final two or three syllables of a declarative utterance in \ can be weakened as a way to mark the end of an utterance. Arjeplogsmål, the local language contactSwedish dialect, features a similar phenomenon.
This weakening is typically realized by completely devoicing the final one, two or three syllables, often to the point that these are essentially whispered. Alternatively, this can be realized as creaky voice instead of voicelessness. For instance, in the example utterance depicted in the waveform in Figure utteranceFinalDevoicingGraphic and transcribed in utteranceFinalDevoicing1, devoicing occurs in the final lexical word giesev ‘summer’, which contains the last two syllables of the utterance.

da’l adnam buorak, buorak giesev\\
t-a=l at̚na-m pʊ͡ɔrakʰ pʊ͡ɔrak kɪ̥͡e̥se̥-v̥\\
dem- 3pl.nom=be 3pl.prs have- prf good good summer- acc.sg\\
They have had a good summer. 090826012

The lack of energy in the waveform corresponding to giesev shows clearly that the word is weakened significantly compared to the rest of the utterance. Note that even the vowels are completely devoiced.

It is not clear what triggers this devoicing, and future study, particularly looking at the possibility of it being a turn marker in discourse, is needed.
summary: In this dialect, the final two or three syllables of a declarative utterance may be weakened to mark utterance boundary, typically by being fully devoiced and sometimes by becoming creaky rather than voiceless. The passage notes that Arjeplogsmål shows this effect clearly in examples such as final *giesev* “summer,” where even the vowels are devoiced, but the trigger for the phenomenon is still unclear and may be related to discourse turn-marking.

aspiration!preaspiration preaspiration|see aspiration
In Pite Saami, preaspirated As is hopefully evident from this discussion on preaspiration, the term ‘preaspiration’ is not entirely accurate from a phonetic-acoustic point of view since the acoustic correlate of this phenomenon is not actually aspiration in all cases. Nonetheless, there are several reasons to select this term: 1. in the majority of cases, the acoustic correlate is in fact preaspiration, 2. this phonemic phenomenon is often referred to as preaspiration in the literature on
other Saami languages (cf. e.g.,
or ), and 3. preaspiration can be reconstructed for the half-long and long Proto-Saami plosive and affricate phonemes that became the current \ preaspirated phonemes.
phonemes only occur in consonant center position. While preaspirated phonemes can be plosives or affricates, the phenomenon that goes along with them is essentially the same.
The period of aspiration aspiration, i.e., the voicelessness preceding the formation of the oral closure, is realized in different ways and depends on the preceding segment. If the preceding segment is a voiced continuant
consonant, then the final part of that segment is devoiced.

While a minimal contrast between a voiceless obstruent preceding a preaspirated consonant phoneme and a voiceless obstruent preceding a plain counterpart phoneme (e.g., /st/ vs. /sʰt/) is theoretically possible, this cannot be detected because such a consonant cannot be devoiced as it is already voiceless (e.g., /st/ [st] and /sʰt/ [st]).
When following a high front vowel /i/, preaspiration is realized as a voiceless palatal fricative [ç].
In all other cases, preaspiration is a voiceless glottal fricative [h]. This is summarized in Table preaspRealization.
summary:
In Pite Saami, the term *preaspiration* is used even though the phenomenon is not always phonetically aspiration; it is retained because most cases do involve aspiration, it is common in the Saami literature, and it reflects a reconstruction for Proto-Saami phonemes. These preaspirated phonemes occur only in consonant-center position and may be plosives or affricates, but the associated voiceless period is realized differently depending on context.  

If preceded by a voiced continuant, the final part of that segment is devoiced; after a high front vowel /i/, preaspiration surfaces as [ç], and elsewhere it is realized as [h].

Geminates are generally longer in duration than singleton consonants, with special patterns for plosives and affricates, where only one stop closure occurs, and for preaspirated consonants, where both preaspiration and closure are lengthened. Comparison of non-voiced plosive durations in the consonant center
While a thorough study of length phenomena in \ is beyond the scope of the current study, it is worth noting the actual duration which the various plosive phonemes are realized with in the consonant center.
Specifically,
a plain geminate geminate plosive and a singleton preaspirated plosive have approximately the same duration for the period of stop closure (around 300ms), and are at least 100ms longer than plain singleton plosives and 100ms shorter than a preaspirated geminate plosive. Singleton voiceless plosives are plain word-initially and in some clusters, postaspirated word-finally, and unreleased before homorganic consonants; geminates occur only in the consonant center, while preaspirated plosives are restricted to the consonant center as sole or final consonant segments. The passage also notes that plain geminate plosives and preaspirated singleton plosives have similar stop-closure durations, though this is said to be phonologically irrelevant.

Dialect variation and the historical voiced dental fricative dialect variation|(
A number of \ lexemes historically featured a voiced dental fricative *ð fricative!voiced dental fricative in Proto-Saamic. These items are subject to variation in the corresponding synchronic phoneme across \ territory.
Specifically, Proto-Saamic *ð can correspond to a singleton or geminate alveolar voiceless plosive /t\,tː/, alveolar trill /r\,rː/, or voiced dental fricative /ð\,ðː/; the selection of phoneme varies from speaker to speaker. The alveolar plosives and trills /t\,tː\,r\,rː/ are realized as described in Plosives and oralSonorants.
For speakers with /ð\,ðː/, these are realized as a voiced dental fricative singleton [ð] or geminate [ðː], respectively. The phonological system of the few speakers who have the voiced dental fricatives /ð\,ðː/ actually has two more phonemes than the systems of speakers with /t\,tː/ or /r\,rː/, as these latter four phonemes are already present in the phonology of all speakers. Note that, because /ð/ is very uncommon and not a feature that all speakers share, it is not included in the consonant inventory presented in Table Cphonemes.

Phonemes subject to this variation are only found in the consonant center.
To illustrate this, the phonemic variation in the word for stone, which goes back to Proto-Saamic *keaðɢē, is presented in Table ethVariationTable.

Generally speaking, the phoneme /t/ is found on the northern side and the phoneme /r/ on the southern side, although the borders are not absolutely clear. The phoneme /ð/ is least common, and seems to only be found in the speech of the eldest speakers.
Speakers are quite aware of this variation.
In the current working version of the \ orthography, the grapheme <r> has been chosen to represent all three variants (thus the word for stone is spelled gärrge), although spellings using the grapheme <d> or even <ð> may be used as well.
summary:
Pite Saami has a fricative system with singleton /f v s ʃ h/ and geminate /fː vː sː ʃː/ fricatives, with the singletons occurring in syllable onsets and word-internal codas and the geminates only in consonant-center position. The voiced fricative /v/ often becomes an approximant [ʋ] or [w], especially after open front vowels and word-initially, while final [h] occurs only in limited morphological and speaker-specific contexts.

The passage also notes dialect variation in reflexes of Proto-Saamic *ð, which may appear as /t tː/, /r rː/, or less commonly /ð ðː/ depending on speaker and region. This variation is restricted to consonant-center position, and current orthography uses <r> to represent the different outcomes.
