text:
consonant cluster|(
In, it is frequently the case that up to three consonants can occur consecutively, particularly in the consonant center. Because syllabification syllable!syllabification does not cross word boundaries, consonant clusters in word-initial and word-final position are necessarily tautosyllabic. However, word-internally, syllabification of the final consonant as a syllable onset (cf. syllabification on syllabification) creates a syllable boundary within a group of consecutive consonants. There are two ways of approaching such word-internal consecutive consonant groups: on the one hand, one can consider the syllable boundary to be a significant fissure dividing such a consonant grouping into two units, and then only study any tautosyllabic consonant clusters that result. On the other hand, one can disregard any syllable boundaries, and thus treat any consonant groupings, even those spanning a syllable boundary (heterosyllabic consonant clusters), as a unit.
In determining whether syllable boundaries are a meaningful part of \ phonotactics, a discussion of the inventories for both tautosyllabic and heterosyllabic consonant clusters is provided below.

In the following, tautosyllabic consonant clusters will be described first, before moving on to heterosyllabic consonant groupings. Note that this does not include consecutive consonants which arise in compounding at an internal root-boundary.
summary: The passage explains that up to three consonants may occur in succession, especially in syllable centers, and that word-initial and word-final clusters are necessarily tautosyllabic because syllabification does not cross word boundaries. Word-internally, however, syllabification can create a syllable boundary within a consonant sequence, so such groups may be analyzed either as two separate units divided by the boundary or as a single cluster including heterosyllabic consonants. The discussion that follows will first treat tautosyllabic clusters and then heterosyllabic groupings, excluding consonant sequences created by compounding at internal root boundaries.

subsubsection: Consonant clusters in syllable onset position
text:
In syllable onset position, 21 CCs and 2 CCCs are attested, as listed in Table syllableOnsetCCCsA and Table syllableOnsetCCCsB;
all are in word-initial position. This is because syllabification results in onsets consisting of a single consonant word-internally; thus tautosyllabic consonant clusters can only occur in word-initial onset position.
Words with an onset cluster tend to be of either unknown or of Germanic origin,
which helps explain why eleven of the word-initial CCs and both of the CCCs would not be attested in word-internal onsets even if syllabification allowed tautosyllabic consonant clusters word-internally.
summary: In syllable onset position, 21 CC clusters and 2 CCC clusters are attested, and all occur word-initially. Word-internally, syllabification yields onsets of only one consonant, so tautosyllabic consonant clusters are restricted to word-initial position. The passage also notes that onset-cluster words are often of unknown or Germanic origin, which helps explain why eleven word-initial CCs and both CCCs would still not occur word-internally even if such clusters were permitted there.

subsubsection: Consonant clusters in syllable coda position
text:
Because syllabification results in syllable onsets of a single consonant segment (cf. syllabification ), only the coda of the initial syllable can host tautosyllabic consonant clusters in the consonant center. An inventory of these CCs is provided in Table tautoCCenterCCs.

Syllable codas in word-final position are more restrictive, as only three CCs and one CCC are frequently found in this position, while four other CCs are found in a very limited set of words; the attested clusters in word-final syllable codas are listed in Table wordFinalCCs.
The regularly occurring word-final coda clusters are quite common suffixes. The suffixes -st elat.sg, -jst elat.sg, -jt acc.pl form an integral part of any noun paradigm. The suffix -lt is limited to a handful of directional particles and may be an old case suffix. It should also be noted that \ speakers from the northern side of \ territory use -s and -js for elative case marking.
The clusters /rt rm lm jk/ are limited to a single, seemingly native lexical item each, but there are not enough data at this point to make any further conclusions.
summary: Because syllabification allows only single-consonant onsets, tautosyllabic consonant clusters can occur only in the coda of the initial syllable in the consonant center. Word-final codas are more restricted: only three CCs and one CCC occur frequently, and the regular word-final clusters are largely common suffixes such as -st, -jst, -jt, and -lt. Other clusters like /rt rm lm jk/ are restricted to a single lexical item each, though the data are too limited for firm conclusions.

subsubsection: Heterosyllabic consonant clusters in the consonant center
text:
The inventories of tautosyllabic consonant clusters in various word positions detailed above are lacking any regularity concerning position within syllable structure (onset or coda). In other words, the sets of coda clusters licensed word-internally only overlap with the coda clusters licensed word-finally to a very limited extent. Specifically, only the clusters /jt lt rt/ are attested both word-internally and word-finally, while all the other clusters are unique to either word-internal or to word-final position.
Furthermore, the relatively large number of word-initial consonant clusters, but complete lack of consonant clusters in other syllable-onset positions word-internally is also asymmetrical.
These facts indicate that perhaps a different approach to explaining the data would be more fruitful.

Keeping the above in mind, as well as the exceptional role that the consonant center consonant center plays in morphophonology morphophonology (consonant gradation, cf. Cgrad ) and phonotactics (geminates, preaspiration, overall length), an inventory of the possible heterosyllabic consonant clusters, e.g., disregarding syllable boundaries, that occur in the consonant center as a unit proves more insightful in describing \ phonology.

In addition to the 21 geminate consonants that can occur alone in the consonant center, there are a total of 213
heterosyllabic CCs attested in the consonant center. Table CCenterCCs
lists the 197 heterosyllabic CCs with either two singleton consonants or a geminate consonant and a singleton consonant.

Most combinations of various natural classes are found; however, it is striking that a nasal as the first element can only have an obstruent as the second element. It is also noteworthy that a single oral sonorant plus a nasal is attested, but no double oral sonorant plus a nasal.

Turning to heterosyllabic consonant clusters with three members (tripartite CCs), there are 16 attested in the consonant center; these clusters are listed in Table CCenterCCCs.
The heterosyllabic consonant clusters in the first two rows of this table
are fairly common, and correspond paradigmatically to consonant clusters lacking the plosive but with only the fricative and sonorant (see above on heterosyllabic CCs and Cgrad on consonant gradation). The other three tripartite consonant clusters /jst mst rtm/ are only attested in one or two words each, Recent loan words from Swedish language contact may also contain tripartite CCs not found elsewhere in, e.g., kɔnstɔ ‘art’ <Swedish konst.
and there are not enough data to reach any further conclusions at this point.

Due to the morphophonological morphophonology process of consonant gradation, which features paradigmatic stem allomorphy characterized by quantitative alternations in the consonant center in many cases (cf. Cgrad ),
almost all of the heterosyllabic CCs can be grouped into short long pairs, e.g., /pt pːt/ or /jʰʦ jːʰʦ/. There are only 16 heterosyllabic CCs which do not seem to have a corresponding quantitative partner; for reasons explained below, it is useful to divide these into the two groups listed in CCgroups:

Group A: /vn vɲ vŋ lm ln lɲ lŋ rm rn rŋ jm jn jŋ/\\
2.6mmGroup B: /sŋ ʃm ɲk/

Members of the first and larger group all have a corresponding morphophonemic partner, but this corresponding partner is a consonant cluster consisting of three consonant segments, and differs qualitatively as well. Specifically, tripartite CCs consisting of /v l r j/ followed by a plosive sonorant pair
correspond to Group A (those lacking the plosive element of the relevant tripartite CC); these pairings are listed in Table CCandCCCpairs.

The remaining heterosyllabic CCs /sŋ ʃm ŋk/(Group B) seem to lack a quantitative partner. It is likely that the corresponding long CCs /sːŋ ʃːm ŋːk/ would be acceptable since CCs with very similar phonemic structures in quantitative pairs exist. However, a lack of data at this point prevents this from being ascertained for certain.

It is worth noting that the only consonant cluster which occurs in a word-medial position other than the consonant center is /st/ from the suffix -st-, a derivational morpheme
which derives a verb, e.g., basestit ‘to fry quickly’ (cf. basset ‘to fry’). Cf. vblzST for more on this verbalizer.

Ultimately, this massive inventory of consonants and consonant clusters in the middle of words can only really make sense when one understands the extent to which morphology is expressed in this position, as becomes clear in Chapters morphWordClassCh through derivMorph. consonant cluster|)
summary: The passage argues that consonant clusters cannot be adequately described by simple onset/coda position, since the distribution of word-initial, word-internal, and word-final clusters is highly asymmetrical and overlaps only minimally. Instead, it proposes analyzing the consonant center as a unit, where many heterosyllabic clusters occur and where morphophonological processes like consonant gradation and quantitative alternations organize the inventory into short-long pairs, with only a small number of exceptions.

text:
\ has eight monophthong vowel phonemes and one diphthong diphthong vowel phoneme. These are listed in
Figure monophthongs, with the monophthongs in the vowel chart on the left, and the diphthong on the right.

A discussion of these phonemes and the distribution of the relevant allophones follows.
Note that there is a short open front vowel /a/ and a long open front vowel /aː/; for the latter case, length is marked with a triangular colon <aː> in phonemic transcription, as according to IPA standards, and with an acute accent <á> when represented in orthography.

The monophthong phonemes /a aː ɛ i u ɔ/ are realized as monophthongs in all cases.
The monophthong phonemes /e/ and /o/ are realized as slight diphthongs in V1 position, namely as [i͡e] and [u͡o],
respectively. They can be very short in duration. There is a relatively minimal difference between the beginning and ending positions of each of the [i͡e] and [u͡o] phones in the oral cavity, a closeness which is even reflected in inconsistencies in the working version of the \ orthography: both <e> and <ie> are used for /e/, and <o> and <uo> for /o/.

The diphthong phoneme /u͡a/ is restricted to V1 position. Due to vowel harmony, /u͡a/ can be realized as [ʊ͡ɛ] or [ʊ͡a], and needs not be particularly long in duration.

Note that farther north within the Pite Saami language territory, dialect variationmonophthong phonemes are often realized as slight diphthongs diphthong. This is closer to Lule Saami within the Saami dialect continuum; indeed, many Lule Saami monophthong vowel phonemes are realized as slight diphthongs.

Because there is no significant difference in behavior between monophthongs and diphthongs which would justify treating them separately, all nine vowel phonemes are dealt with together in the following section.
summary:
The language has eight monophthong vowel phonemes and one diphthong phoneme, with a contrast between short /a/ and long /aː/ marked with a triangular colon in transcription and an acute accent in orthography. While /a aː ɛ i u ɔ/ are consistently monophthongs, /e/ and /o/ are realized as slight diphthongs in V1 position, and the diphthong /u͡a/ is restricted to V1 and may surface as [ʊ͡ɛ] or [ʊ͡a] under vowel harmony.

The passage also notes that farther north in the Pite Saami area, monophthongs are often realized as slight diphthongs, resembling Lule Saami. Since there is no important behavioral difference between monophthongs and diphthongs, all nine vowel phonemes are treated together in the following discussion.

text:
The following sections describe the \ vowel phonemes and their allophonic realizations in the three vowel positions prosodic domains V1, V2 and V3. Table VsSlots
summarizes the distribution of the vowel phonemes in these three prosodic vowel slots.
All vowel phonemes are licensed in V1, and all except /ɛ/ and /u͡a/ occur in V2. The phoneme /ɛ/ only occurs in a limited phonological context in V2 of grammatical words, and is therefore in parentheses in Table VsSlots.; cf. openE.
However, V3 position is the most restrictive and allows only /i ɛ a u/. This distribution reflects the fact that V1 is the most prosodically relevant slot, and V3 the least significant.
summary: The passage describes the distribution of vowel phonemes across three prosodic vowel positions, V1, V2, and V3. All vowel phonemes can occur in V1, all except /ɛ/ and /u͡a/ occur in V2, and V3 is the most restricted, allowing only /i ɛ a u/. This pattern is said to reflect the greater prosodic importance of V1 and the lesser significance of V3.

text:
The segment /i/ is a close front high vowel. In V1 position, it is not realized with a very narrow oral cavity, but closer to [ɪ], while in V2 and V3 position it is even less close and essentially [ɪ], and tends to be shorter in duration. When a palatal approximant /j/ immediately follows, this triggers a slight raising of /i/ so that it is closer to [i].
Some examples are found in decreaseINF through eyeACCPL.

When a following palatal approximant /j/ occurs immediately after /i/, the vowel is slightly raised and becomes closer to [i].

The segment /e/ is a close-mid front vowel. In V1 position, it is realized as a slight diphthongdiphthong [i͡e], while in V2 position it is normally a monophthong [e]. It is not attested in V3 position. Note that, in the current working orthography, the V3 position can contain the grapheme <e>, but this is in fact the phoneme /i/ realized as [ɪ].
Some examples are found in herdNOMSG through fishNOMPL.
herdNOMSGelːoi͡elːoelloreindeer.herd nom.sg0449

It is not attested in V3 position; although the orthography may write <e> there, this actually represents the phoneme /i/ realized as [ɪ]. Examples are given from forms such as “reindeer,” “red fox,” and “fish.”

text:
The segment /ɛ/ is a open-mid front vowel. It normally occurs in V1 position.
Examples can be found in windNOMSG2 and iceFishingLineNOMSG.

The phoneme /ɛ/ can also be found in V2 position, but this is limited to grammatical words and it is never followed by a final consonant. The current working \ orthography is rather inconsistent with the spelling of the /ɛ/ phoneme. In V1 position, it is spelled with <ä>, while in V2 (in grammatical words) it is spelled <e>.
In such cases, /ɛ/ is realized slightly more open than when in V1 position. Examples can be found in where through inside.

In a few recent loan words from Swedish language contact which are originally French or Latin loans words in Swedish language contact that have retained their second syllable stress stress, /ɛ/ can occur as the vowel of the second syllable. However, as this is the stressed syllable in such cases, it is, from a prosodic perspective, still in the V1 position of a normal \ trochaic foot. Two examples are provided in addressNOMSG and professorNOMSG.

It is also found in a few recent Swedish loanwords with second-syllable stress and in certain past tense verb forms with suffixes -jmä and -jdä, where it may occur in the final syllable. Otherwise, /ɛ/ does not occur in V3 position.

The segment /a/ is an open front vowel of short duration. It can occur in V1, V2 and V3 positions. When preceding /v/, such as before the suffix -v acc.sg or -v 1sg.prs, /a/ is usually pronounced more to the back towards [ɑ]. Simultaneously, /v/ is optionally but frequently pronounced as [ʋ] when following /a/ or /aː/; cf. fvssjh.

The segment /aː/ is an open front vowel of long quantity. It can occur in V1 and V2 positions.
When preceding a /v/, such as before the suffix -v acc.sg or -v 1sg.prs, /a/ is usually pronounced more to the back towards [ɑ]. See previous footnote.

The segment /ɔ/ is a open-mid back vowel. It can occur in V1 or V2 position. However, if it is in V2 position, then V1 is also /ɔ/. Examples can be found in nineCARD through streamDIM.

The segment /o/ is a close-mid back vowel.
In V1 position, it is realized as a slight diphthongdiphthong [ʊ͡o], while in V2 position it is the monophthong [o]. It is not attested in V3 position. Some examples are found in good through request1PLPRS.

The segment /u/ is a close back vowel.
In V1 position, it is not realized with a completely narrow oral cavity,
while in V2 and V3 positions it is even less close and essentially [ʊ], and tends to be shorter in duration.

Some examples are found in skiBindingNOMSG through islandDIM.

The passage illustrates this positional variation with several example forms.

subsubsection: Close back to open front vowel
text:
The segment /u͡a/ is a diphthong which begins as a close but slightly centralized back vowel and opens to an open front vowel [ʊ͡a] in most cases. However, the vowel in V2 position can trigger vowel harmony that slightly closes the end position of the oral closure so that it is realized as [ʊ͡ɛ], Despite the orthography being quite phonemic rather than phonetic, these two allophones of /u͡a/ are reflected in spelling: [u͡a] is spelled <ua> and [u͡ɛ] is spelled <uä>.
but the triggering vowels vary between \ dialects. For southern dialects, only a close /i/ or close-mid vowel /e/ in V2 position can trigger this harmony. In northern dialects dialect variation, an open front /a/ in V2 position There are not enough data at this time to know
whether a long /aː/ also triggers this in northern dialects. also triggers this vowel harmony. A few cognate pairs are provided in Table uaVSuae.

Note that this vowel harmony is triggered by a purely phonological context, as opposed to the vowel harmony described in VH in the chapter on morphology, which is triggered morphologically.
summary: The diphthong /u͡a/ is usually realized as [ʊ͡a], but in certain vowel-harmony contexts its final quality is slightly raised to [ʊ͡ɛ]; these two allophones are reflected in spelling as <ua> and <uä>. The vowels that trigger this harmony vary by dialect: southern dialects allow only /i/ or /e/ in V2, while northern dialects also permit /a/, though it is unclear whether /aː/ does so as well. Unlike the vowel harmony discussed elsewhere in the grammar, this one is triggered purely by phonological context rather than morphology.

text:
epenthesis schwa
In a small number of \ words, a vowel is inserted between two non-homorganic consonants in the consonant center consonant center position.
This centralized vowel is exceptionally short in duration, and is transcribed here with a
superscript schwa [ᵊ]. Waveforms for the two examples provided in liverNOMSG and candyNOMPL are found in Figure epentheticSchwaWaveforms.
liverNOMSGripːreripᵊreribbreliver nom.sg1403
candyNOMPLɲaːlkaɲaːlᵊkahnjálgacandy nom.pl1277

In both cases, the epenthetic schwa is clearly linked to more energy, and it stands out from the surrounding consonants.
These waveforms also make visible the shorter duration of the epenthetic schwa (59ms and 47ms, respectively) compared to the other vowels (the shortest of which is 108ms).

Speakers are rarely conscious of this vowel, and it is not reflected in the orthography. In neighboring Lule Saami, a similar epenthetic vowel exists and is predictable based on the prosodic and phonological structure of a word. It therefore seems likely that this epenthetic schwa is not phonemic in \ either. However, more data are needed to confirm this and thoroughly describe its distribution. The fact that this epenthetic vowel seems to be significantly more prevalent in northern \ dialects dialect variation complicates the situation further. The examples in quick through whitefishNOMSG provide dialectal variants, with the more southern variant first (lacking the epenthetic vowel), and the more northern variant second (with the epenthetic schwa).

The passage describes a rare epenthetic schwa that is inserted between two non-homorganic consonants in certain words. It is very short, acoustically prominent, usually unnoticed by speakers, and not written in the orthography; the author suggests it is probably non-phonemic, though more data are needed.

text: Morphology plays an essential role in, a highly synthetic language. Based on morphological patterning and in addition to syntactic criteria, seven word classes can be posited. morphology first provides an introduction to morphological phenomena in, before introWordForms summarizes the word classes.
summary: The passage says that morphology is essential in this highly synthetic language and that word classes can be identified not only by syntactic criteria but also by morphological patterning. It also notes that morphology first introduces morphological phenomena, and that the section on word forms later summarizes the seven word classes.

text:
A number of inflectional categories exist in; Table summaryMorphCats provides a summary of inflectional categories relevant for each sub-category of the relevant word classes.

Derivational morphology is commonly used to create nouns, verbs, and, to a lesser extent, adjectives and adverbs.
Both derivational derivation and inflectional inflection morphology manifest themselves linearly (by suffixing) or non-linearly, via consonant gradation, umlaut and/or vowel harmony. More often than not, linear and non-linear morphological phenomena are combined.

The present section only provides an overview of these various morphological phenomena, and is divided into linearMorphology on linear morphology and morphophonology on non-linear morphological processes.
Because morphological behavior varies between the word classes, it is described in more detail individually in the relevant word class chapters.
summary: The passage says that a range of inflectional categories applies to the relevant word classes, and that derivational morphology is mainly used to form nouns and verbs, and less often adjectives and adverbs. It also notes that both derivational and inflectional morphology may be expressed either linearly, through suffixation, or non-linearly, through processes such as consonant gradation, umlaut, and vowel harmony, often in combination. The section gives only an overview of these phenomena, with more detailed description provided in the individual word class chapters because morphological behavior differs across classes.

Concerning linearly separable morphology, \ is an exclusively suffixing language. Both inflectional and derivational suffixes exist.
According to the general linear morphological structure of \ words, derivational suffixes attach to a root before inflectional suffixes occur on the resulting stem, as illustrated in linearMorphStructure.

morphology!linear|)
summary: The language is exclusively suffixing, with both inflectional and derivational suffixes. In its linear morphological structure, derivational suffixes attach to the root first, and inflectional suffixes are added afterward to the resulting stem.

text:
morphology!non-linear|(
There are three ways
in which non-linear morphology can be expressed in:
itemize
stem consonant alternations (consonant gradation)
stem vowel alternations in V1 position (umlaut)
regressive vowel harmony in V1 and V2 vowels
itemize
These are triggered by a word’s position
within an inflectional paradigm, or in derivation. All inflectional non-linear morphology is restricted to the final foot foot of a given word, while derivational non-linear morphology can also occur in a non-ultimate foot. Non-linear processes may apply simultaneously. The following sections describe these phenomena in more detail: Cgrad for consonant gradation, umlaut for umlaut and VH for vowel harmony. Cf. for historical explanations of these morphophonological processes in Saami.
summary: The passage says that non-linear morphology can be expressed through stem consonant alternations, stem vowel alternations in initial vowel position, and regressive vowel harmony affecting initial and second vowels. These processes are triggered by a word’s place in an inflectional paradigm or in derivation; inflectional non-linear morphology is limited to the final foot of a word, while derivational non-linear morphology may also occur in a non-final foot, and multiple processes can apply at the same time.

text:
consonant gradation|(
The term consonant gradation This term is quite common in Saami linguistics, e.g., in, although it is also known as ‘grade alternation’, e.g., in. As much of the literature on Saami linguistics is in languages other than English, it may be useful to provide some translations of the term ‘consonant gradation’: German: Stufenwechsel, Swedish: stadieväxling, Finnish: astevaihtelu, Hungarian: fokváltakozás and Russian: чередование ступеней.
refers to regular alternations of the consonant phonemes in the consonant center of the final foot of a word. Cf. prosodicDomains on prosodic positions, including the foot and the consonant center.

All consonant phonemes in the consonant center are included in the present classification of such alternations.
These alternations come in pairs of stem allomorphs that differ quantitatively and/or qualitatively.
Alternations can be between a preaspirated aspiration!preaspiration and the corresponding non-aspirated consonant (ʰx x),
a geminate geminate consonant and the corresponding singleton consonant (xː x),
a geminate singleton and the corresponding singleton singleton (xːy xy),
two singletons and only the latter singleton (xy y),
and three singletons and only the initial and final singleton (xyz xz). There are certainly other ways to classify these alternations in the consonant center as well. For instance, one could disregard any consonant phonemes that are present in both alternations (then xː x and xːy xy would be the same type), or consider the xː x and ʰxː x patterns in Table CgradPatternSummary to be the same type as simply a case of alternating consonant phonemes. However, the patterns in the present classification demonstrate the regularity of patterning between phonological features (such as geminate vs. singleton).

These patterns and the attested alternations are provided in Table CgradPatternSummary.

The term strong grade consonant gradation!strong grade (abbreviated ‘str’) is used to refer to the form with preaspiration aspiration!preaspiration, a geminate geminate or more consonant segments than the corresponding form. Likewise, the term weak grade consonant gradation!weak grade (abbreviated ‘wk’) refers to the form lacking a preaspirated or geminate consonant, or having fewer consonant segments, respectively.
To facilitate reading Table CgradPatternSummary, the attested alternations for each pattern are organized by alternations with a non-aspirated element first, followed by patterns with at least one preaspirated element. Furthermore, the individual lists of alternations are organized by mode of articulation and by the order set forth in the consonant phoneme inventory in Table Cphonemes.
Some examples illustrating this can be found below.

The minimal pair in CgradEx3 shows a consonant gradation alternation /ʰp p/, which corresponds to the pattern ʰx x.

pit100324 [pit100324]

The minimal pairs in CgradEx1a and CgradEx1b are examples of consonant gradation patterns which differ in a geminate singleton alternation. The consonant gradation alternations illustrated are /vː v/ and /rːk rk/, respectively, and correspond to the patterns xː x and xːy xy.

pit100323a [pit100323a]

pit090926 [pit090926]

The minimal pairs in CgradEx2a and CgradEx2b are examples of consonant gradation patterns in which a phoneme present in the first form is absent in the second form. The consonant gradation alternations illustrated here are /tn n/ and /jpm jm/, respectively, and correspond to the patterns xy y and xyz xz.

pit101208 [pit101208]

pit110413a [pit110413a]

As may be inferred from the examples above, paradigmatic alternations between nom.sg and nom.pl forms for nouns, or between 2sg.prs and 3sg.prs forms for verbs are often a good source of minimal pairs concerning consonant gradation alternations, and are a useful way to determine consonant gradation patterns.

Note that the geminate geminate plosives plosive and affricates affricate /pː\,tː\,kː\,ʦː\,ʧː/ are lacking in Table CgradPatternSummary for the pattern xː x, although alternations such as pː p could be expected. However, due to a lack of sufficient data and some conflicting data in the corpus, it is not entirely clear what the current status is for consonant gradation in words with a consonant center consisting solely of a geminate plosive or affricate. The fact that \ lacks consonant gradation in a limited number of contexts is one of the main differences to Lule Saami to the north, which does not lack consonant gradation, and Ume Saami to the south, which features consonant gradation even less frequently.
The example in CgradEx4a illustrates a word clearly lacking consonant gradation in the corpus data, here with the geminate velar plosive /kː/.

pit110522 [pit110522]

Corpus data also indicate that variation within the \ area complicates things. For instance, the adjective tjábbe ‘beautiful’ undergoes consonant gradation in the speech dialect variation of speakers from the northern parts of Arjeplog, but does not for southern speakers, as illustrated in CgradEx4b. For northern speakers, the gradation is realized as an alternation in voicing, and not length.

pit110522 [pit110522, sje20131017 sje20131017]

This being the case, some speakers from farther north may have further voiced plosive phonemes /bː dː gː/ that only occur in consonant gradation alternations with the corresponding unvoiced phonemes /pː tː kː/. However, it is not clear based on the corpus data how widespread this feature is, or if it also affects geminate affricates.

Finally, it is not clear from the corpus data what the status of the phonological contexts lacking consonant gradation mentioned in (working from a historical perspective and with older data) is. Further research is needed to complete the picture, and
variation within \ and possible effects of language attrition should also be taken into consideration. consonant gradation|)
summary: Consonant gradation in Saami refers to regular alternations of consonants in the consonant center of the final foot of a word, and the passage classifies these alternations into several types, including preaspirated vs. non-aspirated, geminate vs. singleton, and cases where consonants are deleted. The strong grade is the form with preaspiration, gemination, or more consonant segments, while the weak grade lacks these features or has fewer segments. The text also notes that some patterns are well attested in the corpus, but others—especially with geminate plosives and affricates—remain unclear and vary by dialect, so further research is needed.

text:
umlaut|(
The term umlaut refers to regular allomorphic alternations of the vowels in the V1 position of a stem. Cf. prosodicDomains on prosodic positions, including V1 position.
The two umlaut patterns attested in the corpus are listed in Table umlautPatternSummary.

These umlaut alternations are qualitative and not quantitative.
These alternations are not triggered by the phonological environment, but instead morphologically.
The allomorph /ɛ/ in the first pattern is found in the same paradigmatic slots for each inflectional class as /u͡a/ Note that /u͡a/ has an allomorph [u͡ɛ] triggered by purely phonological vowel harmony; cf. Vua.
in the second pattern, just as the allomorphs /e/ and /o/ also correspond to the same paradigmatic slots.

Word forms for bägge ‘wind’ in umlautEx1 and for buälldet ‘burn’ in umlautEx2 provide examples of the two umlaut patterns.

pit080621 [pit080621]

pit101208 [pit101208]

For lexemes subject to consonant gradation, forms featuring /ɛ/ or /u͡a/ are typically in the strong grade consonant gradation!strong grade, while forms with /e/ or /o/ are normally in the weak grade consonant gradation!weak grade; cf. the word forms in example umlautEx2. umlaut|)
summary: Umlaut is described as a regular allomorphic alternation affecting the vowel in the stem’s V1 position, and the corpus shows two qualitative umlaut patterns. These alternations are morphologically, not phonologically, triggered, with corresponding allomorphs occupying the same paradigmatic slots across inflectional classes; the passage also notes that forms with /ɛ/ or /u͡a/ typically occur in the strong grade, while /e/ or /o/ forms normally occur in the weak grade.

text:
vowel harmony|(
The term vowel harmony (abbreviated ‘VH’) here refers to non-adjacent regressive phonological assimilation assimilation concerning the place of articulation of the V1 vowel of a stem in the context of certain V2 vowels. Cf. prosodicDomains on prosodic positions, including V1 and V2 positions.
Specifically, mid-high or high front vowels in V2 position in specific paradigmatic slots trigger raising of the vowel in V1 position. Because the paradigmatic slots that trigger vowel harmony differ between word classes and inflectional classes, and do not apply across the board, vowel harmony is not a purely phonological process, but morphophonological. Furthermore, the results of harmony on the same underlying vowel are inconsistent, and may be due to a word’s membership is certain morphological classes concerning vowel harmony. However, future research must be conducted to come to a more thorough conclusion on this.

Verbs verb and nouns noun can be subject to vowel harmony, but the assimilation patterns vary both between these word classes and within them.
Table VHsummaryTable summarizes the various patterns and the word classes that they are attested in based on the current corpus.

The morphological categories that trigger vowel harmony also vary. This is the case not only between nouns and verbs (as these have different inflectional categories), but also between inflectional classes for verbs. These categories are presented in Table VHtriggerSummary.

Some examples for vowel harmony are provided here.
In vhEx1, an example is shown of vowel harmony in the Class Ie noun guolle ‘fish’, as it alternates between /o/ in the V1 vowel of the nom.sg form, and /u/ in the nom.pl form.

pit110413a [pit110413a]

In vhEx2, an example of vowel harmony in the class II verb bassat ‘wash’ is provided. Here, a vowel harmony alternation between /a/ in the V1 vowel of the 2sg.prs form, and /i/ in the 2sg.pst form is evident (in addition to a consonant gradation alternation).

pit101208 [pit101208]

Finally, vhEx3 shows an example of vowel harmony in the class III verb buälldet ‘burn’. Here, a vowel harmony alternation between /o/ in the V1 vowel of the 2sg.prs form, and /u/ in the 2sg.pst form is evident (in addition to a consonant gradation alternation).

pit101208 [pit101208]

See JcomponentNounSuffixes for more details on vowel harmony in nouns, and VHPatternSectionVerbs in verbs. Note that, for nouns, vowel harmony is also referred to as ‘ ’.
vowel harmony|)
morphology!non-linear|)
summary:
Vowel harmony is described as a non-adjacent regressive phonological assimilation in which certain front vowels in V2 trigger raising of the V1 vowel. Because the triggering paradigmatic slots differ by word class and inflectional class, and because the outcomes are not fully consistent, the process is treated as morphophonological rather than purely phonological.

Both nouns and verbs can show vowel harmony, but the patterns vary within and between these classes. The passage illustrates this with examples from a noun and two verb classes, where different forms alternate in their V1 vowels depending on the inflectional form.

text:
word class (overview)
By characterizing the morphological and syntactic behavior of words in, and grouping such words based on that behavior, a total of seven word classes can be distinguished. These can be divided into two general categories containing generally open word classes and closed word classes, and are listed in Table wordClassList.
The specific syntactic criteria and inflectional inflection categories defining these are summarized in Table wordClassSummary1.

Some word classes consist of two or more subclasses:
nominals refer to nouns
and pronouns (personal, demonstrative, reflexive, interrogative and relative), and adjectivals include both adjectives and numerals.
Note that pronouns and numerals are closed subclasses belonging to open classes.

This categorization is intended to provide a broad starting point for classifying \ words; details for each word class can be found in the relevant chapters below.

Chapter nouns concerns the nominal subclass nouns, which provide fairly straightforward examples of the morphophonological complexities involved in \ inflection and derivation, while
the nominal subclass pronouns is dealt with in Chapter pronouns.
Chapter adjectivesIntro then covers the adjectival subclasses adjectives and numerals. Following this, Chapter verbs deals with verbs. Finally, the remaining small classes ( adverbials, adpositions, conjunctions
and interjections) are covered in Chapter otherWordClasses.
summary:
The passage outlines a system of seven word classes based on morphological and syntactic behavior, divided into open and closed classes, with the relevant criteria summarized in tables. It also notes that some classes contain subclasses: nominals include nouns and pronouns, while adjectivals include adjectives and numerals, and pronouns and numerals are closed subclasses within open classes.

The text further explains that this classification is a broad framework for word categorization, with later chapters treating nouns, pronouns, adjectives, numerals, verbs, and the remaining smaller word classes separately.

text:
noun|(
Nouns in \ form an open class of words that are formally defined
by their ability to head a nominal phrase. As the head of an NP, a noun inflects for case and number.

Each nouns consists of a lexical stem followed by an inflectional class marker and a portmanteau suffix indicating case and number, as illustrated in nounStructure.

∑ \ class-marker \ case/number

\ noun stems can have up to three allomorphic forms throughout the nominal paradigm due to a complex combination of morphophonological morphophonology processes.
The current chapter first describes the morphological categories number ( numberNouns ) and case ( case ) in a general way in order to provide a background for the variables discussed in NumCaseNouns on morphological case and number marking.

A description of the inflectional class markers and the resulting inflectional classes for nouns is given in nounClasses. Cf. nDerivation for derivational morphology creating nouns.
The final section ( possSuffixes ) deals briefly with the possessive suffixes, an infrequent set of archaic suffixes that indicate number and case and signify the possessor of the head noun’s referent.
summary:
Nouns form an open class and are defined by their ability to head a nominal phrase; as heads of NPs, they inflect for case and number. Each noun consists of a lexical stem, an inflectional class marker, and a portmanteau suffix marking case and number, and noun stems may show up to three allomorphic forms across the nominal paradigm because of morphophonological processes.

The chapter first introduces the categories of number and case, then describes noun inflectional class markers and the resulting classes. It also briefly discusses rare archaic possessive suffixes that mark number and case and indicate the possessor of the noun’s referent.

text:
number
\ nouns inflect inflection!nominal for singular and plural in all grammatical cases except the essive case!essive and possibly the abessive case!abessive case. Dual number!dual is not a relevant category for nouns, despite being an integral category in verb morphology
and for some pronoun classes. Number is expressed along with case by portmanteau suffixes, stem alternations, or a combination of both.
NumCaseNouns on number and case marking
treats this in more detail.

There is no formal distinction between count and mass nouns in, as illustrated by the example in uncountableEx1, in which the words for ‘flour’, ‘sugar’ and ‘food’ are all inflected for plural.

dán ájten inimä jáfojd ja suhkurijd ja gárvojd ja iehtjá biebmojd\\
d-á-n ájte-n ini-mä jáfo-jd ja suhkuri-jd ja gárvo-jd ja iehtjá biebmo-jd\\
dem- prox- iness.sg shed- iness.sg have- 1pl.pst flour- acc.pl and sugar- acc.pl and clothing- acc.pl and other food- acc.pl\\
In this shed we had flour and sugar and clothing and other food. 100310b100-104

When the singular form is used, a noun’s referent is either generic, as illustrated by both nouns in uncountableEx2, or it refers to a single unit,
as the noun ájten ‘shed’ in example uncountableEx1 above.

men vuästa, del káfan njallge\\
men vuästa del káfa-n njallge\\
but cheese nom.sg definitely coffee- iness.sg tasty\\
But cheese, (it’s) definitely tasty in coffee. 080924139
summary:
Nouns inflect for singular and plural in all grammatical cases except the essive, and possibly the abessive, while dual is not a noun category even though it is important in verb morphology and some pronouns. Number and case are marked together by portmanteau suffixes, stem alternations, or both, and there is no formal count/mass distinction since nouns like ‘flour,’ ‘sugar,’ and ‘food’ can appear in the plural.

When singular is used, the referent is either generic or a single unit.

text:
case|( noun!case|see case
\ has nine cases: nominative, genitive, accusative, illative, inessive, elative, comitative, abessive, and essive. The terminology chosen here for the nine cases reflects the names used traditionally in Uralic studies.
Nouns inflect inflection!nominal for these cases, in addition to number, via portmanteau suffixes, stem alternations, or a combination of both.

A general description of the cases is provided here.
Note that the case system is valid for pronouns (also a subclass of nominals) as well, but not for adjectives and numerals.
Case is expressed along with number by portmanteau suffixes, stem alternations, or a combination of both.
NumCaseNouns on treats this in more detail.
summary: The language has nine cases: nominative, genitive, accusative, illative, inessive, elative, comitative, abessive, and essive, using terminology traditional in Uralic studies. Nouns, including pronouns, inflect for case and number through portmanteau suffixes, stem alternations, or both, while adjectives and numerals do not show this case system.

text:
case!nominative
In addition to being used as the citation form, most commonly in singular, nominative case ( ) marks the grammatical subject of a verbal clause (typically the most agent-like argument for transitive verbs)

as in nom1 and
nom2.

dä stuor sarves båhta\\
dä stuor sarves båhta\\
then big moose nom.sg come 3sg.prs\\
Then a big moose arrives. 090702319

ja dä dáhka almatj dålåv\\
ja dä dáhka almatj dålå-v\\
and then make 3sg.prs person nom.sg fire- acc.sg\\
And then one makes a fire. 100404102

The possessed possession noun in a possessive copular clause (cf. copulaClauses ) is also in the nominative case, as in nom3.

muvne lä bijjla\\
muvne lä bijjla\\
1sg.iness be 3sg.prs car nom.sg\\
I have a car.(lit.: ‘at-me is car’) 08092601m44s
summary: Nominative case is used not only as the citation form, usually in the singular, but also to mark the grammatical subject of a verbal clause, especially the most agent-like argument in transitive clauses. It also marks the possessed noun in possessive copular clauses, as in the equivalent of “I have a car” literally expressed as “at me is car.”

text:
case!genitive
The genitive case ( ), the only adnominal case in,
marks the possessor modifying the head of a noun phrase (the possessed noun), as in gen1.

gokt lä dan almatja namma majna ságasta?\\
gokt lä d-a-n almatj-a namma ma-jna ságasta\\
how be 3sg.prs dem- dist- gen.sg person- gen.sg name nom.sg rel- com.sg talk 2sg.prs\\
What is the name of that person who you are talking with? 110521b1040

Furthermore, the nominal complement!phrasecomplement in a postpositional phrase phrase!postpositional occurs in the genitive case, as the noun gåde ‘hut’ in gen2.

gåde sinne suovastit\\
gåde sinne suovasti-t\\
hut gen.sg in smoke- inf\\
to smoke (something) inside a hut 100405a157
summary: The genitive case is the only adnominal case, and it marks the possessor modifying the head of a noun phrase, as in the example meaning “the name of that person.” It is also used for the nominal complement in postpositional phrases, such as the genitive noun meaning “hut” in the phrase meaning “to smoke inside a hut.”

text:
case!accusative
The accusative case ( ) marks the object of a transitive valency!transitive verb, as illustrated by the monotransitive clause in acc1.

dä virtiv válldet giehpajd ja ribrev ja dagarijd ulgos\\
dä virti-v vállde-t giehpa-jd ja ribbre-v ja dagari-jd ulgos\\
then must- 1sg.prs take- inf lung- acc.pl and liver- acc.sg and such- acc.pl out\\
Then I have to take out the lungs, the liver and such things. 080909103

In ditransitive valency!ditransitive clauses, the accusative marks the object referring to the theme while the recipient is marked by the illative, as in acc2.

mån vaddav gajka buhtsujda biebmov\\
mån vadda-v gajka buhtsu-jda biebmo-v\\
1sg.nom give- 1sg.prs all ill reindeer- ill.pl food- acc.sg\\
I give food to all the reindeer. 110413b137

The case!accusativeaccusative can also mark nouns functioning as a clause-level temporal adverbial phrase phrase!adverbial denoting a period of time,
as in acc3.

jo dan vuolen udemä ijav\\
jo d-a-n vuolen ude-mä ija-v\\
yes dem- dist- gen.sg under sleep- 1pl.pst night- acc.sg\\
Yes, and we slept under that for a night. 090702305
summary: The accusative case marks the object of a transitive verb, and in ditransitive clauses it marks the theme while the recipient is expressed by the illative. It can also be used for clause-level temporal adverbials denoting a period of time, such as “for a night.”

text:
case!illative
The illative case ( ) marks nouns that are the goal of the action expressed by a verb of motion, as in ill1.

muhten båtsoj ij både gärrdáj\\
muhten båtsoj ij både gärrdá-j\\
some reindeer nom.pl neg 3pl.prs come conneg corral- ill.sg\%yes dem.iness.sg under eller? sleep-1pl.pst night-acc.sg
Some reindeer don’t come into the corral. 080909007

In addition, the illative case marks nouns that refer to the addressee of communication, as in ill2, and the recipient of ‘giving’ actions valency!ditransitive, as in ill4.

muv áhttje hålloj såmes raddnáj…\\
muv áhttje hållo-j såmes raddná-j\\
1sg.gen father nom.sg say- 3sg.pst some friend- ill.sg\\
My father said to some friend… 090702505

vadde Jåssjåj aj \\
vadde Jåssjå-j aj \\
give sg.imp Josh- ill.sg also \%
Give (one) to Josh, too! 090519033

Finally, familial relations can also be expressed using an illative construction. In such cases, the ‘ego’ of the family relation is in the illative, as in ill5.

dån lä eddno munje \\
dån lä eddno munje\\
2sg.nom be 2sg.prs maternal.uncle nom.sg 1sg.ill \%
You are my maternal uncle.(lit.: you are maternal uncle to me) 110413b035

In this example, the illative nominal is a pronoun, but it is plausible that full nouns are possible in this function as well, although there are no such tokens in the corpus.
summary: The illative case marks nouns that are the goal of motion verbs, the addressee in communication, and the recipient of giving actions. It is also used in constructions expressing familial relations, where the “ego” of the relation appears in the illative, as in “You are my maternal uncle,” though the text notes that only pronouns are attested in the corpus for this use.

text:
case!inessive
The inessive case ( ) marks nouns that function as adjuncts to verbal clauses indicating the location of the event or action, as in iness1.

nå, mav enabov dihki Áhkkabakten? \\
nå ma-v enabo-v dihki Ahkkabakte-n \\
well what- acc.sg more- acc.sg do 2sg.pst Ahkkabakte- iness.sg \\
Well, what more did you do in Áhkkabakkte? 080924021

Similarly, as the complement!phrasecomplement of the copular verb verb!copular, an inessive noun indicates the location of the subject referent, as in iness2.

vággen Sálvojåhkå'l\\
vágge-n Sálvo-jåhkå=l\\
valley- iness.sg Sálvo-creek nom.sg=be 3sg.prs\\
Sálvo Creek is in the valley. 100404007

The possessor noun in a possessive possession copular clause (cf. copulaClauses ) is also in the inessive case, as in iness3.

sámen lä bena\\
sáme-n lä bena\\
Saami- iness.sg be 3sg.prs dog nom.sg\\
The Saami man has a dog.(lit.: at Saami is dog) 080917a068
summary: The inessive case marks nouns used as adjuncts to verbal clauses to indicate the location of an event or action. It also appears as the complement of the copular verb to show where the subject is located, and as the possessor noun in possessive copular clauses, expressing possession in the sense of “at X is Y.”

text:
case!elative
The elative case ( ) marks nouns as the source of an action of transfer, as in elat1, as well as the origin, as in elat2a and elat2b.

váldav tjåjvev ribrist luovas\\
válda-v tjåjve-v ribri-st luovas\\
take- 1sg.prs stomach- acc.sg liver- elat.sg loose\\
I loosen the stomach from the liver. 080909079

nå gåsse dija älgijdä Örnvikast vuodjet vadnásav?\\
nå gåsse dija älgi-jdä Örnvika-st vuodje-t vadnása-v\\
well when 2pl.nom begin- 2pl.pst Örnvik- elat.sg drive- inf boat- acc.sg\\
Well when did you start taking the boat from Örnvik? 080924563

dån båda Amerigist\\
dån båda Amerig-ist\\
2sg.nom come 2sg.prs America- elat.sg\\
You come from America. 08062128m02s

The elative also marks the addressee of a question (the source of information), as in elat5.

Eddest galgav gatjadit\\
Edde-st galga-v gatjadi-t\\
Edgar- elat.sg will- 1sg.prs ask- inf\\
I will ask Edgar. 090519357

Similarly, in a copular clause clause!copular, the elative case can mark a noun whose referent is a source of pain, as in elat6.

mån lev åjvest\\
mån le-v åjve-st\\
1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs head- elat.sg\\
I have a headache.(lit.: ‘I am from head’) 110331b079

The noun referring to the material that something consists of or is made of is in the elative case, as in elat3 and elat4.

mån iv tuhtje dav färska málest\\
mån i-v tuhtje d-a-v färska mále-st\\
1sg.nom neg-1sg.prs like conneg dem- dist- acc.sg fresh blood- elat.sg\\
I don’t like that (made) of fresh blood. 080924271

dá lä sasnest gårroduvum\\
d-á lä sasne-st gårro-duvu-m\\
dem- prox nom.pl be 3pl.prs furless.leather- elat.sg sew- pass-prf\\
These are sewn out of furless leather. 080708_Session08080708_Session08001

The elative case can be used to mark the agent which carries out the action referred to by a passivized passive verb, as in elat5b.

gåhte lä tsiggijduvvum mánájst\\
gåhte lä tsiggij-duvvu-m máná-jst\\
hut nom.sg be 3sg.prs build- pass- prf child- elat.pl\\
The hut has been built by children. 110518a28m41s

In comparative adjective!comparative constructions, elative marks a noun whose referent is the standard in the comparison, as in elat7.

mån lev stuorab Svienast\\
mån le-v stuora-b Sviena-st\\
1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs big- comp Sven- elat.sg\\
I am bigger than Sven. 110331b087
summary: The elative case marks nouns that function as a source or origin, including the source of a transfer, the place something comes from, the addressee of a question, and even a source of pain in copular clauses. It is also used for the material something is made of, the agent in passive constructions, and the standard of comparison in comparative adjective phrases.

text:
case!comitative
The comitative case ( ) marks nouns referring to someone or something participating in an action together with the agent as in com1, or some other participant, as in com1b.

men ådtjo sáme gielav ságastit duv årbenij?\\
men ådtjo sáme giela-v ságasti-t duv årbeni-j\\
but may 2sg.pst Saami gen.sg language- acc.sg speak- inf 2sg.gen sibling- com.pl\\
But were you allowed to speak the Saami language with your siblings? 080924366

válda káfav suhkorijn jala suhkorahta?\\
válda káfa-v suhkori-jn jala suhkor-ahta\\
take 2sg.prs coffee- acc.sg sugar- com.sg or sugar- abess\\
Do you take your coffee with sugar or without sugar? 110509b11m41s

The comitative also marks nouns referring to an instrument instrumental used to carry out an action, as in com2.

del vuodja bijlajn Örnvikaj ja dä vádnasijn Tjeggelvasa badjel\\
del vuodja bijla-jn Örnvika-j ja dä vádnasi-jn Tjeggelvas-a badjel\\
now drive 3sg.prs car- com.sg Örnvik- ill.sg and then boat- com.sg Tjeggelvas- gen.sg over\\
Now one drives to Örnvik by car, then by boat over Lake Tjeggelvas. 080924471

When two persons or things are equated with respect to a certain characteristic, the comitative marks the noun whose referent is the standard of comparison adjective!comparative, as in com3.

Svenna lä akta vuoras Ingerijn\\
Svenna lä akta vuoras Inger-ijn\\
Sven nom.sg be 3sg.prs one old Inger- com.sg\\
Sven is as old as Inger.(lit.: Sven is one age with Inger) 110331b135
summary: The comitative case marks a noun that accompanies the agent in an action, as in “with your siblings,” and it can also mark an instrument used to carry out an action, such as “by car” or “by boat.” It is additionally used in comparative constructions to mark the standard of comparison, as in “Sven is as old as Inger.”

text:
case!abessive
The referent of a noun marked by the abessive case ( ) is lacking or missing, as illustrated by abess1 This example is also found in com1b above but is repeated here for convenience, as well as to focus on the abessive noun.
and abess2.

válda káfav suhkorijn jala suhkorahta?\\
válda káfa-v suhkori-jn jala suhkor-ahta\\
take 2sg.prs coffee- acc.sg sugar- com.sg or sugar- abess\\
Do you take your coffee with sugar or without sugar? 110509b11m41s

dån lä vájmodak dal\\
dån lä vájmo-dak dal\\
2sg.nom be 2sg.prs heart- abess now\\
You are heartless now. 110413a226

Note that nouns in abessive case!abessive are rare in natural speech, and limited to elicitation sessions in the corpus.
The ’s wordlist indicates that the word ájnát can also be used to express ‘without’ (entry explExs4367; cf. orthography ), but the corpus does not provide any tokens of this.
While the meaning of nouns in the abessive case is quite clear, their morphophonological morphophonology behavior is problematic; see abessiveProblematic for more details.
summary: The abessive case marks a noun whose referent is lacking or missing, as shown in examples meaning “with sugar or without sugar” and “You are heartless now.” The passage notes that abessive nouns are rare in natural speech and mostly occur in elicitation sessions, and that although the meaning is clear, their morphophonological behavior is problematic.

text:
case!essive
The essive case ( ) generally marks predicative nouns functioning as complements complement!phrase of verbs such as sjaddat ‘become’, as in ess1a and ess1b, and gähtjoduvvat ‘be called’, as in ess2. Note that nouns in the essive case do not inflect for number number.

bednan sjaddav\\
bedna-n sjadda-v\\
dog- ess become- 1sg.prs\\
I become a dog. 110509b05m49s

jegŋa sjaddá tjáhtsen\\
jegŋa sjaddá tjáhtse-n\\
ice nom.sg become 3sg.prs water- ess\\
Ice becomes water. 110331b160

dut såhke vadnásan gåhtjoduvva\\
d-u-t såhke vadnása-n gåhtjo-duvva \\
dem- rmt- nom.sg birch nom.sg boat- ess call- pass 3sg.prs\\
Yonder birch is called a boat. 110509b14m02s

Furthermore, the complement of the particle dugu ‘like’ can be in the essive case, as illustrated by the example in ess3.

dat vuodja dugu goullen\\
d-a-t vuodja dugu goulle-n\\
dem- dist- nom.sg swim 3sg.prs like fish- ess\\
He swims like a fish. 110413a059

However, while my main consultant accepted constructions like in ess3, her initial response normally consisted of nearly the same construction, only with the noun in nominative case!nominative case, as in ess4.

vuodja dugu goulle\\
vuodja dugu goulle\\
swim 3sg.prs like fish nom.sg\\
He swims like a fish. 110413a052

Finally, it should be pointed out that essive is not particularly common in the corpus; tokens for this case are only found in elicitation sessions. In summary, there are not enough data to come to any definitive conclusions concerning the status of essive in current \ usage.
case|)
summary: The essive case primarily marks predicative nouns used as complements of verbs such as *sjaddat* ‘become’ and *gähtjoduvvat* ‘be called’, and these nouns do not inflect for number. It can also occur after the particle *dugu* ‘like’, though nominative is often used instead, and the case appears to be rare in the corpus, occurring only in elicitation data.

section: Number and case marking on nouns
text:
inflection!nominal

As indicated in the previous sections, \ nouns inflect for nine cases case and two number number categories (only the essive and possibly the abessive cases do not inflect for number). While case and number are generally marked by nominal suffixes, they are often supplemented by other morphophonological marking strategies, or even expressed solely by non-linear morphology. These other strategies are:
itemize
consonant alternations in the stem (also known as consonant gradation)
stem-vowel alternations (umlaut)
vowel harmony
itemize
Concerning nouns, the segmental alternations are discussed in detail in nonlinearNounMorph, while vowel harmony is presented in NclassIe. First, a short discussion of the nominal suffixes follows here.
summary: Nouns inflect for nine cases and two number categories, although the essive and possibly the abessive do not show number marking. Case and number are usually expressed by nominal suffixes, but they may also be marked or reinforced by consonant alternations in the stem, stem-vowel alternations, and vowel harmony. The passage notes that these alternations are treated elsewhere in detail, and the section that follows begins with nominal suffixes.

section: Number and case marking on nouns
text:
suffix!nominal
\ has a number of portmanteau suffix!portmanteau suffixes expressing case case and number number.
Only nom.sg, nom.pl and gen.sg are generally
not marked by any linear morphology morphology!non-linear.
The nominal suffixes marking case and number are listed in Table nounSuffixes. Note that the status of the abessive case!abessive suffixes is unclear, including whether they inflect for number, as discussed in abessiveProblematic. Nouns in essive case!essive case do not inflect for number.

In nom.pl and gen.sg, the -h suffix is optional in \ (and therefore appears in parentheses in Table nounSuffixes ).
The paradigms in also indicate an optional -h, while does not indicate any -h at all.
The com.sg suffix has two allomorphs: -jn and -jna, which seem to be in free variation in the corpus, and not determined phonologically.
summary: The passage says that nominal suffixes in this language are mostly portmanteau markers of case and number, with only nominative singular, nominative plural, and genitive singular generally lacking overt linear marking. It also notes that the status of the abessive suffixes is unclear, including whether they inflect for number, while essive nouns do not inflect for number. In nominative plural and genitive singular, the suffix -h is optional, and the comitative singular has two free-variant allomorphs, -jn and -jna, which do not appear to be phonologically conditioned.

text:
When looking at the inflectional inflection suffixes, it is noticeable that a number of suffixes suffix!nominal contain a -j component, as highlighted by Table nounSuffixesWithJ.
It is tempting to posit a plural marking suffix -j because it occurs in gen.pl, acc.pl, ill.pl, iness.pl, elat.pl and com.pl; however, the ill.sg suffix -j and the com.sg suffix -jn(a) both have a similar -j element, but are clearly not plural.

Furthermore, as illustrated in Table nounSuffixesWithJandUmlaut,
the plural cases with a -j component in the suffix trigger vowel harmony in stem consonants in Class Ie nouns (cf. NclassIe ),

but so does the. \ suffix, while the ill.sg suffix does not trigger \ (despite being segmentally identical to. \ and. \ suffixes).
Thus, -j suffixes that trigger vowel harmony also fail to align with number marking. As a result, I do not analyze any -j suffix as a plural marker, but do point out this nearly pervasive plural pattern. Cf. ‘eidemic resonance’ in.
summary: The passage notes that many nominal inflectional suffixes contain a -j element, and although this seems at first like a plural marker because it appears in several plural cases, similar -j forms also occur in singular suffixes. It also observes that while some -j plural suffixes trigger vowel harmony in Class Ie nouns, other suffixes with comparable segmental shapes do not, so the author concludes that -j should not be analyzed as a plural marker, even though it is a near-regular plural pattern.

section: Number and case marking on nouns
text:
morphology!non-linear
In addition to the suffixes described above, most nouns are also marked for case and number by non-linear stem allomorphy (cf. morphophonology ).

Because nom.sg, nom.pl and gen.sg lack suffixes completely, As mentioned in nominalSuffixes above, there is an optional -h suffix marking nom.pl and gen.sg.
nouns in these three case/number categories can only be marked by non-linear morphology.

To illustrate this, the inflectional inflection!nominal paradigm for the noun bärrgo ‘meat’ is provided in Table meatParadigm and described here. Note that, due to /o/ occurring in V2 position in all forms as the inflectional class marker, the stem has two allomorphs: bärrg- and bierg-.

In summary, the inflectional paradigm for bärrgo is characterized by both consonant gradation consonant gradation and umlaut umlaut in the stem,
and the morphological environment determines which of these allomorphs is selected.
As a result, the acc.pl form biergojd is marked for case/number by the weak bierg- stem consonant gradation!weak grade and the -jd suffix simultaneously, and the ill.sg form bärrgoj is marked by the strong bärrg- stem consonant gradation!strong grade and the -j suffix. The most obvious evidence that the choice of stem allomorph is morphologically meaningful can be found in a comparison of the nom.sg form bärrgo and the nom.pl As the nom.pl form is always syncretic with the gen.sg form, a comparison of the latter with the nom.sg form would be equally insightful.
form biergo. These forms differ exclusively in the choice of the strong versus the weak stem allomorph and in the choice of umlaut. Thus, the nom.sg form bärrgo is marked for case/number by the fact that the stem is in the strong grade and features the vowel ä, while the nom.pl stem is in the weak grade and features the vowel ie.

This pattern of non-linear case/number marking throughout the paradigm for bärrgo is illustrated in Table meatParadigmPattern.
Here, two patterns are manifest: the forms for nom.sg, ill.sg and ess show one pattern, while all other case/number combinations exhibit the other pattern. This alignment of stem allomorph selection is more or less prevalent throughout \ noun paradigms whenever stem allomorphy is a part of a noun’s inflection!nominalinflectional paradigm.
Note, however, that not every noun undergoes consonant gradation and/or umlaut; instead, their presence are determined by the phonological form of a noun. Consonant gradation is described in detail in Cgrad, and umlaut in umlaut; some examples of nouns with consonant gradation and umlaut alternations are shown in Table CGpatterns and Table umlautPatterns, respectively.
summary: Most nouns are marked for case and number not only by suffixes but also by non-linear stem allomorphy, and in some categories such as nom.sg, nom.pl, and gen.sg the stem alternation is the only overt marking. The noun *bärrgo* ‘meat’ illustrates this with two stem allomorphs, *bärrg-* and *bierg-*, which are selected by the morphological environment and combine with consonant gradation and umlaut to distinguish forms such as nom.sg *bärrgo* and nom.pl *biergo*. Not all nouns show these alternations, since consonant gradation and umlaut depend on the phonological shape of the noun.

section: Number and case marking on nouns
subsection: Problematic case/number marking in abessive case
text:
case!abessive
Unlike the other cases, the behavior of nouns in the abessive case is a bit of an enigma, even if its meaning, which typically translates as ‘without’, is quite clear (cf. abessive ).
Indeed, it is difficult to come to any certain conclusions about the relationship between abessive as a case per se and the morphophonological marking of nouns in the abessive case. It seems to be rarely used in natural speech, and is only attested in the corpus in elicitation sessions. Even in elicitation sessions, language consultants were often hesitant or uncertain of the word forms they produced, and often produced conflicting forms for a single item. Indeed, the slipperiness of the abessive case is nothing new, as both and only provide incomplete treatments of abessive.

One potential source of the confusion (even for speakers) is the fact that abessive suffixes are unique in two ways.
First, there is significant allomorphy, and, secondly, some of the allomorphs are the only bisyllabic nominal inflection!nominalinflection suffixes in.
The attested forms are -dak, -daga, -gat, -gahta and -ahta (cf. examples abess1 and abess2 on page abess1).
Furthermore, the weak grade consonant gradation!weak grade usually accompanies abessive, but sometimes the strong grade consonant gradation!strong grade does. In some cases of Class Ie nouns, vowel harmony is triggered, in others it is not. In some cases, number is clearly marked, in other cases, there is no distinction between singular and plural.

As a result, the following sections on inflectional noun classes are only able to provide a limited and preliminary description concerning abessive.
summary: The abessive case, meaning ‘without,’ is described as especially unclear in its behavior and morphological marking, with few reliable attested examples because it is rarely used in natural speech and mainly appears in elicitation data. It shows substantial allomorphy, unusual bisyllabic suffixes, and variable patterns of consonant gradation, vowel harmony, and number marking, so the grammar can only offer a limited preliminary description of its inflectional behavior.

inflection!nominal noun!inflection class|(
Nouns in \ can be grouped into three main inflectional classes, with several subclasses, based on recurring patterns across case/number inflectional paradigms. Each noun is marked by a class suffix suffix!inflectional class I am indebted to phonologist and Lule Saami scholar Bruce Morén-Duolljá Mor\'en-Duollj\'a, Bruce for inspiring me to consider an approach to the data involving post-stem class marking morphology.
which is attached directly after the noun stem and precedes case/number suffixes (cf. Figure nounStructure). For the majority of nouns, this suffix consists only of a vowel (in V2 position); however, the class marking suffixes in the less frequent classes II and III deviate from this pattern.
The presence of umlaut alternations and/or consonant gradation for a given noun is not dependent on the noun’s membership in a specific class, but is determined by whether the phonemes occupying the V1 position and the consonant center of the final foot, respectively, are susceptible to umlaut and/or consonant gradation. Furthermore, some derivational suffixes (such as the diminutive suffix -tj) can block consonant gradation and umlaut from happening in the new derived form.

Note that membership in a specific noun class does not seem to be semantically motivated.

The following sections present the four inflectional noun classes based on a preliminary analysis of the corpus; it is possible that, with more research, more noun classes may result, or that the present classes may need revision. Because each noun paradigm consists of seventeen inflectional forms, most of the data on which these classes are based come from elicitation sessions, as it is far beyond realistic for a single, non-native-speaker linguist to collect a sufficiently large natural (i.e., un-elicited, spontaneous) spoken language corpus which includes all inflectional forms for a large variety of nouns.

There are two main criteria for positing the different noun classesː
itemize
the allomorphy of the nom.sg form of a noun stem in relation to the rest of the inflectional paradigm (i.e., consonant gradation consonant gradation, umlaut umlaut)
the regularity of the pattern of vowels occurring between the stem and case/number suffixes (i.e., the class marking suffix suffix!inflectional class)

itemize
To illustrate these differences, it is sufficient to look at the class suffix in nom.sg and the alignment of consonant gradation allomorphs, as summarized in
Table nounClassSummary.

The header grade alignment refers to the choice of stem allomorph in nom.sg versus nom.pl whenever consonant gradation is relevant for a specific noun paradigm: the value ‘str-wk’ indicates that nom.sg is marked by the strong grade and nom.pl by the weak grade, while ‘wk-str’ is the opposite pattern.

Class I is a sort of default class
and is therefore dealt with first in NclassI,
while classes II and III are described in NclassII and NclassIII. The final section ( summaryNounClasses ) provides a brief summary of the noun classes, including a table listing examples from each class.
summary:
Nouns are grouped into inflectional classes based on recurring case/number paradigms, with each noun carrying a post-stem class suffix before the case/number endings. Most nouns have a class suffix that is just a vowel, and membership in a class is not semantically motivated; umlaut and consonant gradation depend instead on phonological conditions in the stem and can be blocked by some derivational suffixes.  

The classes are identified mainly by two criteria: the allomorphy of the nominative singular stem relative to the rest of the paradigm, and the regularity of the vowel pattern between stem and suffixes. The author notes that the classification is preliminary, based largely on elicited data, and that Class I is the default class, with Classes II and III described separately.

Subclasses Ia–Id behave similarly, with an invariant class-marking suffix across the paradigm, while subclass Ie is exceptional because of vowel harmony and is treated separately. itemize
vowel harmony
allomorphy in the class markers suffix!inflectional class ( e, i, á)

The inflectional paradigm for the words guolle ‘fish’ and vágge ‘valley’ are provided as examples for Ie nouns in Table fishValleyParadigm; note that vágge is not subject to consonant gradation.
For nouns with consonant gradation and/or umlaut in Class Ie, nom.sg, ill.sg and ess are in the strong grade and have ä or ua/uä in V1 position, while other case/number slots have the weak grade and ie or uo in V1 position, just as with all Class I nouns.

As mentioned above, nouns in Class Ie are subject to. This refers to non-adjacent regressive vowel harmony triggered by the presence of /j/ in certain case/number suffixes. In this, certain V1 vowels and the V2 vowel are raised in accommodating the palatal position of the /j/ in the suffix. The vowel in V2, which is e in Class Ie nouns, is raised to i, while the vowel in V1 is raised depending on its initial value: ä i, uo/uä u,
a ä, á ä and å u. Other V1 vowels in Class Ie are not affected, but the V2 vowel is always raised from /e/ to /i/ in the relevant paradigm slots.

The class marking suffixes and consonant gradation consonant gradation pattern for Class Ie are summarized in Table NclassIeSuffixes.
summary:
Class Ie nouns are a special subset of Class I nouns characterized by vowel harmony and allomorphic class-marking suffixes. In nouns with consonant gradation and/or umlaut, nom.sg, ill.sg, and ess show the strong grade with ä or ua/uä in V1, while the other case/number forms show the weak grade with ie or uo in V1.

The passage also explains that Class Ie nouns undergo non-adjacent regressive vowel harmony triggered by /j/ in certain suffixes, raising V2 from e to i and raising V1 in specific ways depending on its original quality. Other V1 vowels are not affected, but the V2 vowel is always raised from /e/ to /i/ in the relevant forms.

The examples båtsoj ‘reindeer’ and ålmaj ‘man’ illustrate this pattern, but the corpus data are sparse and inconclusive, and several irregularities remain unexplained, including vowel alternations and the illative singular gradation pattern in båtsoj.

This class is divided into two subclasses, IIIa and IIIb, which are discussed in the following sections.

Examples include *sabek* ‘ski’ and *vanás* ‘boat’; *vanás* is similar to *sabek* but shows consonant gradation. All denominal nouns formed with the diminutive suffix *-tj* belong to Class IIIa, as illustrated by *guolátj* ‘little fish’.

The less common subclass of Class III nouns exhibits a nom.sg form which also lacks a class marker but ends in an open syllable; thus, the stem-final consonant, which is present in all other slots in the paradigm, is lacking.
The word bena ‘dog’ is provided in Table dogParadigm as a example for this second subclass.
summary: A less common subclass of Class III nouns has a nominative singular form that lacks a class marker and ends in an open syllable. In this form, the stem-final consonant found in all other paradigm slots is absent, as shown by the example *bena* ‘dog’.

However, elicited abessive forms were consistently in the strong grade, while elicited essive forms were sometimes in the strong grade consonant gradation!strong grade, sometimes in the weak grade consonant gradation!weak grade, without any seemingly consistent patterns. A special set of possessive suffixes exists in \ which indicate, in addition to case and number for the host noun, the person and number of the possessor of the referent of the host noun.
While the possessive suffixes go back to Proto-Saami, they seem to have nearly fallen out of use in contemporary, and are only attested in three recordings from the corpus. These examples from the corpus are presented first, and a discussion follows.

While there are technically nine tokens of possessive pronouns in the corpus, these nine tokens can be grouped into two identical sets, so that effectively only two examples are available. Specifically, there are three tokens of áhttjes ‘my father’ in nominative case by one speaker in two different recordings, and three tokens of the parallel construction mammaset ja pahpaset ‘your mother and your father’ by another speaker in one recording. The passage describes a set of special possessive suffixes that mark not only the case and number of the noun but also the person and number of the possessor. Although these suffixes are inherited from Proto-Saami, they appear to be nearly obsolete in the contemporary corpus, occurring only in a few tokens, while most possession is expressed with genitive nouns or pronouns.

The examples suggest that the suffixes attach after the inflectional class marker and may function as portmanteau forms, but the corpus is too small to establish a full paradigm. The text also notes possible effects of alienability and lexicalization, and points out that some loanwords still take possessive suffixes, which may indicate residual productivity or analogical use.
