summary:
The language has a closed class of pronouns, including personal, demonstrative, reflexive, interrogative, and relative pronouns. Pronouns are nominal elements defined by their ability to substitute for a nominal phrase, and they inflect for case; personal and reflexive pronouns show singular, dual, and plural number, while demonstrative, interrogative, and relative pronouns show only singular and plural.

The passage also notes that there is insufficient corpus data to determine the status of pronouns in the abessive and essive cases. In addition, there are non-nominal interrogative pro-forms that do not inflect for case or number, and these are treated separately from interrogative pronouns.

text:
pronoun!personal|(

Personal pronouns inflect inflection for person person and number number (singular, dual or plural) as well as for case case. They are listed in Table PersPronTable. Personal pronouns do not inflect for the biological sex of their referents, but are restricted in referring only to humans (demonstrative pronouns are used when the referent is not human).
The nominative case!nominative forms all have two possible forms, e.g. mån månnå ‘ 1sg.nom’. In general, the monosyllabic form is the default, while the bisyllabic form is typically used as a citation form and when the pronoun is emphasized.

The person marking morphemes in personal pronouns are completely systematic and are
listed in Table PersPronPersonMorph.

Case and number marking is not quite as systematic, but certain segmental patterns are present which closely resemble the singular case/number suffixes suffix!nominal for nouns, particularly those in inflectional class I (cf. NclassI ).
Specifically, note the lack of a final consonant for all full forms of nominative pronouns (cf. the lack of a nom.sg or nom.pl nominal case suffix), genitive pronouns in dual and plural (cf. the lack of a gen.sg nominal case suffix), the final -v in the case!accusativeaccusative personal pronouns (cf. -v for nouns in acc.sg), a final or nearly final j-element for illative pronouns (cf. -j for nouns in ill.sg), a final or nearly final n-element for inessive pronouns (cf. -n for nouns in iness.sg), a final or nearly final st-element for elative pronouns (cf. -st for nouns in elat.sg and elat.pl) and a final or nearly final jn-element for comitative pronouns (cf. -jn(a) for nouns in com.sg).
pronoun!personal|)
summary:
Personal pronouns inflect for person, number (singular, dual, plural), and case, but not for the biological sex of their referents, and they are restricted to human referents. Nominative forms have two variants: a monosyllabic default form and a bisyllabic form used as a citation form and for emphasis.

The person-marking morphemes are fully systematic, while case and number marking are less regular but show clear parallels to nominal suffixes, especially in class I nouns. These parallels include patterns such as no final consonant in nominative forms, -v in accusative, and final or near-final elements like j, n, st, and jn in illative, inessive, elative, and comitative forms, respectively.

text:
pronoun!demonstrative|( demonstrative pronoun|see pronoun
Demonstrative pronouns are based on the stem d-. They inflect inflection for case case and number number (singular and plural, but not dual), as well as the proximity of the entity they refer to. The data from the corpus indicate that there is a three-way distinction between referents close to the speaker (proximal spacial deixis!proximal), those away from the speaker (distal spacial deixis!distal), and those particularly far away (remote spacial deixis!remote).
The demonstrative pronouns are listed in Table DemProTable. Note that due to a lack of sufficient data on the remote forms in the corpus (either no forms exist or speakers were too uncertain to warrant inclusion here), this part of the paradigm is not complete; forms based on tentative data are marked by a question mark.

Morphologically, demonstrative pronouns consist of the stem d-, followed by -á-, -a- or -u- for proximal, distal and remote, respectively. This
is then followed by a case/number suffix, as summarized in Table DemProSuffixTable.

Both distal and remote demonstrative pronouns have a referent which is away from the speaker, but remote demonstrative pronouns indicate a greater distance than distal demonstrative pronouns so that the referent of a remote demonstrative pronoun is clearly not located near the addressee.
On the other hand, the referent of a proximal demonstrative pronoun is very close to the speaker.
Distal demonstrative pronouns are not as specific in indicating the location of the referent, and do not necessarily rule out a referent which is near the addressee.
Indeed, distal demonstrative pronouns are the most common in the corpus and are a sort of unmarked default demonstrative pronoun.
Note that demonstratives demonstrative are identical in form to demonstrative pronouns, but differ syntactically because they modify the head of an NP; they are discussed in demonstratives.

Demonstrative pronouns typically have non-human referents, as in demProWithNonHumanReferent1.

muhtin sa del vuoptin dajt\\
muhtin sa del vuopti-n d-a-jt\\
sometimes so then sell- 1du.pst dem- dist- acc.pl\\
So sometimes we sold those. 080924300

However, they can also be used to refer to third-person human referents, as in the example in demProWithHumanReferent1.

da lä jabmam, ber muv äddne'l viessomin dále\\
d-a lä jabma-m ber mu-v äddne=l viesso-min dále\\
dem- dist nom.pl be 3pl.prs die- prf only 1sg.gen mother nom.sg=be 3sg.prs live- prog now\\
They have died, only my mother is living today. 100310b145

Distal demonstrative pronouns can also be used for anaphoric text deixis. For instance, dat in example demProTextDeixis refers to the fact that the speaker has just dropped her ski pole.

oj! ij dat aktagav dága\\
oj ij d-a-t aktaga-v dága\\
oh neg 3sg.prs dem- dist- nom.sg none- acc.sg make conneg\\
Oh! That’s no problem.(lit.: that makes nothing) 100404156

pronoun!demonstrative|)
summary:
Demonstrative pronouns are formed from the stem **d-** and inflect for case and number, with a three-way contrast in deixis: **proximal** (near the speaker), **distal** (away from the speaker), and **remote** (farther away, not near the addressee). Morphologically, the stem takes **-á-**, **-a-**, or **-u-** for proximal, distal, and remote forms, followed by case/number suffixes, though the remote paradigm is incomplete in the corpus.

The passage also notes that distal forms are the most common and function as an unmarked default. Demonstrative pronouns usually refer to non-human entities but can also refer to human third persons and can be used anaphorically in text deixis.

text:
pronoun!reflexive|(
The reflexive pronouns in Pite Saami are based on the stem etj- and inflect for the number (singular, dual and plural) and person of the noun they are coreferential with. Reflexive pronouns also inflect for case. These are listed in Table ReflPronTable.
The stem etj- can be translated as ‘self’, which could imply that it is a noun, but it is different from nouns for several reasons: 1) it is monosyllabic, 2) it has its own case and number marking suffixes, and 3) it inflects for dual number.
Note that reflexive pronouns are not common in the spontaneous language recordings in the corpus, but are mostly found in elicitation sessions. Even in elicitation sessions, my main consultant was not completely sure about some of the forms for less common cases (i.e., everything except nominative case!nominative, accusative case!accusative However, note the form etjav ‘ refl-1sg.acc’ was provided by a different speaker (A) than the speaker (B) who provided the forms in the rest of the paradigm, and speaker A was very uncertain of this form. lists etjam and etjamav, and I suspect that the form etjav indicates that a simplification of the system has taken place (at least for speaker A) in which the root etj- is simply treated as a noun (such as ‘self’) which inflects using standard nominal case/number suffixes (here the acc.sg suffix -v), but ultimately more data are needed to verify this.
and genitive case!genitive). Furthermore, a number of the elicited forms deviate from the forms provided in the complete paradigm in. But note also that the paradigm in indicates a lack of consensus in the reflexive pronouns across speakers, as well. Whether the forms found in the \ corpus indicate a simplification of the system or simply another speaker’s ideolect is impossible to determine at this point.

For these reasons, the forms in Table ReflPronTable should be considered preliminary at this point, and potentially subject to modification as a result of more thorough study. My consultants were particularly uncertain about the forms marked by a question mark, while forms listed in parenthesis are not attested in the corpus, but taken from the paradigms in and adapted to the current \ orthography.

One example of a reflexive pronoun is shown in reflPron1.

mån ságastav etjan birra\\
mån ságasta-v etja-n birra\\
1sg.nom speak- 1sg.prs refl-1sg.gen about\\
I talk about myself. 110521b2010

Reflexive pronouns are frequently used to add emphasis to the phrase!nominalnoun phrase they are coreferential with (as an intensifier), as in reflPron3.

mån lev etj sábme\\
mån le-v etj sábme\\
1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs refl 1sg.nom Saami nom.sg\\
I myself am Saami. 080703023

The noun phrase that a reflexive pronoun is coreferential with does not have to be realized overtly,
as illustrated by the utterance in reflPron2 (here as an intensifier as well).

etj lä lerram\\
etj lä lerra-m\\
refl 2sg.nom be 2sg.prs learn- prf\\
(You) yourself have learned. 080924407

pronoun!reflexive|)
summary:
Pite Saami reflexive pronouns are based on the stem **etj-** and inflect for person, number (singular, dual, plural), and case, with forms that are partly uncertain and likely variable across speakers. Although etj- means roughly ‘self,’ it differs from nouns because it is monosyllabic, has its own case and number suffixes, and inflects for dual number, so the paradigm is considered preliminary.  

These pronouns are uncommon in spontaneous corpus data and are mostly found in elicitation, where some forms are inconsistent or unclear; this may reflect simplification of the system or speaker-specific usage. Reflexive pronouns can function as intensifiers, emphasizing the noun phrase they refer to, and the coreferential noun phrase does not need to be overtly expressed.

text:
pronoun!interrogative|( interrogative!pronoun|see pronoun
\ has several classes of interrogative pronouns as well as a set of interrogative pro-forms which do not refer to NPs. While the latter set of non-nominal pro-forms refer to other word classes, they are covered in this section nonetheless due to their syntactic status as pro-forms.
The pronouns can be divided into those with human referents (cf. QpronounHUM ), which use the stem ge-, and those with non-human referents (cf. QpronounNoHUM ), which use the stem m-.
Furthermore, there are two classes of interrogatives which enquire about the selection of a particular item (semantically equivalent to English ‘which’; described in QpronounDEM ): the first refers to a choice from a selection in general and uses the stem mikkir-, while the other refers to a choice of one or two items and uses the stem gåb-.
Interrogative pro-forms not referring to NPs mostly feature the stem g- (cf. interrogativeProForms ). This classification is summarized in Figure interrogativeProFormSummary, which also indicates the stem for each type.
summary: The passage says that the language has several classes of interrogative pronouns, plus interrogative pro-forms that do not refer to noun phrases but are included because of their syntactic status. Interrogative pronouns are divided into human forms with the stem **ge-** and non-human forms with the stem **m-**. It also distinguishes two “which”-type interrogatives: one for a general selection with **mikkir-**, and one for a choice of one or two items with **gåb-**; most non-NP interrogative pro-forms use the stem **g-**.

text:
Interrogative pronouns with human referents use the stem ge- and inflect for the number (singular or plural) of the intended referent and for case. These pronouns are listed in Table QpronounHUMtable; examples are provided in QpronounHUMex1 and QpronounHUMex2.

nå, gejna dä tjuovo?\\
nå ge-jna dä tjuovo\\
well who- com.sg then accompany 2sg.pst\\
Well, who did you go with? 080924071

gen gabmaga lä dá?\\
ge-n gabmag-a lä d-á\\
who- gen.sg shoe- nom.pl be 3pl.prs dem- prox nom.pl\\
Whose shoes are these? 100404326
summary: Interrogative pronouns referring to humans are built on the stem **ge-** and inflect for both **number** (singular or plural) and **case**. The passage gives examples showing forms such as **gejna** “who” in the comitative singular and **gen** “whose” in the genitive singular.

text:
Interrogative pronouns with non-human referents use the stem m- and inflect for the number number (singular or plural) of the intended referent and for case case. These pronouns are listed in Table QpronounNoHUMtable; an example is provided in QpronounNoHUMex.

mav dån sida?\\
ma-v dån sida\\
what- acc.sg 2sg.nom want 2sg.prs\\
What do you want? 090519194
summary: Interrogative pronouns with non-human referents are formed with the stem **m-** and inflect for both **number** (singular or plural) and **case**. The passage points to a table listing these forms and gives an example sentence showing **mav** in the accusative singular, meaning “what” in the question “What do you want?”

text: The two selective interrogative pronouns are used to enquire about the selection or choice of an item. The stem mikkir- refers to a selection in general, while the stem gåb- limits the selection to one or two choices. These are described in the following two sections.
summary: The passage explains that the two selective interrogative pronouns are used to ask about the selection or choice of an item. The stem **mikkir-** refers to selection in general, whereas **gåb-** restricts the choice to one or two options.

text:
Interrogative pronouns based on the stem mikkir- are used to enquire about a choice or selection in general. They inflect for the number (singular and plural) of their referent and for case. These forms are listed in Table QpronounDEMGeneralTable.
Note that the inessive forms are not attested in the corpus. Two examples are provided in QpronounDEMGeneralEx1 and QpronounDEMGeneralEx2.

mikkirist lä dat dágaduvvum?\\
mikkir-ist lä d-a-t dága-duvv-um\\
which- elat.sg be 3sg.prs dem- dist- nom.sg make- pass-prf\\
What is that made of? 110521b1203

nå, mikkira lidjin dan Ákabakten?\\
nå mikkir-a lidji-n d-a-n Ákabakte-n\\
well which- nom.pl be- 3pl.pst dem- dist- iness.sg Ákkabakkte- iness.sg\\
Well which (people) were in Ákkabakkte? 080924032

They can also modify the head of an NP, and are then a ‘pro-adjective’ Cf. for more on non-pronoun ‘pro-forms’. enquiring after a further characterization of the referent. In this case, they do not inflect for number or case (as is true of all attributive adjectives), and so the form is always mikkir, as illustrated by the examples in QpronounDEMGeneralEx3 and QpronounDEMGeneralEx4.

mikkir málle lij?\\
mikkir málle li-j\\
which blood nom.sg be- 3sg.pst\\
Which (kind of) blood was it? 080924256

mikkir gulijd åtjojde?\\
mikkir guli-jd åtjo-jde\\
which fish- acc.pl buy- 2pl.pst\\
Which (kinds of) fish did you buy? 080924025

Another possible form of the stem seems to be makkar-, but this is only attested twice in the corpus and by one speaker, while mikkir- was consistently preferred in elicitation sessions.
An example with makkar is provided in QpronounDEMGeneralEx5; here, makkar is a pro-adjective modifying a noun in a subordinate interrogative clause.

ja dä lä aj väha gähtjamin makkar sarvajd gilgin njuovat aj\\
ja dä lä aj väha gähtja-min makkar sarva-jd gilgi-n njuova-t aj\\
and then be 3sg.prs also a.little look- prog which reindeer.bull- acc.pl will- 3pl.pst slaughter- inf also\\
And then he is also checking a bit which reindeer bulls they should also slaughter. 080909006
summary:
Interrogative pronouns based on the stem **mikkir-** are used to ask about a choice or selection in general, and they inflect for number and case. When they modify a noun as a pro-adjective, however, they do not inflect and appear in the fixed form **mikkir**; inessive forms are not attested in the corpus.  

A possible alternative stem, **makkar-**, is attested only twice from one speaker, whereas **mikkir-** was consistently preferred in elicitation.

text:
A further interrogative pronoun used to limit a selection to only one or two is based on the stem gåb-. It inflects for case case and for number number (singular and plural), as described below. Table QpronounDEMLimitedTable lists the various forms.

When marked for singular, it indicates a selection of one out of two possible choices, as in QpronounDEMLimitedEx1.

gåban sajen lä dån årrom?\\
gåba-n saje-n lä dån årro-m\\
which- iness.sg place- iness.sg be 2sg.prs 2sg.nom be- prf\\
At which of the two places have you been? 110521b1161

When marked for plural, it indicates a selection of two out of three or more choices,
as in QpronounDEMLimitedEx2.

gåbaj birra ságasta?\\
gåba-j birra ságasta\\
which- gen.pl about speak 2sg.prs\\
Which two are you talking about? 110521b1037

This interrogative pronoun is only attested in elicitation sessions in the corpus. A more thorough description must be left to future research.
pronoun!interrogative|)
summary: The passage describes an interrogative pronoun based on the stem *gåb-*, which inflects for case and number and is used to restrict a choice to a limited set. In the singular it asks about one of two possibilities, while in the plural it refers to two out of three or more possible choices. It is only attested in elicitation data, so a fuller description is deferred to future research.

text:
interrogative!pro-form|(
There are a number of non-nominal interrogative pro-forms. These enquire about information typically expressed by a clause-level adverbial, an adjunct or a complement clause. They are listed and glossed in Table otherQpronounTable, and three examples are provided in otherQpronounEx1 through otherQpronounEx3.

gånne dajt tjogijdä?\\
gånne d-a-jt tjogi-jdä\\
where dem- dist- acc.pl pick- 2pl.pst\\
Where did you pick them? 080924168

gukte almatj hålla ‘reta’?\\
gukte almatj hålla reta\\
how person nom.sg say 3sg.prs ‘reta’\\
How does one say ‘reta’? 080924377

man mälgat lij gu lij hiejman, iv mån diede\\
man mälgat li-j gu li-j hiejm-an, i-v mån diede\\
how far be- 3sg.pst when be- 3sg.pst home- iness.sg neg- 1sg.prs 1sg.nom know conneg\\
How far it was, when one was home, I don’t know 100404317

The list in Table otherQpronounTable is likely not complete, as there are several other non-nominal interrogative pro-forms listed in the \ wordlist (cf. orthography ) which are not attested in the corpus. Furthermore, the data do not indicate what the difference is between the various alternate forms for ‘to where’ and ‘how’.
interrogative!pro-form|)
summary: The passage describes several non-nominal interrogative pro-forms used to ask about information normally expressed by clause-level adverbials, adjuncts, or complement clauses, and illustrates them with examples such as “where,” “how,” and “how far.” It also notes that the inventory in the table is probably incomplete, since some forms appear in the wordlist but not the corpus, and that the data do not show the difference between alternate forms meaning “to where” and “how.”

text:
pronoun!relative|(
Relative pronouns in \ are identical in form to the interrogative pronoun!interrogative pronouns with non-human referents (cf. QpronounNoHUM ). However, unlike interrogative pronouns, relative pronouns do not reflect the human-ness of their referents. They agree in number number with their referent, and inflect for the case case
required by their syntactic function within the relative clause.
The relative pronouns are listed in Table relativePronounsTable.

See relativeClauses for a number of examples with relative pronouns as well as a description of relative clauses.

pronoun!relative|)

pronoun|)
summary: Relative pronouns are formally identical to interrogative pronouns with non-human referents, but unlike interrogative pronouns they do not mark whether their referent is human. They agree with their referent in number and take the case required by their syntactic role within the relative clause.

text:
Adjectivals in \ are defined syntactically by their ability to head an adjectival phrase phrase!adverbial (AP). They can be divided into four sub-categories based on both syntactic and morphological behavior, as summarized in Table adjectivalsSummary.

While attributive adjectives generally do not inflect, in elliptical phrases in which the head of an NP is not realized overtly, they do inflect for case and number.
Predicative adjectives are marked for number, and are morphologically similar to nominals.
Demonstratives agree in number and case with the noun they modify.
Numerals, on the other hand, are consistently uninflected.
Finally, the two types of adjectives form an open sub-class, while numerals are a closed sub-class.

The rest of this chapter covers adjectives, demonstratives and numerals as follows: adjectivesATTR provides a description of attributive adjectives,
while predADJ deals with predicative adjectives, before notePredNounsAdjs takes up the formal relationship between these two types.
compSuperlADJs then goes on to describe comparative and superlative forms,
before comparingNPs illustrates the implementation of such forms in making comparisons.
Syntactic restrictions on the adjectives corresponding to ‘small, little’ are described in smallADJs.
Quantifiers (a semantic sub-class of adjectives) are discussed in quantifiers, while
demonstratives are presented in demonstratives.
Finally, numerals covers numerals.
summary: Adjectivals are defined syntactically by their ability to head an adjectival phrase, and they are divided into four subcategories according to their syntactic and morphological behavior. Attributive adjectives usually do not inflect, except in elliptical noun phrases where they show case and number; predicative adjectives are marked for number and are morphologically similar to nominals; demonstratives agree in number and case with the noun they modify; and numerals are consistently uninflected. The passage also notes that adjectives form an open subclass, while numerals form a closed subclass.

text:
adjective!attributive|( adjective|(
Attributive adjectives form the head of an AP modifying the head of the matrix nominal phrase phrase!nominal, and are normally not subject to inflectional inflection morphology.

As part of an attributive AP, an attributive adjective occurs before the head noun it modifies, but after a demonstrative demonstrative, if present (cf. nominalPhrases on the structure of NPs). Examples are provided in adjEx1 through adjEx3.

dat lä tjähppis båtsoj ja villges åjjve\\
d-a-t lä tjähppis båtsoj ja villges åjjve\\
dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.prs black reindeer nom.sg and white head nom.sg\\
It is a black reindeer and a white head. 100405b043

guolle'l nåv njalga bäbbmo\\
guolle=l nåv njalga bäbbmo\\
fish nom.sg=be 3sg.prs so tasty food nom.sg\\
Fish is such tasty food. 100310b025

dat villges båtsoj\\
d-a-t villges båtsoj\\
dem- dist- nom.sg white reindeer nom.sg\\
that white reindeer 090930a014

As the head of an AP, attributive adjectives can be modified by adverbs adverb of grade, as illustrated by the AP hoj buorak ‘really good’ in adjEx4, or nåv njalga ‘so tasty’ in adjEx2 above.

ja dat lä årrom hoj buorak giesse\\
ja d-a-t lä årro-m hoj buorak giesse\\
and dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.prs be- prf really good summer nom.sg\\
And it has been a really good summer. 080909009

A number of adjectives end in -s (cf. the two adjectives tjähppes ‘black’ and villges ‘white’ in adjEx1), which is often considered an ‘attribution’ marking suffix in the literature. deals in detail with this final -s, which is common to all Saami languages. Rießler claims that it was grammaticalized from a 3 \ possessive suffix, and originally only marked the attributive form of adjectives. However, note that Rießler also points out that “the system of attributive and predicative marking is highly irregular in the Saamic languages”.
However, as njalga ‘tasty’ in adjEx2 illustrates, not all adjectives are marked this way. Furthermore, corresponding predicative adjective!predicative adjective forms (cf. predADJ below) often also have a final -s, sometimes even to the exclusion of the attributive adjective form. Because no consistent relationship between forms with and forms without a final -s exists, it is no longer a productive way to mark or derive either attributive or predicative adjectives. For this reason, it is not considered to be morphologically meaningful in the present discussion. Nonetheless, it is worth noting that adjectival forms (both attributive and predicative) ending in -s are common.

Note also that some attributive adjectives appear to have two possible forms. For instance, guhka and guhkes ‘long’ were both encountered in elicitation sessions with a single speaker who insisted that both forms were equally valid (cf. recording pit080819apit080819a starting at 33m14s).
summary:
Attributive adjectives head an adjective phrase that modifies a nominal phrase, normally without inflection, and they occur before the noun but after any demonstrative. They can themselves be modified by degree adverbs, as in examples like *hoj buorak* ‘really good’ and *næv njalga* ‘so tasty’.  

The passage also notes that many adjectives end in *-s*, but this ending is irregular, not consistently tied to attributive versus predicative use, and is therefore not treated as a productive morphological marker here. Some adjectives even show two possible attributive forms, such as *guhka* and *guhkes* ‘long’.

text:
If the context of the wider discourse is sufficiently unambiguous, it is possible that the nominal head of an NP is not realized, but implied.
When such elliptic constructions (sometimes called ‘headless NPs’) feature an AP, the head adjective is then inflected for case and number.

For instance, in the elliptic construction in adjNPheadEx1, the adjective ruopsis ‘red’
is marked for singular number and as the object of the verb form bårov ‘I eat’ for accusative case!accusative case. In adjNPheadEx2, the subject NP also lacks an overt nominal head, but features the adjective tjähppis ‘black’ (cf. the example in adjEx1 above), which receives. \ marking.

båråv ruopsisav\\
bårå-v ruopsisa-v\\
eat- 1sg.prs red- acc.sg\\
I eat the red one. 090930a119

tjähppisa lä njallge\\
tjähppis-a lä njallge\\
black- nom.pl be 3pl.prs tasty nom.sg\\
The black ones are tasty. 090930a112

Adjectives in elliptic NPs can be preceded by a demonstrative,
as in adjNPheadEx3.

dat tjábba máhtta sáme gielav\\
d-a-t tjábba máhtta sáme giela-v\\
dem- dist- nom.sg beautiful nom.sg can 3sg.prs Saami gen.sg language- acc.sg\\
That beautiful one can (speak) the Saami language.(referring to a girl) 090930a148

As the host of case case/number number inflection, such adjectives look morphologically like nouns.
However, syntactically, these adjectives remain adjectives for two reasons. First, they can be modified by adverbs adverb of grade, while nouns cannot be. Second, they generally have a referential antecedent that is the bearer of the property they denote. The quantifier aktak ‘none, any’ can be used in an elliptic NP without a referential antecedent; cf. quantifiers, specifically example noneEx3.
Semantically, they do not denote an entity (as nouns do), but a property, as with all adjectives.
A further example is provided in adjNPheadEx4.
Here, the choice of the attributive adjective form tjábba ‘beautiful’ (as opposed to the corresponding predicate adjective form tjábbe) indicates that this is indeed an elliptical NP construction, and not predication.

lä huj tjábba, dat, dat lä jävvja\\
lä huj tjábba d-a-t d-a-t lä jävvja\\
be 3sg.prs quite beautiful nom.sg dem- dist- nom.sg dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.prs white.reindeer nom.sg\\
It is a quite beautiful one, it, it is a white reindeer.(referring to a reindeer) 100405b036-037

adjective!attributive|)
summary: In sufficiently clear discourse contexts, an NP may lack an overt nominal head and be interpreted elliptically, with an adjective serving as the head and inflecting for case and number. Such adjectives can also be preceded by demonstratives, and although they look morphologically noun-like in these constructions, they remain syntactically adjectives because they can be modified by adverbs and usually refer back to an antecedent rather than denoting an entity.

adjective!predicative|(
While attributive adjectives form the head of an attributive AP embedded in an NP phrase!nominal, predicative adjectives form the head of an AP which is the complement!phrasecomplement of the copular verb verb!copular årrot ‘be’ and ascribe a property to the subject referent.

In adjPredEx1 and adjPredEx2, for instance, the predicative adjective corresponding to the attributive adjective tjähppis ‘black’ (cf. the example in adjEx1 above) is tjáhpat.

fáhttsa lä tjáhpat\\

fáhtsa lä tjáhpada\\
fáhtsa lä tjáhpad-a\\
mitten nom.pl be 3pl.prs black- pl\\
The mittens are black. 090930a063

Morphologically, predicative adjectives are much like nouns because they inflect for number number. In fact, many predicative adjectives inflect for number in ways that clearly align with the.. \ inflectional marking of certain noun classes.

The case could be made that they also inflect for case, although they are always in nominative case (cf. copulaClauses on copular clauses).
However, because no paradigmatic opposition to other case forms exists for predicative adjectives (they are only attested in the corpus as a nominative complement!phrasecomplement to a copular clause), I conclude that they only inflect for number.

Nonetheless, these are syntactically adjectives, as they head adjectival phrases and can be modified by adverbs adverb of grade, such as nav ‘so’ as in adjPredEx3.

buhtsu lä nav buojde ja tjábbe\\
buhtsu lä nav buojde ja tjábbe\\
reindeer nom.pl be 3pl.prs so fat pl and beautiful pl\\
The reindeer are so fat and beautiful. 080703014

particularly since noun classes with similar segmental structures exhibit clear number marking strategies. Examples of such predicative adjectives are presented in Table noPredAdjTable.

The variety evident in morphological correlations between the attributive and the predicative forms indicates that there is no regular form-to-function relationship between the attributive and predicative forms. Therefore, on formal grounds, the attributive and predicative forms of these property words are assigned to different, though formally and semantically related, adjectival lexemes, as argued for in the following section ( notePredNounsAdjs ).

adjective!predicative|)
summary: Predicative adjectives in this grammar head an adjectival phrase that functions as the complement of the copular verb *årrot* ‘be’ and predicate a property of the subject. They often inflect for number, sometimes in ways that resemble noun-class marking, but some predicative adjectives do not inflect for number at all; because of this morphological variation and the lack of a consistent form-function relation, the attributive and predicative forms are treated as different but related adjectival lexemes.

section: A note on attributive and predicative adjectives
text:
adjective!attributive adjective!predicative

In the literature on Saami languages, a convention prevails by which predicative adjectives are treated as having more or less derivable attributive forms. Cf., and.
From a historical point of view, this may be reasonable, particularly if there was a point in the history of the Saami languages at which attributive forms were derived by adding -s and selecting the phonologically relevant stem allomorph, and thus the attributive forms were derivable from the predicative forms. For, however, there is no clear or consistent morphological relationship synchronically between attributive adjectives and the corresponding predicative adjectives, as shown above. This is particularly exemplified by the existence of more than one acceptable attributive form, (as pointed out in adjectivesATTR for the attributive adjective forms guhkes guhka ‘long’), as well as by the existence of a number of predicative forms ending in -s, but attributive forms lacking -s (cf. pattern vii above).
Due to cases like those illustrated by subgrouping ix in Table noPredAdjTable, it is not clear that it is sensible to claim that all adjectives have corresponding predicative adjectives that differ at all.
Because of the wide variety of and the inconsistencies in morphological patterns between corresponding attributive and predicative adjectives, it is ultimately more elegant to analyze these two sets of adjectives simply as semantically and etymologically related -- but not morphologically derivable -- adjectives.
summary: The passage says that although Saami adjectives have often been analyzed as if predicative forms underlie derivable attributive forms, this may only be historically plausible. Synchronically, there is no clear or consistent morphological relationship between attributive and predicative adjectives, since some adjectives have multiple acceptable attributive forms, and others show predicative -s forms without a matching attributive -s. The author therefore argues that these two adjective sets are best analyzed as semantically and etymologically related, but not morphologically derivable.

The comparative adjective!comparative and superlative adjective!superlative
forms of attributive and predicative adjectives are derived using suffixes. It seems that, morphosyntactically speaking, comparative and superlative forms can be derived from all adjectives, even when a semantic restriction could lexically prevent such forms from occurring; cf., e.g., guäktegierdakap ‘more pregnant’ ( pit090927pit090927.07m01s).

The singular comparative or superlative predicative form is identical
to the respective comparative or superlative attributive form. However, the plural comparative or superlative predicative form is always marked by a suffix consisting of a single vowel (mostly -a). In many cases, the stem to which comparative and superlative suffixes are attached is identical
to the stem of the positive plural predicative form, but a number of exceptions exist.

Table compSuperlADJsTable provides some example paradigms.
To help illustrate the morphophonemic relationship to positive forms, the singular predicative adjective form is also indicated.
Furthermore, the paradigms are divided into subgroupings (each marked with a Roman numeral) based on suffix allomorph patterns. The third and fifth columns in Table compSuperlADJsTable provide the singular comparative and superlative adjectives (the attributive and predicative singular forms are syncretic), respectively, while the fourth and sixth columns only indicate the suffix used to mark the plural predicative comparative and superlative adjectives, respectively. Note that there are allomorphic alternations in the superlative suffix for subgroupings iii and iv.

Comparative adjective!comparative adjectives are derived in a relatively straightforward way: the suffix -p Note that, in the current working orthography, the comparative suffix -p is written -b- when intervocalic, such as in plural predicative forms.
is added to an adjective root. If the root has a closed final syllable, then an epenthetic vowel -u- is inserted between the root and the suffix. In predicative position, plural is always marked by a suffix consisting of a vowel; in most cases (groups i, ii and iv), the vowel is -a, but sometime it is -o (group iii). It is not clear what determines the choice of plural suffix for comparative forms. While all forms marked by -o in the corpus have a stem final -s, not all forms with a stem final -s are marked by -o (cf. nanos ‘strong’).

The superlative adjective!superlative suffix has four allomorphs. For the attributive and the singular predicative forms, the allomorph -mos is chosen when the root has a closed final syllable, as in groups iii and iv. Roots with an open final syllable have either the superlative suffix allomorph -mus or -jmus; however, it is not clear what drives the selection of these latter two allomorphs.

The allomorph -bmus- occurs whenever the resulting form has an odd number of syllables, as is the case for roots with a final odd syllable in the plural predicative form.
Essentially, the superlative suffix always forms the final foot of a word, and thus is the location for consonant gradation alternations. If a final, odd syllable is present (e.g., for the plural predicative form), then the -bmus- allomorph is chosen. Cf. prosodicDomains on prosodic domains and Cgrad on consonant gradation.

Examples for comparative and superlative adjectives in attributive position can be found in compATTRADJex1 and superlATTRADJex1, respectively. Instances for predicative usage can be found in comparingNPsEx3 and comparingNPsEx5 in comparingNPs.

summary:
Comparative and superlative adjectives are formed with suffixes and can morphosyntactically be derived from all adjectives, even where semantics might normally block them. Singular predicative forms are identical to the singular attributive forms, while plural predicative forms always take an extra vowel suffix, though the stem and suffix allomorphs vary by subgroup and sometimes show irregular patterns.

The comparative is built with -p, with epenthetic -u- inserted after closed final syllables and -b- used intervocalically in the working orthography. The superlative has four allomorphs (-mos, -mus, -jmus, -bmus), chosen partly by syllable structure and prosodic conditions, and comparative/superlative forms can also occur in elliptic noun phrases where they inflect for case and number.

summary: Predicative adjectives are used in copular constructions to compare nominal referents. If the referents are equal in the relevant quality, the comparison uses akta ‘one’ plus the adjective, with the compared NP in the comitative case; if they are unequal, the comparative adjective is used and the reference NP appears in the elative case. Superlative comparison is formed with the superlative predicative adjective, optionally preceded by gajk ‘all’ for emphasis.

The paradigms for the two \ words for ‘small’ provided in Table noPredAdjTable do not sufficiently indicate the restrictions placed on these specific adjectives. The root smáv-, a North Germanic loan word, only modifies plural nouns, while unn-,
the native word, usually only modifies singular nouns.
No other \ adjectives underlie such a restriction; however, the Swedish language contact adjective små (cognate with the source of smáv-) is also restricted to modifying plural nouns. The Swedish adjective stem lite- is used for singular nouns.
Therefore, it seems that this syntactic restriction was probably also borrowed. While a few examples exist in the corpus of unn- modifying a plural noun, smáv- is the preferred item and much more frequent in the corpus.
A corpus search (including elicitation sessions) resulted in 1 token of unn- and 10 tokens of smáv- modifying a plural noun (carried out on 12 th November 2012).
Examples are provided in smallADJex1 through smallADJex4.

jå, månnå aj mujhtav gu liv unna mánátj\\
jå månnå aj mujhta-v gu li-v unna máná-tj\\

Yes, I also remember when I was a small child. 080924632

bena lä unne\\
bena lä unn-e\\

summary:
The passage argues that the two words for “small” have different distributional restrictions: the loanword **smáv-** modifies only plural nouns, while the native **unn-** usually modifies only singular nouns, with no other adjectives showing this kind of restriction. Because Swedish contact adjective **små** is also restricted to plural nouns and **lite-** to singular nouns, the author suggests that this syntactic restriction was likely borrowed.  

Corpus and elicitation data show that **smáv-** is much more frequent with plural nouns than **unn-**, though a few plural examples of **unn-** do occur. In non-elicited corpus tokens, **unn-** appears only with diminutive nouns.

Quantifiers include
edna ‘many, much’, gajk ‘all’, omasse ‘all kinds of’, färt ‘every’, nagin ‘some’, såmes ‘some’, suhta ‘some, several’ and binna ‘a bit, a little’.

summary: Quantifiers in this language are semantically similar to numerals, but formally they are treated as adjectives. In attributive position they normally do not inflect for case or number, though *gajk* ‘all’ can optionally take plural *-a*, and quantifiers in elliptic noun phrases do inflect; the special quantifier *aktak* ‘none, any’ is also analyzed as an adjective for this reason. The passage also notes that at least *edna* ‘many, much’ has a distinct predicative form, *ednak*, showing that attributive and predicative quantifier forms can differ.

demonstrative

Demonstratives
modify a noun phrase by further specifying the head noun concerning the distance of the referent relative to the speaker. Just as with demonstrative pronouns pronoun!demonstrative, the corpus data indicate that there is a three-way distinction between referents close to the speaker (proximal spacial deixis!proximal), those away from the speaker (distal spacial deixis!distal), and those particularly far away (remote spacial deixis!remote).
Indeed, they are identical in form with the demonstrative pronouns listed in Table DemProTable in the section on demonstrative pronouns ( demonstrativePronouns ), and are therefore not listed separately here.
Unlike adjectives, demonstratives always agree with the noun they modify in number number (singular and plural, but not dual) and in case case.

are provided in demonstrativeAdjectivesEx2 through demonstrativeAdjectivesEx3.

text:
numeral|(
Numerals in \ form a closed class and a distinct closed sub-class of adjectives. Syntactically, they are adjectives because they head an adjectival phrase phrase!adjectival; however, morphologically, they differ from other adjectives by never inflecting inflection (neither for number in predicative APs, nor for case case and number number in ellipsis constructions).

Furthermore, numerals do not consist of attributive/predicative sets differing in form.
Instead, numerals are consistent in form, regardless of being in attributive or predicative position.

\ numerals form a decimal system consisting of the basic numerals for the numbers one through ten, hundred and thousand. All other numerals are compounds based on these basic terms, with the exception of nolla ‘zero’. Basic and complex numerals are dealt with in basicNums and complexNums, respectively; the derivation of ordinal numeral!ordinal numerals is described in ordinalNums.
summary: Numerals form a closed subclass of adjectives: syntactically they head adjectival phrases, but morphologically they do not inflect, unlike other adjectives. They also have the same form in both attributive and predicative positions. The numeral system is decimal, built from the basic numerals one through ten, hundred, and thousand, with all other numerals formed as compounds except *nolla* ‘zero’.

text:
The basic numerals for the numbers one through ten in \ are reconstructable native Saamic numerals, and tjuohte ‘hundred’ is at least from Proto-Saami. indicates that tjuohte ‘hundred’ was originally a borrowing from Proto-Indo-European into Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Finno-Saamic.
The numerals nolla ‘zero’ and tuvsan ‘thousand’ are likely more recent borrowings, although it is not entirely clear whether they are from North Germanic or
Finnic. The entries for the numerals ‘zero’ and ‘thousand’ in only provide etymologies for North Saami and Inari Saami; however, while Finnic is clearly a contact language for these two languages, North Germanic is a contact language for, and therefore also a potential source for these two numerals; cf. Swedish language contact nolla ‘zero’ and tusen ‘thousand’.

These basic cardinal numerals are listed on the left side of Table basicNumsTable.
summary: The passage says that the Saamic numerals for one through ten are reconstructable as native Saamic forms, and that *tjuohte* ‘hundred’ is at least Proto-Saami, though it was originally borrowed from Proto-Indo-European into Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Finno-Saamic. It also notes that *nolla* ‘zero’ and *tuvsan* ‘thousand* are likely later borrowings, probably from either North Germanic or Finnic, with the evidence especially relevant for North Saami and Inari Saami.

subsubsection: Derivation and suppletion in ordinal numerals
text:
derivation!numeral
In general, ordinal numeral!ordinal numerals, which are listed on the right side of Table basicNumsTable, can be derived derivation from the corresponding cardinal numeral by replacing the vowel in V2 position and any final consonant with the suffix -át (and its allomorph -et in giehtjet ‘seventh’). In addition, the weak stem allomorph is selected and umlaut of V1 occurs, if applicable (cf. morphophonology on stem allomorphy).
The ordinal numerals corresponding to tjuohte ‘hundred’ and tuvsan ‘thousand’ are not attested in the corpus.

However, there are exceptions. First, the ordinals vuostas ‘first’ and mubbe ‘second’ are suppletive forms compared to the corresponding cardinal numerals akkta ‘one’ and guäkte ‘two’. Note that vuostas ‘first’ and mubbe ‘second’ are also reconstructable to at least Proto-Saami.
These two ordinals are used exclusively for the single-digit numbers ‘first’ and ‘second’; any ordinal numeral referring to a number of two or more digits uses a form derived from the cardinal numeral, as described above. This is illustrated in Table firstSecondOrdinals.

Second, the cardinal numeral giehtjav ‘seven’ differs in the final two segments from the ordinal numeral gietjet ‘seventh’ (i.e., -av and -et).
summary: Ordinal numerals are generally formed from the corresponding cardinal numeral by replacing the vowel in V2 and any final consonant with the suffix -át, or -et in *giehtjet* ‘seventh’, with weak-stem allomorphy and umlaut of V1 when relevant. However, *vuostas* ‘first’ and *mubbe* ‘second’ are suppletive forms rather than derivatives of *akkta* ‘one’ and *guäkte* ‘two*, and they are used only for single-digit ordinals; ordinals for numbers of two or more digits follow the regular pattern. The forms for *tjuohte* ‘hundred’ and *tuvsan* ‘thousand’ are not attested, and *giehtjav* ‘seven’ and *gietjet* ‘seventh’ differ in their final two segments.

text:
Any numerals other than those listed in Table basicNumsTable are complex numerals formed by combining the basic numerals.
Multiples of ten are composed of the relevant cardinal numeral followed by lågev ‘ten’; examples are provided in Figure multiplesTen.

Note that lågev is often shortened to låk in fast speech, as in complexNumEx1.

… gokt lij dánne giehtjavlåk jage maŋŋus\\
gokt li-j dánne giehtjav-låk jage maŋŋus\\
how be- 3sg.pst here seven-ten year nom.pl ago\\
… how it was here seventy years ago. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a001

There are two ways to compose two-digit numerals that are not multiples of ten.
One method appends the relevant numeral representing the ‘ones-digit’ to the multiple of ten, while lågev ‘ten’ is shortened to låk.
This is illustrated in Figure twoDigitNumsA,
with examples of two-digit numerals from the corpus presented in complexNumEx2 and complexNumEx3.

sån lä gakktselåkgiehtjav jage\\
sån lä gakktse-låk-giehtjav jage\\
3sg.nom be 3sg.prs eight-ten-seven year nom.pl\\
She is eighty-seven years old. 100310b146

dä lij del tjuojgadam ja gåddam nälljalåkgakktse stalpe sájtejna\\
dä li-j del tjuojgada-m ja gådda-m nällja-låk-gakktse stalpe sájte-jna\\
then be- 3sg.pst then ski- prf and slay- prf four-ten-eight wolf gen.pl spear- com.sg \\
Then he skied and slew forty-eight wolves with a spear. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a088-089

Alternatively, complex numerals may be formed phrasally. According to this strategy, the ‘ones-digit’ precedes a postpositional phrase headed by the postposition nanne Note that nanne is often shortened to nan in rapid speech.
‘on’ with the multiple of ten as the dependent låge (in gen.sg case), as illustrated in Figure twoDigitNumsB.
However, this latter method was only attested in elicitation sessions with one consultant, and is not found in non-elicited data from the corpus.

Native ordinal numerals referring to numbers between ten and one hundred are only attested in the corpus in elicitation sessions, and speakers are quite inconsistent and unsure about them.
The same is true for cardinal numerals larger than one hundred.
The only example in the corpus for a numeral larger than one thousand is not native, but a Swedish language contact borrowing (in an NP with \ case and number marking); this is provided in complexNumEx4. With the exception of the case/number suffix -n, the entire phrase nittonhundratalan ‘in the nineteen-hundreds’ in complexNumEx4 is borrowed from Swedish nittonhundratalet ‘the nineteen-hundreds’.

nittonhundratálan álgon ja dä viesoj\\
nitton-hundra-tála-n álgo-n ja dä vieso-j\\
nineteen-hundred-century- iness.sg beginning- iness.sg and then live- 3sg.pst\\
He lived in the nineteen-hundreds, at the beginning. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a070-072
summary:
Numerals not listed in the basic table are formed by combining basic numerals. Multiples of ten use the relevant cardinal numeral followed by lågev ‘ten’ (often shortened to låk in fast speech), and two-digit numerals can be built either by attaching the ones digit to this ten-form or, less commonly and only in elicitation data, by using a phrasal construction with nanne ‘on’.  

Ordinals between ten and one hundred, as well as cardinals above one hundred, are only poorly attested and speakers are inconsistent about them. The only numeral over one thousand in the corpus is a Swedish borrowing, with only the case/number suffix native.

However, there are two exceptions: the numeral *akta* ‘one’ inflects for case when modifying a noun or standing alone elliptically, and the ordinal *vuostas* ‘first’ can appear in a superlative form, *vuostamos*, meaning ‘the very first.’

text:
verb|( verb!aspect|see aspect verb!tense|see tense verb!mood|see mood verb!valency|see valency
Verbs in Pite Saami form an open class of words which are defined syntactically by their ability to head a verb complex phrase!verb complex, as well as morphologically by inflecting for person, number, tense and mood.
Verbs consist of a stem which is followed by a class marker and an inflectional suffix or suffixes,
as illustrated in verbStructure.

∑ \ class-marker \ mood/tense/person/number

Verb stems can have up to five allomorphic forms throughout the verbal para\-digm due to a complex combination of morphophonological morphophonology alternations.
Verbs form at least five inflectional classes.
The inflectional suffixes are exponents for person, number, tense and/or mood.
\ distinguishes three number categories (singular, dual and plural), two tense categories (present and past) and the three modal categories (indicative, imperative and potential).

The first sections of this chapter ( inflectionalCatsVerbs on the inflectional categories number, tense and mood; nonFiniteVerbforms on non-finite forms and periphrastically marked categories of future, aspect and negation; passiveVinflection on passive voice) provide a description of relevant morphological categories as a background for the discussion of morphological marking strategies for verbs in markingVerbs. Finally, verbInflectionalClasses draws on the initial sections to posit inflectional classes for verbs.
summary:
Pite Saami verbs are an open class defined both syntactically, by heading a verb complex, and morphologically, by inflecting for person, number, tense, and mood. A verb consists of a stem plus a class marker and inflectional suffixes, and stems may have up to five allomorphic forms across the paradigm because of morphophonological alternations.  

The language distinguishes singular, dual, and plural; present and past; and indicative, imperative, and potential, and verbs fall into at least five inflectional classes. The chapter sections introduce these categories, as well as non-finite forms and periphrastic marking of future, aspect, negation, and passive voice, before discussing verbal marking strategies and inflectional classes.

text:
All finite verbs agree in number number with the subject of the clause and inflect inflection!verbal for singular, dual or plural.
Finite verbs in the indicative and the potential mood mood also agree in person person.
Inflectional morphology is present even if the subject of the clause is not overt.
For instance, in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx1, the finite verbs minne and gillge both agree with da, the 3 \ subject; in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx2, the finite verb lijmen agrees with the 1 \ subject månnå ja Jåssjå.

ja dä da tjåhken minne gu gillge gåddålit nagan juhtusav\\
ja dä d-a tjåhken minne gu gillge gåddåli-t nagan juhtusa-v\\
and then dem- dist nom.pl together go 3pl.prs when will 3pl.prs kill- inf some animal- acc.sg\\
And then they go together when they are going to kill some animal. 080703047-048

månnå ja Jåssjå lijmen ulgon sirijd tjåggemin\\
månnå ja Jåssjå li-jmen ulgon siri-jd tjågge-min\\
1sg.nom and Josh nom.sg be- 1du.pst outside blueberry- acc.pl pick- prog\\
Josh and I were picking blueberries outside. 100310b032

Note that there are a few examples in the corpus in which speakers do not consistently inflect for dual number!dual, but instead use the corresponding plural form.

The imperative mood!imperative is not marked for person person, but distinguishes the three number categories singular, dual and plural.
For example, in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx3 the finite verb tjaske is inflected for the implied (2 nd person) singular subject.

tjaske munje sobev\\
tjaske munje sobe-v\\
throw sg.imp 1sg.ill pole- acc.sg\\
Throw a ski-pole to me! 100404206
summary: Finite verbs agree in number with the subject and are inflected for singular, dual, or plural; in the indicative and potential moods, they also agree in person. This inflectional marking appears even when the subject is not overt, though the corpus contains some cases where speakers use plural forms instead of dual. The imperative does not mark person, but it distinguishes singular, dual, and plural, as shown by forms with an implied second-person subject.

text:
tense
For indicative clauses, verbs can inflect inflection!verbal for present tense!present tense, as in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx1, or tense!pastpast, as in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx2 above.
Verbs marked for present tense generally signify that a situation is true in the present, as in presentEx1 below, or they express general truths, as in example inflectionalCatsVerbsEx1 above (which indicates a general truth about wolves’ behavior). However, present tense can also be used to indicate historical present, as in presentEx2, or planned future situations, as in presentEx3. It is therefore not strictly a present tense!present tense and could be considered non-past.
Nonetheless, the glossing standard ‘ ’ is chosen to mark this, as it covers the most common function.

dale lä bar bievadak mij sudda muahtagav\\
dale lä bar bievadak mij sudda muahtaga-v\\
now be 3sg.prs only sunshine nom.sg which nom.sg melt 3sg.prs snow- acc.sg\\
Now it’s only the sun which melts the snow. 100405a036

tjävlav valdav ja dä tjanáv virbmev dan tjävvlaj ja hålåv raddnaj…\\
tjävla-v valda-v ja dä tjaná-v virbme-v d-a-n tjävvla-j ja hålå-v raddna-j\\
bobber- acc.sg take- 1sg.prs and then tie- 1sg.prs net- acc.sg dem- dist-? ill.sg bobber- ill.sg and say- 1sg.prs friend- ill.sg\\
I take the bobber and then I tie the net to that bobber and I say to my friend… 090702029

ja dä maŋŋel dä vuolga Västeråsaj\\
ja dä maŋŋel dä vuolga Västeråsa-j\\
and then after.that then drive 2sg.prs Västerås- ill.sg\\
And then after that you’ll drive to Västerås. 080924677

In the example in presentEx2, it is not clear why the demonstrative dan is used, as this resembles either the genitive or the inessive demonstratives, but not the expected illative demonstrative dasa. Perhaps it is simply an error in natural speech.
summary: In indicative clauses, verbs may inflect for present or past tense. Present tense typically refers to present situations or general truths, but it can also be used for historical present and planned future events, so it is not strictly limited to the present and could be considered non-past.

text:
mood|(
\ has three moods: indicative, imperative and potential. Indicative mood is by far the most common mood and is considered the default, unmarked mood, as it is not overtly expressed morphologically, as in the examples in tense above.
The following two sections deal with imperative and potential mood.
summary: The language has three moods: indicative, imperative, and potential. Indicative is by far the most common and functions as the default, unmarked mood, since it is not overtly marked morphologically. The next sections discuss imperative and potential mood.

text:
mood!imperative|(
Verbs inflectedisinflection!verbal for imperative mood indicate that the speaker is instructing or commanding the addressee to carry out the action referred to by the verb; the implied subject is always 2 nd person. Verbs in the imperative are not marked for person, but do inflect for number number (singular, dual and plural), as in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx3 above as well as in imperativeEx1 and imperativeEx2 below; see Table verbSuffixes in inflectionalSuffVerbs for the imperative number suffixes.

nå, giehto naginav dan Luoddauvre birra\\
nå giehto nagina-v d-a-n Luoddauvre birra\\
well tell sg.imp something- acc.sg dem- dist- gen.sg Luoddauvre gen.sg about\\
Well, say something about this ‘Luoddauvre’! 080924314

dáhken dal dav\\
dáhke-n dal d-a-v\\
do- du.imp now dem- dist- acc.sg\\
Do that now! 101208188

The example in imperativeEx3 below indicates that imperative can also be used as a kind performative speech-act.

gijtov ednet\\
gijtov edne-t\\
thank- acc.sg have- pl.imp\\
Thank you all!(lit.: have thank) 101208290

Note that includes a second imperative category in his verb paradigms that inflects for all three person categories and is marked by a stem-final -u-; Lehtiranta terms this ‘imperative II’. mentions ‘imperative II’ in passing as well, explaining that it is “less severe and more like a wish” (my translation), but Lagercrantz only includes examples for 2.
The \ corpus does not have any tokens of such verbs, so more study is needed to determine their current status.
mood!imperative|)
summary:
Verbs inflected for imperative mood express commands or instructions directed to a second-person addressee. They are not marked for person, but they do inflect for number (singular, dual, and plural), and the imperative can also function as a performative speech act, as in “Thank you all!”

The passage also notes a second imperative category, “imperative II,” described by Lehtiranta as less forceful and more like a wish, but this form is not found in the corpus. Further study is needed to determine its current status.

text:
mood!potential|(
Verbs can also be inflected for potential mood, indicating that the action referred to by the verb is likely to happen. Verbs in the potential mood are marked by a linearly segmentable morpheme -tj- followed by a person person/number number suffix. Cf. potClauses for syntactic aspects of clauses in the potential mood.
Examples are provided in potentialEx1 through potentialEx3.

nå hålåv, vuolgetjip del\\
nå hålå-v vuolge-tji-p del\\
well say- 1sg.prs go- pot- 1pl obviously\\
Well then I say we should obviously go. 090702013

nä, virtitjav nuollat\\
nä virti-tja-v nuolla-t\\
no must- pot- 1sg undress- inf\\
Oh no, I’ll probably have to take off some clothes. 090519029

ikeb dat vuosjatja káfav\\
ikeb d-a-t vuosja-tj-a káfa-v\\
maybe dem- dist- nom.sg prepare.coffee- pot- 3sg coffee- acc.sg\\
Perhaps he’ll make some coffee. 110404270

As the examples in potentialEx4 and potentialEx5 illustrate, the potential mood can be used as a friendly request.

vuosjatja káfav\\
vuosja-tj-a káfa-v\\
prepare.coffee- pot- 2sg coffee- acc.sg\\
Perhaps you could make some coffee. 110404267

gulatja dav mav mån hålåv\\
gula-tj-a d-a-v ma-v mån hålå-v\\
hear- pot- 2sg dem- dist- acc.sg rel- acc.sg 1sg.nom say- 1sg.prs\\
Please hear what I am saying! 110404056

The person/number suffixesisinflection!verbal for potential mood!potential mood are homophonous
with those used in present tense!present tense for Class V verbs (cf. VclassV ); cf. POTinflection for a discussion of the status of verbs in the potential mood as inflectional and derivational forms.
mood!potential|) mood|)
summary: Verbs can be inflected for potential mood to indicate that an action is likely to happen, and this mood is marked by the segmentable morpheme **-tj-** followed by a person/number suffix. The potential mood can express prediction or likelihood, as well as a friendly request. The text also notes that the person/number suffixes in the potential mood are homophonous with present tense suffixes in Class V verbs.

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
verb!non-finite|(
A number of non-finite verb forms exist in. The most common of these are the infinitive, connegative, perfect and progressive forms. Each of these non-finite verb forms can co-occur with an auxiliary verb to periphrastically express the verbal categories of future tense tense!future, perfect or progressive aspect aspect, and negation negation; these categories are described in futureTense, aspect and negationVerb, respectively.
Syntactic aspects of clauses involving these non-finite forms are described in multiVdeclarativeClauses on declarative clauses with more than one verb form, as well as in clausalSubordination on clausal subordination.
Table nonFiniteVTable summarizes the morphological and syntactic features of these four non-finite forms, while examples of verbs in these forms are provided in Table nonFiniteVTableExs.

The literature on Saami languages often treats non-finite verb forms in addition to those mentioned above. These include the verb genitive, verb abessive or gerunds, for instance. Cf. and for North Saami, or for Lule Saami.
For, describes the morphological form a number of such non-finite forms, These non-finite forms are also included in the verb paradigms in.
while does not describe such verb forms.

With this in mind, it is certainly plausible that \ has other non-finite verb forms other than those mentioned here. However, there is no evidence of such forms in the present corpus.
Ultimately, the morphological and syntactic behavior of other non-finite verb forms must be left for future study.
verb!non-finite|)
summary:
The passage says that the most common non-finite verb forms are the infinitive, connegative, perfect, and progressive, and that these forms can combine with auxiliaries to express future tense, perfect or progressive aspect, and negation. It also notes that clauses with these forms are discussed elsewhere in relation to multi-verb declarative clauses and clausal subordination.  

The text adds that Saami-language literature sometimes includes other non-finite forms such as verb genitive, verb abessive, or gerunds, but although such forms may plausibly exist, there is no evidence for them in the present corpus, so their behavior is left for future study.

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
tense!future
The verb gallgat ‘will’ plus the infinitive form of the lexical verb can together express a future activity. The examples in futureTenseEx1 through futureTenseEx3 illustrate this.

nå gukte galga dåhkå ållit dajna\\
nå gukte galga dåhkå ålli-t d-a-jna\\
well how will 2sg.prs to.there reach- inf dem- dist- com.sg\\
Well how are you going to reach it with that? 080909052

dä galgav mån gähttot\\
dä galga-v mån gähtto-t\\
then will- 1sg.prs 1sg.nom tell- inf\\
Then I will tell a story. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a115

man ednag biejve galga danne årrot?\\
man ednag biejve galga danne årro-t\\
how many day nom.pl will 2sg.prs there be- inf\\
How many days are you going to be there? 080924658

Note that, as mentioned in tense above, the present tense!present tense is also used to express planned future events.
summary: The future can be expressed with **galgat** ‘will’ plus the **infinitive** of the lexical verb, as shown in examples meaning ‘be going to reach,’ ‘will tell,’ and ‘are you going to be.’ The passage also notes that the **present tense** can be used to refer to **planned future events**.

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
aspect
\ features two aspects, perfect and progressive, as described in perfectAspect and progressiveAspect below. Both aspects are formed periphrastically using a combination of the auxiliary verb årrot ‘be’ and the relevant non-finite verb form.
See also auxV on the syntactic structure of clauses with perfective and progressive verbs.
summary: The passage states that the language has two aspects, perfect and progressive. Both are formed periphrastically with the auxiliary verb **årrot** ‘be’ plus the appropriate non-finite verb form, and the syntax of clauses with these forms is discussed elsewhere.

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
aspect!perfect
The perfect verb form is marked by the suffix -m (glossed as ); the verb stem is in the strong grade when consonant gradation consonant gradation is relevant. Verbs in the perfect generally indicate that an action in the past still has relevancy in the present situation. For instance, in perfectEx1 the speaker is slaughtering a reindeer, and is now able to cut out the stomach because the esophagus has been tied in a knot, preventing the stomach’s contents from running out.

men mån lev tjåjvev ruhtastemin ullgus, tjådågov lev tjadnam tjieboten\\
men mån le-v tjåjve-v ruhtaste-min ullgus tjådågo-v le-v tjadna-m tjiebote-n\\
but 1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs stomach- acc.sg cut- prog out esophagus- acc.sg be- 1sg.prs knot- prf neck- iness.sg\\
But I am cutting out the stomach, I have knotted the esophagus in the neck. 080909054-055

In perfectEx2, the speaker indicates that one can dip potatoes in fish fat only after one has fried the fat, thus melting it.

gu lä dav bassam, dä máhta pironijd budnjut\\
gu lä d-a-v bassa-m dä máhta pironi-jd budnju-t\\
when be 2sg.prs dem- dist acc.sg fry- prf then can 2sg.prs potato- acc.pl dip- inf\\
Once you have fried it, you can dip potatoes (in it). 090702088

Finally, in perfectEx3, the perfect form of the verb jábmet ‘die’ is used to mark the state of being dead resulting from the event of dying as opposed to the present state of being alive.

da lä jábmam, ber muv äddne'l viessomin dále\\
d-a lä jábma-m ber muv äddne=l viesso-min dále\\
dem- dist nom.pl be 3pl.prs die- prf only 1sg.gen mother nom.sg=be 3sg.prs live- prog now\\
They have died, only my mother is still living now. 100310b145
summary: The perfect verb form is marked by the suffix **-m**, with the verb stem appearing in the strong grade when consonant gradation applies. It typically expresses that a past action remains relevant in the present situation, as shown by examples where a completed action enables a current action or where dying is presented as the resulting state of being dead rather than being alive.

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
aspect!progressive
Verbs in the progressive indicate that an activity is ongoing. The progressive verb form is marked by the suffix -min (glossed as ) appended to the verb stem, which is in the strong grade when consonant gradation is relevant.
In perfectEx1 above, the speaker uses the progressive form rhtastemin because he is in the middle of cutting out the stomach as he utters the sentence. In perfectEx3, the speaker’s mother is still living, as opposed to the deceased.
The action expressed by a progressive verb does not have to be simultaneous with the moment of the utterance, but can be past tense, as shown by the
example in inflectionalCatsVerbsEx2b.
Here, the speaker is describing a picture which was taken while picking blueberries.

månnå ja Jåssjå, lijmen ulgon sirijd tjåggemin\\
månnå ja Jåssjå li-jmen ulgon siri-jd tjågge-min\\
1sg.nom and Josh nom.sg be- 1du.pst outside blueberry- acc.pl pick- prog\\
Josh and I were picking blueberries outside. 100310b032
summary: The progressive aspect indicates that an activity is ongoing and is marked by the suffix **-min** attached to the verb stem, which appears in the strong grade when consonant gradation applies. The text notes that progressive forms can describe actions occurring at the time of speech or in the past, as in an example where the speaker says “Josh and I were picking blueberries outside” while describing a picture.

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
The progressive aspect!progressive form of a verb can also be used in an adverbial phrase!adverbial function. For instance, tjájbmamin ‘laughing’ in ADVverbsEx1 and gullamin ‘listening‘ in ADVverbsEx2 are each used as a modal adverbial to indicate a simultaneous activity.

tjájbmamin vádtsa\\
tjájbma-min vádtsa\\
laugh- prog go 3sg.prs\\
She walks while laughing. 11052229m10s

gullamin mån tjálav\\
gulla-min mån tjála-v\\
listen- prog 1sg.nom write- 1sg.prs\\
I write while listening. 110404089
summary: The progressive form of a verb can be used adverbially, where it functions as a modal adverbial to express a simultaneous activity. The examples show tjájbmamin ‘laughing’ and gullamin ‘listening’ used to mean “while laughing” and “while listening.”

section: Non-finite verb forms and periphrastically marked verbal categories
text:
negation
Negation in \ is expressed periphrastically by a finite negation verb and a non-finite verb form. The inflectionalisinflection!verbal behavior of the negation verb is presented in theNegationVerb, while syntactic aspects of negation in \ are covered in more detail in negation; however, a brief description of negation is provided here.

As with any finite verb, the negation verb agrees in person person and number number with the subject of the sentence and inflects for tense tense or mood mood. The complement!phrasecomplement verb occurs in a special non-finite verb form called the connegative verb!non-finite!connegative (glossed as ), which is in the weak grade (when gradation is relevant) and otherwise lacks any additional morphological marking. Examples for present tense!present and past tense!past indicative as well as imperative mood!imperative forms are provided in connegEx1 through negImpEx1.

mån iv vasja lipsusijd ja daggarijd válldet dán muddon\\
mån i-v vasja lipsusi-jd ja daggari-jd vállde-t d-á-n muddo-n\\
1sg.nom neg- 1sg.prs feel.like conneg rumen.fat- acc.pl and such- acc.pl take- inf dem- prox- iness.sg time- iness.sg\\

The data from the corpus concerning passive verbs are quite limited, but indicates that passive verbs can be finite verbs inflecting for tense, person and number, as in passEx4, or non-finite forms, such as the perfect, as in passEx1a and passEx1b. However, due to a lack of data, it is not clear whether passives can be used for progressive aspect, or inflect for either imperative mood!imperative or potential mood!potential mood.

That being said, these examples do make clear that the passive marker is restricted to lexical verbs.
