summary:
The passage explains that passive verbs are derived from other verbs with the suffix -duvv, followed by the class-marking vowel for Class IV verbs. Corpus examples show both finite passive forms inflected for tense, person, and number, and non-finite perfect forms, but the data are too limited to determine whether passives can occur with progressive, imperative, or potential forms.

It also states that the passive marker is restricted to lexical verbs, so passives are treated as valency-decreasing derivations rather than part of inflectional paradigms.

text:
inflection!verbal
As shown in inflectionalCatsVerbs above, finite verbs can be marked for four inflectional categories:
itemize
agreement in person with the subject
agreement in number with the subject
tense
mood
itemize
Just as with nouns, inflectional categories for verbs can be expressed by suffixes and by non-linear morphology, and frequently a combination of both. In the following, inflectionalSuffVerbs focusses on inflectional suffixes, while nonLinearMorphVerbs goes on to describe the behavior of non-linear morphology found in stem-consonant alternations (consonant gradation), stem-vowel alternations (umlaut),
and vowel harmony. The final section ( verbInflectionalClasses ) then uses the various morphophonological inflectional patterns found across verb paradigms to posit five preliminary inflectional classes for verbs.

[1] 1x80pt#1
summary: Finite verbs can be marked for four inflectional categories: agreement with the subject in person and number, tense, and mood. These categories may be realized through suffixes, non-linear morphology, or both; the passage then distinguishes suffixal inflection from non-linear processes such as consonant gradation, umlaut, and vowel harmony, and says these patterns are used to propose five preliminary verb inflectional classes.

text:
inflection!verbal verb!inflectional class|(
The portmanteau suffix!portmanteau suffixes expressing agreement in person person and number number as well as tense tense or mood mood in finite verbs are listed in Table verbSuffixes.
In this table, if only one suffix is given in a slot, then it is found in all inflectional classes. When more than one suffix is included in a slot, then the first allomorph is for inflectional classes I, II and III, the second allomorph for class IV, and the third allomorph for class V verbs.

The suffixes for the non-finite verb!non-finite infinitive, connegative verb!non-finite!connegative and perfect aspect!perfect verb forms are included here and in the following sections because they are common verb forms in the corpus and particularly useful in recognizing patterns in verb paradigms.
summary: Finite verbs use portmanteau suffixes that express person and number agreement together with tense or mood. In the suffix table, a single suffix applies across all inflectional classes, while multiple suffixes indicate class-specific allomorphs: the first for classes I–III, the second for class IV, and the third for class V. The non-finite infinitive, connegative, and perfect forms are also included because they are frequent in the corpus and helpful for identifying verb-paradigm patterns.

text:
suffix!verbal inflection!verbal
Several of the verbal inflectional suffixes, considered by themselves, are homophonous:
itemize
-v for 1sg.prs and 1sg.pst in classes I, II and III
-n for 1du.prs, 3pl.pst in all classes, and also du.imp in classes I, II and III
-t for inf and pl.imp in classes I, II and III
no suffix for 2sg.prs, sg.imp and conneg in all classes; 3sg.prs, 3pl.prs in classes I, II, III and V; and 2sg.pst in classes I, II and III

itemize

Despite these similarities, only the morphology of 1du.prs and 3pl.pst verb forms is syncretic in all verb classes because in most cases homophonous suffixes combine with different non-linear morphology and/or with different class marking suffixes.
summary: Several verbal inflectional suffixes are homophonous across classes: for example, -v marks both 1sg present and 1sg past in classes I–III, -n marks 1du present, 3pl past, and also dual imperative in classes I–III, while -t marks infinitive and plural imperative in classes I–III. However, only 1du present and 3pl past are truly syncretic in all verb classes, because in the other cases the identical suffixes occur with different non-linear morphology and/or class-marking suffixes.

text:
morphology!non-linear
In addition to using the inflection!verbalinflectional suffixes described above, inflectional inflection categories for verbs can be marked
by one or more of the following stem allomorphy strategies:
itemize
stem consonant alternations (consonant gradation consonant gradation)
V1 vowel alternations (umlaut umlaut)
V1 vowel raising when followed by a close/close-mid V2 vowel (vowel harmony vowel harmony)

itemize
Because 2sg.prs, 3sg.prs, 3pl.prs, 2sg.pst, 3sg.pst, sg.imp and conneg forms often lack suffixes (cf. verbalSuffixesSyncretism above), verbs in these inflectional categories are typically marked exclusively by these essentially non-linear morphological marking strategies.
To illustrate this, the inflection!verbalinflectional paradigm for the verb buälldet ‘ignite, burn’ is provided in Table verbBurn and described here.

[1] 1x90pt#1

Note that the vowel in V2 position ( a, e and i) in all forms is the inflectional class marker for Class III verbs (cf. VclassIII ); thus the stem has five allomorphs: buälld-, bualld-, buold-, bulld- and buld-. The examples used in this description of non-linear verb morphology is based on the current \ orthography, which is still a work in progress. Because the orthography is to a great extent phonemic, orthographic representations are sufficient for the current discussion.

This reflects a consonant gradation pattern that alternates between strong lld and weak ld, and an umlaut pattern that alternates between ua/uä and uo in the vowel in V1 position. Note that ua and uä are allophones of /ua/; cf. Vua.
Furthermore, the forms for 1du.prs, 3pl.prs and all past tense!past forms are subject to vowel harmony; here, the vowel in V1 position is raised to u in the presence of a close-mid front ( e) or a close front ( i) vowel in V2 position. Note, however, that this vowel harmony is morphologically selected by these slots in the paradigms; the e in V2 in other inflected forms does not trigger vowel harmony (cf. 2du.prs or du.imp forms).

In summary, the inflectional paradigm for buälldet ‘ignite, burn’ is characterized by consonant gradation, umlaut and vowel harmony in the stem, and the morphological environment determines which of these allomorphs is selected.
For instance, as a result, the 1sg.prs form buoldav is marked for person, number and tense/mood by the weak buold- stem (with the -uo- umlaut form) and the -v suffix simultaneously, and the 1pl.pst form buldijmä is marked by the weak buld- stem subjected to vowel harmony, and the -jmä suffix.

The pattern of non-linear inflectional inflection!verbal marking throughout the paradigm for buälldet is illustrated in Table burnParadigmPattern.
The patterns for both consonant gradation and for umlaut in verb classes subject to these morphophonological strategies align seamlessly.
However, each of the two verbal inflection classes subject to vowel harmony has its own unique vowel harmony pattern.

Not every verb undergoes consonant gradation consonant gradation and/or umlaut umlaut; instead, their presence are determined by the phonological form of a verb. Consonant gradation is described in detail in Cgrad and umlaut in umlaut.
Some examples of verbs with umlaut alternations and consonant gradation are shown in Table umlautPatternsVerbs below and Table CGpatternsVerbs, respectively. Note that ua and uä are allophones of /ua/; cf. Vua.
summary:
The passage explains that, besides suffixes, verbal inflectional categories may be marked by non-linear stem alternations such as consonant gradation, vowel alternation (umlaut), and vowel raising due to vowel harmony. It illustrates this with the verb *buälldet* ‘ignite, burn’, whose paradigm shows multiple stem allomorphs selected by specific inflectional slots, while some forms are marked by both stem alternation and suffixes.

It also notes that consonant gradation and umlaut follow regular patterns across relevant verb classes, but vowel harmony has distinct patterns in the two classes that exhibit it. Not all verbs show these alternations; their occurrence depends on the phonological form of the verb.

text:
Vowel harmony vowel harmony in verb forms refers to a regressive assimilation assimilation of place of articulation between the two vowels of the final foot in a word. Specifically the raising of the vowel in V1 position triggered by the presence in specific, class-dependent paradigmatic slots of a close-mid /e/ (orthographic e) or a close front /i/ (orthographic i) vowel in V2 position.
There are six attested vowel harmony patterns in the V1 vowel of a verb stem from Class II or Class III, as illustrated by Table VHPatternsVerbs.

The data from the corpus indicate that Class I and Class IV verbs do not exhibit vowel harmony, but there are no tokens of Class I or Class IV verbs with one of the vowels listed in Table VHPatternsVerbs in V1 position. Consequently, the data must be considered inconclusive in this respect. On the other hand, it is quite evident that Class V verbs are not affected by vowel harmony because the V2 vowel in Class V verbs is never subject to the allomorphic alternations which trigger vowel harmony in the V1 vowel.

It is not clear why á and a have different vowel harmony alternations ( i/ ä and i/ e, respectively, as illustrated by the first four examples in Table VHPatternsVerbs ); these alternation patterns do not align with verb classes.
Further research is needed to come to a better understanding of this vowel harmony.
summary: Vowel harmony in these verb forms is described as a regressive assimilation in which a vowel in V1 is raised by a class-dependent /e/ or /i/ in V2 within the final foot of a word. Six vowel-harmony patterns are attested in Class II and III verb stems, while Class V verbs clearly do not participate because their V2 vowels never undergo the alternations that trigger harmony. Evidence for Class I and IV verbs is inconclusive, and the different alternations of á and a do not appear to align with verb classes, so further research is needed.

subsection: The potential mood: inflection or derivation?
text:
mood!potential inflection!verbal
The potential mood Cf. POTmood for a general description, including examples, of the potential mood.
is not attested very often in the corpus, particularly outside elicitation settings,
and was not considered in most elicitation sessions focussing on verb paradigms. As a result, the amount of data from the corpus available to inform a description of the inflectional inflection behavior of the potential forms are quite limited. Nonetheless, the paradigm for the potential forms of the verb gullat ‘hear’ is provided in Table hearPOTforms.
[1] 1x80pt#1

Taking the potential forms presented in the verb paradigms in and in the examples in into consideration, the paradigm of class marking suffixes and person/number suffixes used for potential verb forms is presented in Table POTinflections.
The stem allomorph of the verb is in the weak stage, when applicable.

In the literature on Saami languages, potential mood is normally treated as an inflectional category, Cf., e.g.,,, and.
and, for this reason as well as due to its seeming opposition to imperative mood!imperative or tense-marked forms, is treated as such in the present study.

However, three morphosyntactic aspects of potential mood verb forms make its classification as an inflectional category potentially questionable.
First, verbs in the potential mood feature a segmentally separable marker ( -tj-), rather than being part of a portmanteau morpheme simultaneously indicating mood/tense, number and normally person as is the case for other tenses and moods.
Second, the stem allomorph chosen in all potential forms is consistently the weak form consonant gradation!weak grade, which is quite consistent with the morphosyntactic behavior of other derived verbs which consistently have a specific consonant gradation consonant gradation type, while the mood and tense paradigms for non-derived verbs contain both strong and weak stem allomorphs.
Finally, it is striking that the potential mood class marking suffixes and person/number suffixes (listed in Table POTinflections) are homophonous with the class marking and present tense!present tense person/number suffixes for Class V verbs (cf. Table speakParadigm). Note that 3sg potential forms in
do not have a class marker or person/number suffix. This deviates from the 3sg. \ forms of Class V verbs (even though mentions that the potential forms are inflected in the same way as indicative present tense!present forms). On the other hand, all instances of 3sg potential forms in the \ corpus are marked with -a, just like the 3sg. \ forms of Class V verbs. Perhaps this 3sg potential marker is a recent change to the \ potential verb forms based on analogy to these present tense forms.
In all of these three aspects, the potential forms of verbs are identical in behavior to a number of derivational verb forms (cf. verbDIM, vblzST and vblzD ), and unlike other inflectional tense/mood forms.
At this point, the only morphological motivation to classify the potential mood as an inflectional category is its complementary distribution with other tense and mood forms. These characteristics are summarized in Table POTcomparison.

With these facts in mind, potential forms could be analyzed as derived verb forms consisting of a lexical verbal root plus a verbalizer (the potential mood morpheme) followed by Class V inflectional inflection!verbal suffixes. This possible analysis is illustrated in POTparsedEx,
in which the morphological components of the form gulatjav ‘I will likely hear’ are parsed and labeled.

gula-tj-a-v \\
hear- pot-V- 1sg \\
∑-mood-class-person/number\\

In such an analysis, potential verbs no longer stand in opposition to tense and imperative mood!imperative mood forms, but instead are subject to a semantic restriction to a non-past time, and are thus only marked for tense!presentpresent (i.e., non-past) tense, and are marked according to the present tense slots of the inflectional paradigm for Class V verbs.

It should be pointed out that the corpus contains insufficient data concerning the potential forms of any verbs in Class V. This is relevant because Class V verbs have bisyllabic stems that, together with the potential marker, may trigger allomorphy in other person/number suffixes, in which case not all potential forms would follow the standard Class V paradigm. Such information would be essential in fully evaluating the analysis proposed here.

Due mainly to this lack of truly conclusive data, I continue to follow the standard classification of the potential mood as an inflectional category for the means of the present study, but point out this potentially problematic analysis for \ as described above as a topic worthy of future study.
summary:
The potential mood is only sparsely attested in the corpus, so the description of its inflectional behavior is based on limited evidence. Although it is normally treated as an inflectional category, the passage argues that several features of potential forms—such as a separable potential marker, consistent weak-grade stem allomorphy, and suffixes homophonous with Class V present-tense endings—make this classification questionable and suggest they could instead be analyzed as derived verb forms plus Class V inflection.

Because the corpus lacks sufficient data, especially for Class V verbs, the author does not adopt this alternative analysis definitively. Instead, the study retains the standard classification of potential mood as inflectional, while noting the issue as a topic for future research.

text:
inflection inflection!verbal
Verbs in \ can be grouped into inflectional classes based on recurring patterns across inflectional paradigms. I am indebted to phonologist and Lule Saami scholar Bruce Morén-Duolljá Mor\'en-Duollj\'a, Bruce for inspiring me to consider an approach to the data involving post-stem class marking morphology.
Each verb is marked by a class suffix suffix!inflectional class which is attached directly after the verb stem and precedes inflectional suffixes (cf. Figure verbStructure).
Unlike nouns, the potential to have umlaut alternations and/or consonant gradation present for a given verb is dependent on the verb’s membership in a specific class. However not every verb in the umlaut/gradation classes is subject to these alternations, as that is determined by whether the phonemes occupying the V1 position and the consonant center of the final foot, respectively, are susceptible to umlaut and/or consonant gradation.

Furthermore, some derivational derivation suffixes (such as the diminutive diminutive suffix -tj) can block consonant gradation consonant gradation and umlaut umlaut from occurring in the derived form.
Membership in a specific verb class does not seem to be semantically motivated.

As described in the previous section, \ verb paradigms present complex combinations of linear morphology (inflectional inflection!verbal suffixes) and non-linear morphology (consonant gradation, umlaut, vowel harmony), and consist of a minimum of 21 finite forms and several non-finite forms. This minimum includes 1 st, 2 nd and 3 rd person forms for singular, dual and plural in both present tense!present and tense!pastpast, as well as singular, dual and plural forms for mood!imperativeimperative. Because of insufficient data concerning the potential forms of verbs, but also due to their regular predictability across classes (cf. POTinflection ), these were not considered in determining inflectional classes for verbs.
These are by far the most common forms in non-elicited data from the corpus. Furthermore, the three non-finite forms infinitive, connegative and perfect were also considered in determining inflectional classes.
The non-elicited portions of the \ corpus are simply too limited to even come close to providing complete paradigms for even a single verb, and so a majority of the verb forms composing the paradigms for the current study are from elicitation sessions. Approximately 30 more or less complete verb paradigms were recorded, which provides sufficient data to posit five inflectional classes. However, the true extent and finer details of the morphophonological patterns found across verb paradigms in \ must be left to future study; it is possible that, with more research, more verb classes may result, or that the present classes may need revision. As a result, what follows must be considered of a preliminary nature.

There are five main criteria for positing five different verb classesː
itemize
the regularity of the pattern of vowels occurring between the stem and inflectional suffixes (i.e., the class marking suffix suffix!inflectional class)
the number of syllables in the infinitive form syllable!syllabic structure

the presence of deviant person/number suffixes relative to the other verb classes
V1 and consonant center consonant center stem allomorphy patterning throughout the inflectional paradigm (i.e., umlaut umlaut and consonant gradation consonant gradation)
whether some verb forms are subject to vowel harmony vowel harmony, and which slots trigger such vowel harmony
itemize
To summarize these differences, it is sufficient to look at the class suffix and the syllable count in the infinitive form, the regularity of person/number suffixes across classes, the presence of consonant gradation (‘C-grad’) and umlaut, and the presence/absence of vowel harmony, Note that, particularly historically, the verbs in inflectional classes I, II and II are similar to nouns in inflectional class I, while verbs in class IV are similar to nouns in class II, and verbs in class V correspond to nouns in class III. Cf. nounClasses for inflectional classes for nouns.
as illustrated in Table verbClassSummaryTable.

Class I is the least complex class,
and is therefore dealt with first in VclassI,
while classes II, III, IV and V are described in VclassII
through VclassV.
otherVerbClasses briefly discusses the possibility of the existence of other verb classes. The verb årrot ‘be’ and the negation verb are dealt with in theCopulaVerb and theNegationVerb. The final section ( verbInflectionalClassesSummary ) provides a brief summary of the verb classes, including a table listing examples from each of the verb classes.
summary:
Verbs in this language are divided into inflectional classes, each marked by a class suffix placed after the stem and before inflectional endings. Class membership affects whether umlaut and consonant gradation can occur, though these alternations also depend on the specific sounds in the stem; some derivational suffixes can block them, and class membership does not appear to be semantically motivated.

The author proposes five verb classes based on the class suffix, infinitive syllable count, irregular person/number suffixes, patterns of umlaut and consonant gradation, and vowel harmony behavior. This classification is preliminary, since the corpus is incomplete and further research may alter the number or details of the classes.

text:
Verbs in Class I are relatively simple, and characterized as follows:
itemize
a bisyllabic infinitive form syllable!syllabic structure
the class marking suffix suffix!inflectional class is consistently -o
potentially subject to consonant gradation consonant gradation and umlaut umlaut, but not vowel harmony vowel harmony
itemize

The verb viessot ‘live, feel’ is provided in Table liveParadigm as an example. Other examples of Class I verbs include: årrot ‘reside’, gårrot ‘sew’, gähttjot ‘tell’, lávvlot ‘sing’ and såggot ‘drown’.

Table VclassIsummaryTable
summarizes the gradation pattern and class suffixes for Class I verbs. Note that umlaut alternations align with consonant gradation alternations.

There are a number of verbs which seem to be marked by -u as a class marker in infinitive, such as
gävdnut ‘exist’ and pruvkut ‘use; usually do’. While the data in the corpus are incomplete, such verbs likely pattern in essentially the same way as the verbs mentioned above marked by -o, only they are consistently marked with -u as the class marking suffix.
summary:
Class I verbs are generally bisyllabic in the infinitive, take the class suffix **-o**, and may show consonant gradation and umlaut, but not vowel harmony. Examples include *viessot* ‘live, feel’ and several other verbs such as *årrot* ‘reside’ and *gårrot* ‘sew’; the passage also notes that umlaut alternations correspond to consonant gradation patterns.  

A smaller set of verbs appears to take **-u** as the infinitive class marker, such as *gävdnut* ‘exist’ and *pruvkut* ‘use; usually do’, and these likely behave like the **-o** verbs apart from this consistent suffix difference.

text:
The characteristics of verbs in Class II are:
itemize
a bisyllabic infinitive form with a class suffix suffix!inflectional class -a or -å
potentially subject to consonant gradation consonant gradation, umlaut umlaut and vowel harmony vowel harmony
itemize

For most inflected forms, the class marking suffix is consistent with the class marking suffix in the infinitive form; however, eight forms are assigned a specific class-marking vowel, as listed in Table deviantClassSuffixesVClassIITable.

Class II verbs can further be divided into two sub-classes, based on the class marking suffix in the infinitive form: Class IIa is marked by a, while Class IIb is marked by å.
The verb bassat ‘wash’ is provided in Table washParadigm as an example for a Class IIa verb, and bårråt ‘eat’ for a Class IIb verb in Table eatParadigm.

Other examples of Class IIa verbs include: juhkat ‘drink’, tjájbmat ‘write’, barrgat ‘work’, gullat ‘hear’, gähtjat ‘look’ and sávvat ‘wish’.
The corpus only provides sufficient data for the Class IIb verb bårråt; the verbs dåbbdåt ‘recognize’, gåpptjåt ‘close’, hållåt ‘say’ and låhkåt ‘read’ are also likely candidates for Class IIb. Verbs in Class IIb all have å as the initial stem vowel while the class marking post-stem vowel is also å, just as the nouns in noun Class Id (also marked by å).

Table VclassIIsummaryTable summarizes the gradation pattern, class suffixes and locations for vowel harmony for Class II verbs; here, V stands for the vowel which marks the infinitive form ( a for Class IIa and å for Class IIb). Note that umlaut alternations align with consonant gradation alternations.
summary: Class II verbs have bisyllabic infinitives marked by the suffix -a or -å and may undergo consonant gradation, umlaut, and vowel harmony. Most inflected forms keep the infinitive class vowel, though eight forms take a special class-marking vowel; Class II is divided into Class IIa with -a and Class IIb with -å, with examples and likely members listed for each. The passage also notes that in Class IIb, the stem vowel and post-stem vowel are both å, and that umlaut alternations correspond to consonant gradation alternations.

text:
Verbs in Class III are characterized as follows:
itemize
a bisyllabic infinitive form with a class suffix suffix!inflectional class -e
potentially subject to consonant gradation consonant gradation, umlaut umlaut and vowel harmony vowel harmony
itemize

Twelve forms are subject to vowel harmony (the same six as for Class II verbs, plus six more).

The verb basset ‘fry’ is provided in Table fryParadigm as an example for a Class III verb. Other examples of Class III verbs include: vádtset ‘go’, adnet ‘have, possess’, diehtet ‘know’, båhtet ‘come’, buälldet ‘ignite, burn’ and máhttet ‘can’.

When the consonant center of a Class III stem consists of a single segment in the 1. \ and 2. \ forms and the V1 vowel is neither á nor ua/uä/uo, the class marking vowel is á instead of a, as illustrated in Table fryParadigm.

Table VclassIIIsummaryTable summarizes the gradation pattern, class suffixes and locations for vowel harmony for Class III verbs. Note that umlaut alternations align with consonant gradation alternations.
summary: Class III verbs have a bisyllabic infinitive with the class suffix -e and may undergo consonant gradation, umlaut, and vowel harmony. Twelve forms show vowel harmony, and when the stem’s consonant center is a single segment in the 1st and 2nd forms and the V1 vowel is neither á nor ua/uä/uo, the class-marking vowel is á rather than a. The passage gives *basset* ‘fry’ as an example and notes that umlaut alternations align with consonant gradation alternations.

text:
Class IV verbs are characterized by:
itemize
a bisyllabic infinitive form syllable!syllabic structure
no allomorphic variation in the stem and in the class marker suffix!inflectional class

deviant person person/number number suffixes with a -j- element vowel harmony

itemize

The stem and the class marking suffix are consistent in all forms throughout a paradigm, i.e., there is no allomorphy in the stem or class marker.
The person/number suffixes for 3sg.prs, 1du.prs, 3pl.prs, 1sg.pst, 2sg.pst and 3pl.pst deviate from the corresponding person/number suffixes in other verb classes in featuring an initial -j- element.
A nearly complete paradigm for the verb välldut ‘marry’ is provided in Table marryParadigm.

However, the data in the corpus are not nearly sufficient to provide much more than the paradigm in Table marryParadigm.

Class IV is likely a relatively small class of verbs; other potential candidates are årrat The verb årrat ‘fall asleep’ should not be confused with the Class III verb årret ‘sleep’.
‘fall asleep’, ádnot ‘request’ and tjerrot ‘cry’. includes a paradigm for tjerrot, which appears to pattern like välldut. But even the paradigm in for tjerrot is marked by inconsistent forms across dialects. Furthermore, one of my main consultants from the northern side of the \ territory stated that her dialect does not use the lexeme tjerrot, but instead vállut ‘cry’.
The class marking vowel in the infinitive form is thus not restricted to the -u- indicated in Table marryParadigm.

Table VclassIVsummaryTable summarizes the preliminary class suffix pattern for Class IV verbs, as well as the presence of a person/number suffix which deviates from the corresponding person/number suffixes in other verb classes.
This is based on the paradigm for välldut in Table marryParadigm and the paradigm for tjerrot provided in. Note the difference in orthographic forms between those used here, with tjerrot for the infinitive form, and the forms used in, with tjierˈrut for the infinitive form.
summary: Class IV verbs have a bisyllabic infinitive and show no stem or class-marker allomorphy: the stem and class suffix remain consistent across the paradigm. Several person/number suffixes, however, differ from other verb classes by beginning with a -j- element, and the class appears to be small, with examples such as *välldut* ‘marry’ and possibly *årrat*, *ádnot*, and *tjerrot*.

text:
Verbs in Class V are characterized by:
itemize
a trisyllabic infinitive form with the class marking suffix -i syllable!syllabic structure
absence of consonant gradation consonant gradation, umlaut umlaut and vowel harmony vowel harmony
itemize
Many Class V verbs are derived verbs based on a bisyllabic verb (cf. gullat ‘hear’ and gulladit ‘be in touch’ (lit.: let someone hear from you)). Because many derived verbs are in Class V, the semantic aspects accompanying the relevant derivational suffixes align in Class V, but their membership in Class V is due to their (morpho-)phonemic structure, not their semantics. Cf. vDerivation on verbal derivation.

The paradigm in Table speakParadigm provides an example for the verb ságastit ‘speak’;
other Class V verbs include bargatjit ‘work a little’, gatjadit ‘ask’, gullalit ‘listen’, málestit ‘cook, boil’, gávnadit ‘meet’ and leradit ‘teach’.
Table VclassVsummaryTable then summarizes the gradation pattern and class suffixes for Class V verbs.

[1] 1x60pt#1
summary: Class V verbs are defined by a trisyllabic infinitive with the class suffix -i and by the absence of consonant gradation, umlaut, and vowel harmony. Many are derived from bisyllabic verbs, but their membership in Class V depends on their morphophonemic form rather than their meaning; examples include *ságastit* ‘speak’ and other verbs such as *gatjadit* ‘ask’ and *gávnadit* ‘meet’.

text:
The data in the corpus are unfortunately not sufficient to be entirely confident concerning the five inflectional classes for verbs proposed here. With this in mind, the data concerning several verbs seem unusual, but also contradictory and inconsistent. Specifically, limited data on the verbs årret ‘sleep’, årrat ‘fall asleep’
and ádnot ‘request’
exist in the corpus indicating that these may belong to Class IV or some subset of Class IV verbs. Furthermore, a number of verbs with bisyllabic infinitive forms marked by -i- as a post-stem class-marking suffix exist in the data in the wordlist compiled by the \ (cf. orthography ); however, in many cases, it seems that these verbs in fact belong to Class III, and the -i- class marker is simply an inconsistent spelling of e, as the realizations of /i/ and /e/ in unstressed syllables are more centralized, and thus easily confusable, particularly when applying what are otherwise Swedish graphemes representing more distinctly front Swedish vowels. For instance, the verb virrtit ‘must’ should perhaps be spelled virrtet and likely belongs to Class III. More data on this and other bisyllabic verbs with the -i- spelling need to be gathered to determine whether another inflectional class exists, or if these are only subclasses for Class IV and perhaps Class I, II or III.
summary: The corpus data are too limited to be fully confident about the proposed five verb inflectional classes, and several verbs show unusual or inconsistent patterns. Some verbs such as årret ‘sleep’, årrat ‘fall asleep’, and ádnot ‘request’ may belong to Class IV, while many bisyllabic verbs spelled with -i- as a class marker may actually belong to Class III, with the -i- reflecting inconsistent spelling of e rather than a separate class. Further data are needed to determine whether these forms indicate a new inflectional class or only subclasses within the existing classes.

verb!copular
The verb årrot ‘be’ can be used both as a copula (cf. copulaClauses ) and as an verb!auxiliaryauxiliary (cf. auxV ); its paradigm is presented in Table beParadigm.
It is an unusual verb in a number of ways; these are listed on the following page.
[1] 1x80pt#1

itemize
årrot ‘be’ is suppletive, featuring the two stems årr- and l-.
Many of the l- stem forms are monosyllabic.
The 2., 3. \ and 3. \ forms can be shortened to ’l and encliticized onto the preceding word of an utterance if the preceding word has an open final syllable, as in cliticBE.

duvne'l aj ‘svála’ båkså\\
duvne=l aj svála båkså\\
2sg.iness=be 3pl.prs also arctic.fox gen.sg pant nom.pl\\
You also have Fjällräven \ pants on. 090519073

Fjällräven refers to a Swedish clothing company named after ‘the arctic fox’ (lat.: Vulpes lagopus); in cliticBE, the speaker literally translates language contact the company’s name into.

The 1. \ form lidjiv is often shortened to lijiv, and the 3. \ form lidjin is often shortened to lin.

The infinitive and perfect forms are the only forms in this basic paradigm which use the årr- stem,
which is homophonous (and cognate) with the verb årrot ‘reside, live’.
Finally, the verb årrot ‘be’ is unique in having a contracted connegative and perfect form: lam ‘be- prf conneg’ is a shortened form of lä ‘be conneg’ and urrum ‘be- prf’, and is thus only used in conjunction with the verb of negation, as illustrated by the example in beVerbPRFex2.

men iv lam dä månnå del skålån giesen\\
men i-v l-am dä månnå del skålå-n giese-n\\
but neg- 1sg.prs be- prf conneg then 1sg.nom then school- iness.sg summer- iness.sg\\
But I haven’t been in school during the summer. 080924622
itemize
summary:
The verb *årrot* ‘be’ functions both as a copula and as an auxiliary, and it has an unusual suppletive paradigm with two stems, *årr-* and *l-*. Many *l-* forms are monosyllabic and some can be shortened and encliticized onto a preceding word, while the infinitive and perfect use the *årr-* stem, which is also cognate with ‘reside, live’.  

It is also unique in having a contracted connegative and perfect form: *lam* is a shortened combination of *lä* and *urrum* and is used only with the negation verb. The passage gives examples of these shortened and encliticized forms in use.

text:
interrogative!question marker|(
In several Saami languages, including closely related Lule Saami, a grammatical unit often referred to in the literature as a ‘question particle’ is used to mark polar interrogative clause!interrogative!polar clauses. Cf. North Saami -go and Lule Saami -ga/-k/-ge, which are cognate with \ gu gus. According to, the question marker was originally borrowed from Finnish. Skolt Saami also has a question marker -a, which is not cognate.
For Pite Saami,
indicates that \ also has a question marker gu identifying polar interrogatives, although he shows that it is not obligatory. notes that polar questions often are only marked by being verb-initial, so even in 1921 (when he conducted fieldwork for his book) the question marker was not obligatory in Pite Saami.
In the entire \ corpus, there are only three clear tokens of a polar interrogative with the question marker, and even then, the marker has two forms: gu and gus. These tokens are provided in examples Qpart1 Note that the question marker in example Qpart1 was recorded serendipitously in an elicitation session concerning a different topic.
through Qpart3.

lä gu nällgomin?\\
lä gu nällgo-min\\
be 2sg.prs Q hunger- prog\\
Are you hungry?(lit.: are you hungering) 110518a18m36s

aná gus dån naginav, mujtojd?\\
aná gus dån nagina-v mujt-o-jd\\
have 2sg.prs Q 2sg.nom something- acc.sg remember- nmlz1- acc.pl\\
Do you have something, memories? 090702483

nå, juga gu guäsmagav?\\
nå juga gu guäsmaga-v\\
well drink 2sg.prs Q coffee- acc.sg\\
Well, do you drink coffee? 130530b015

Based on this lack of data, and on the description provided in,
one can only conclude that the question marker is no longer required to identify polar interrogative clauses, and has all but disappeared from current \ usage.

In determining which word class the question marker belongs to, several facts should be considered.
Most importantly, like the adverbs adverb in examples ADVsEx1 through ADVsEx5 above, the scope of the question marker is the entire sentence; gu gus indicates an epistemic lack on behalf of the speaker concerning the proposition expressed by the interrogative clause it marks. While its monosyllabicity is remarkable, and implies a strong degree of grammaticalization (since lexical items in general are minimally bisyllabic), a number of other monosyllabic lexical adverbs also exist (cf. Table lexicalAdverbTable). On this basis, the question marker can be classified as a lexical adverb.

However, although the data are much too limited to be certain, the question marker in all three examples occurs directly after the finite verb. If it indeed can only occur here, then this may be sufficient reason to consider the question marker to be the sole member of a unique word class (perhaps best named ‘particle’) defined by its clause-level scope and syntactic position restriction. Note that the brief description of the cognate Lule Saami ‘question particle’ in indicates that the Lule Saami equivalent may in fact be a focus particle used exclusively in polar interrogatives, as it “is placed near the word on which the most emphasis rests”, while always occurring “after the helping verb” (my translations).

interrogative!question marker|)
adverb|)
summary: In Pite Saami, a question marker gu/gus is attested that can mark polar interrogatives, but the evidence suggests it is now optional and nearly obsolete, since many polar questions are identified only by verb-initial order and only three clear marked examples are found in the corpus. The marker has clause-wide scope and may be analyzed as a lexical adverb, though its fixed postverbal position could also justify treating it as a special particle-like word class.

Adpositions in \ constitute a closed class of words that are defined syntactically by their ability to head an adpositional phrase (abbreviated ‘PP’ as these are either postpositional phrase!postpositional or prepositional phrases phrase!prepositional).
Postpositions, which are clearly preferred over prepositions, are covered in postpositions. The limited data on prepositions, which, with one exception, can all be used as postpositions as well, are described in prepositions.
summary: Adpositions in this language form a closed class and are defined syntactically by their ability to head an adpositional phrase (PP), which may be either postpositional or prepositional. Postpositions are the preferred type and are discussed separately, while the few prepositions are treated in a separate section because, except for one case, they can also function as postpositions.

a few words that are normally used as postpositions may also occur as prepositions.

The corpus provides only a very limited amount of data concerning the existence and behavior of prepositions; the two examples are presented here.

However, the complement!phrasecomplement nällje kronor ‘four crowns’ (referring to the Swedish currency) consists of the \ numeral nällje and a Swedish language contact borrowing kronor which is inflected according to Swedish grammar ( kron-or ‘crown- ’), and not \ grammar, so it is impossible to know with these data which case badjel governs as a preposition.

summary:
The passage says that, apart from dugu ‘like’, only a few normally postpositional words can also appear as prepositions, and the corpus gives only two clear examples: birra ‘about, around’ and badjel ‘over’. In the birra example, the complement is in the genitive, but in the badjel example the governing case cannot be determined because the complement contains a Swedish borrowing inflected by Swedish grammar.  

It also notes that both birra and badjel are much more frequently found as postpositions, so prepositions are rare and marginal in this language, as in other Saami languages.

Conjunctions in \ form a closed class of words that connect phrases or clauses. A list of some conjunctions, what they can connect, as well as their English translation equivalents can be found in Table conjunctionTable. Note that the conjunctions att, eller and men are borrowings from language contactSwedish.

Conjunctions connecting clauses are discussed in clausalCoordination on coordination and clausalSubordination on subordination.
Conjunctions connecting phrases are briefly described here.
NPs phrase!nominal, APs phrase!adjectival and verbs verb can be connected to another phrase of the same type by a conjunction; however, it is not clear from the data whether PPs phrase!postpositional or AdvPs phrase!adverbial can be connected.
Some examples can be found in conjunctionEx1 through conjunctionEx6.

In conjunctionEx1 and conjunctionEx2, ja ‘and’ connects NPs and APs, respectively.

The passage focuses on phrase-level coordination, noting that NPs, APs, and verbs can be linked by conjunctions, while it is unclear whether PPs or AdvPs can be coordinated from the available data. Examples show *ja* ‘and’ connecting NPs and APs, *jala* ‘or’ connecting numeral-APs, NPs, and non-finite verbs, and *eller* ‘or’ connecting NPs.

interjection|(
An interjection is an individual word that is syntactically an utterance of its own at the same level as entire clauses. As such, interjections are not a part of another clause. Interjections often indicate a speaker’s feelings or attitude towards an event. The data in the corpus are quite limited, and it is beyond the scope of the current study to describe interjections in detail, so the
list of interjections
and their English translation equivalents provided in Table interjectionTable is preliminary and subject to amendment pending future study.

Nonetheless, examples from the corpus of nå and jå are provided below.
Note that the interjections jå, nä, så, å/ oj, mmm and jaha are borrowings from language contactSwedish.

The interjection nå ‘well, yes, ok’ is very common in the corpus. It has at least three possible meanings. At the beginning of the conversation presented in particleEx3, nå is a kind of declaration that a speaker is beginning to speak. As in the final utterance in this example, nå also indicates a switch to a new topic.

A: nå buris, Henning\\
nå buris Henning\\
well hello Henning\\
Well hello, Henning!\\
B: nå, buris dä\\
nå buris dä\\
well hello then\\
Well hello there!\\
A: nå, guste dån bådá?\\
nå guste dån bådá\\
well from.where 2sg.nom come 2sg.prs\\
Well where are you coming from? 080924001-003

The interjection nå can also be a confirmation of the preceding utterance, as in particleEx4.

A: ja dä muv bena Rahka\\
ja dä muv bena Rahka\\
and then 1sg.gen dog nom.sg Rahka\\
And then my dog Rahka.\\
B: nå, duv bena aj\\
nå duv bena aj\\
well 2sg.gen dog nom.sg also\\
Ok, your dog, too. 080924037-038

Finally, nå can be used to indicate that a speaker is finished speaking, usually at the conclusion of a narrative and after a pause. One example can be found in the narrative in the recording ‘ pit100404pit100404’ between utterance ‘.324’ and utterance ‘.361’; due to space constraints, only the last two utterances of this long narrative are presented in noEx1.

The interjection jå ‘yes’, also a language contactSwedish borrowing, < Swedish jå, a common pronunciation of ja ‘yes’.
is often used to confirm something, or contradict a negative utterance, as in particleEx7, in which two speakers debate about what the correct \ word for ‘esophagus’ is.

summary: The passage explains that interjections are standalone utterances, not parts of larger clauses, and often express a speaker’s feelings or attitude. Because the corpus data are limited, the list of interjections is preliminary, but examples show that **nå** can mark a speaker beginning to talk, shift topics, confirm a previous utterance, or signal that the speaker is finished, while **jå** is used to confirm or oppose a negative statement. It also notes that several interjections, including **jå**, **nä**, **så**, **å/oj**, **mmm**, and **jaha**, are borrowings from Swedish.

text:
derivation
\ is rich in derivational morphology. While it is beyond the scope of the present work to provide a thorough description of all the various derivational processes and of their semantic nuances and productivity productivity, Israel Ruong (himself a native speaker of ) dedicated his entire PhD thesis to verbal derivation in \.
the following should provide a general impression of how derivational morphology works in, as well as an overview of some of the more common derivational morphemes attested in the corpus and extant in the wordlist compiled by the \ (cf. orthography ).

In the following, derivational meanings are assigned to suffixes for simplicity in classification; however, as with inflectional inflection suffixes, derivational suffixes coincide with non-linear morphology morphology!non-linear when the derivational base is subject to non-linear morphological alternations.

There are many nominalizing and verbalizing derivational processes, and derivations can apply to already derived forms.

On the other hand, there are only two adjectivizers and one adverbializer.

Nominal derivation and verbal derivation are especially complex because the semantics of a derived word do not consistently equal the sum of the meanings of its components. Furthermore, the borderline between polysemy and homonymy of suffixes cannot always be clearly determined, and the decision whether two formally identical, but semantically different forms should be ascribed to the same morpheme or to distinct morphemes is not always obvious.
This is reflected in the glossing standards used here in which most nominalizers and verbalizers are simply allotted numbers, as in nmlz1 or vblz3, as opposed to more meaningful glosses such as dim.

In the following, nominal derivation is dealt with first, in nDerivation, before moving on to verbal derivation
in vDerivation, while adjectival and adverbial derivation are described briefly in adjDerivation and advDerivation, respectively. The final section ( derivMorphSummary ) provides a summary of the derivational morphemes discussed here.

Note that examples in the present chapter include references to either the documentation corpus or an entry in the database from the \ (cf. orthography ). Nearly all references to the documentation corpus are for elicitation sessions, and these are marked accordingly. Unlike examples in the other chapters, in which references indicate a particular utterance of a recording, references here may not be not more specific than the recording name alone because the relevant data were obtained during the course of a longer discussion, and not just in a single utterance. References referring to the ’s database consist only of the four-digit entry number.
summary: The passage says that the language has rich derivational morphology, with many nominalizing and verbalizing processes, while adjectivization and adverbialization are much more limited. It also notes that derivational suffixes can interact with non-linear morphology, can apply to already derived forms, and often have meanings that are not transparently compositional, making the boundary between polysemy and homonymy difficult to determine.

summary:
The nominalizer suffix **-k** (spelled **-g-** intervocalically) is a very frequent and productive derivational morpheme that can attach to nouns, verbs, adjectives, and numerals to form nouns referring to entities characterized by the base meaning. The passage gives examples such as nouns meaning ‘moose,’ ‘yearling,’ ‘police,’ ‘knowledgable person,’ ‘white reindeer,’ and ‘five-crown coin,’ and notes that some place names may also be derived with -k.  

Morphophonologically, **-k** triggers weak consonant grade where relevant, but the vowel before it varies inconsistently, which may reflect different noun classes or possibly more than one suffix of the form **-Vk**.

The nominalizing suffix suffix!derivational -däddje (glossed as nmlz2) creates an agent noun, indicating that the referent of the noun is involved in the activity denoted by the base. Examples are provided in agentNMLZex1 through agentNMLZex5.

The base is typically a verb verb, but can be a noun, as in agentNMLZex4. The stem of the derived agent noun is in the weak grade consonant gradation!weak grade.
As illustrated by agentNMLZex2 and agentNMLZex3, the resulting agent noun (with a root máles and åhpa) may no longer be directly derivable from the comparable verb (there is no verb *málle-t ‘cook- inf’, only málestit, nor a verb *åhpa-t, but instead åhpådit ‘teach- inf’).

Note that the noun báhkojådedäddje ‘chairperson’ in agentNMLZex3 is a compound calque based on the Swedish language contact equivalent ordförande, which literally means ‘word-driver’. It is not clear whether jådedäddje ‘driver’ exists on its own.
summary: The suffix **-däddje** (nmlz2) forms **agent nouns**, referring to someone or something involved in the action expressed by the base. The base is usually a verb, but can also be a noun; the derived noun typically shows **weak-grade consonant gradation**, and some forms are no longer directly derivable from the corresponding verb because the verb has a different stem. One example, **báhkojådedäddje** ‘chairperson’, is a compound calque influenced by Swedish *ordförande* ‘word-driver’, and it is unclear whether **jådedäddje** ‘driver’ occurs independently.

derivation!verbal|(
Verbal derivation in \ is a particularly complex area, and the interested reader is first and foremost referred to Israel Ruong’s PhD thesis Lappische Verbalableitung dargestellt auf Grundlage des Pitelappischen ‘Saami verbal derivation as illustrated by the Pite Saami language’ (my translation).. This work presents a comprehensive typology of non-derived verbs and verbal derivation suffixes in.
It includes an extensive semantic sub-classification of the derivational suffixes into the varied and overlapping meanings each one can have. The forty suffixes Ruong presents, and the myriad functions he assigns them to, further attest to the complicated nature of verbal derivation in.

The present discussion cannot hope to improve on Ruong’s work, and instead attempts to use the \ corpus to achieve the following:
itemize
Using the diminutive verbalizer -tj as a starting point, illustrate the complexity of verbal derivation in \ due to the persistent irregularities between forms and functions ( verbDIM );
Present a sample of verbal derivations ( vblzST through vblzDALL );
Provide a basic description of the important valency-decreasing verbal derivation creating passive verb forms ( VdervPassives ).
itemize
summary: The passage says that verbal derivation in the language is highly complex, and points readers especially to Israel Ruong’s PhD thesis, which offers a comprehensive typology of non-derived verbs and derivational suffixes, including a detailed semantic classification of their overlapping meanings. The present discussion does not try to surpass Ruong’s work, but instead uses the corpus to illustrate irregularities in verbal derivation, present examples of verbal derivations, and give a basic description of valency-decreasing passive derivation.

subsection: The diminutive verbalizer suffix -tj and the complexities of \ derivational verb morphology
text:
derivation!verbal diminutive
The diminutive verbalizing suffix suffix!derivational -tj (glossed as dim) expresses doing the activity referred to by the verbal base a little bit or to a limited extent, as in verbDIMex1 through verbDIMex3. Note the similarity in form and semantics to the diminutive nominalizing suffix -tj discussed in dim.

barrga-twork- infbarga-tji-twork- dim- infwork a little bit110404285

vádtse-twalk- infvádtsa-tji-twalk- dim- infwalk slowly2047

bällke-tquarrel- infbielka-tji-tquarrel- dim- infhave a small quarrel4698

The weak form of the base verb is selected by -tj, and the final vowel in the base becomes a.
The i following the -tj suffix is the verb class marker for the resulting Class V verb.

Note, however, that other derivational suffixes can produce diminutive meanings as well, as illustrated by the examples in verbDIMex4 through verbDIMex6.

gähtja-tsee- infgietja-sti-tsee- vblz1- infglance2530

gåsså-tcough- infgåsså-di-tcough- vblz2- infcough a little bit4898

rassjo-train- infrässjo-dalla-train- vblz3- infrain lightly5073

In these three examples, the derivational suffixes -st, -d and -dall, respectively, The vowel following each of these verbalizers is a class marker.
also derive deverbal verbs which add similar diminutive meanings to the base.

If these suffixes were restricted to a diminutive meaning, then this would simply be a case of many forms corresponding to a single function. However, these suffixes, which are all quite common, only occasionally carry a diminutive meaning. In other instances, they impart a variety of different meanings to the base form. This is illustrated by just a few examples below, and is even more obvious throughout. Despite the variety of and inconsistencies in the meanings that verbal derivational suffixes express, their limited number relative to the number of functions they fulfill is reason enough to describe each of these suffixes as a single derivational affix with multiple functions, rather than multiple, homonymous affixes, each aligned to a separate function.
summary:
The diminutive verbalizing suffix **-tj** expresses performing an activity only a little or to a limited extent, and it patterns in form and meaning with the diminutive nominalizing suffix. The passage also notes that other derivational suffixes such as **-st**, **-d**, and **-dall** can sometimes add similar diminutive meanings, though these suffixes are more generally associated with a range of different meanings.  

Because these common suffixes are not restricted to diminutive senses, the author argues that they should be analyzed as single derivational affixes with multiple functions rather than as separate homonymous affixes.

passive derivation!verbal
Transitive valency!transitive verbs can be passivized using the suffix suffix!derivational -duvv (glossed as pass).
The resulting derived verb belongs to the inflectional verb Class IV, and thus features the class marker -a following the passivizing suffix in the infinitive form, and -u in the perfect form.
For instance, compare the verb in passEx2 (in the active voice) with the equivalent passivized verb in passEx3, including the oblique agent (in \ case).

máná lä tsiggim gådev\\
máná lä tsiggi-m gåde-v\\
child nom.pl be 3pl.prs build- prf hut- acc.sg\\
Children have built the hut. 110518a28m14s

gåhte lä tsiggijduvvum mánájst\\
gåhte lä tsiggij-duvvu-m máná-jst\\
hut nom.sg be 3sg.prs build- pass- prf child- elat.pl\\
The hut has been built by children. 110518a28m41s

Passivization is a valency-decreasing device because the resulting verb is intransitive valency!intransitive, as it only features the patient-like argument as its sole core argument in nominative case. Note that claims, for North Saami, that “one cannot indicate the agent in any way” (my translation) in passive clauses using the cognate North Saami passivizing suffix. \ differs significantly from North Saami in this respect, as Ruong -- himself a native speaker of \ -- verifies. It is very possible that the \ strategy of placing the agent in an oblique case could be due to extensive language contact language contact with Swedish, a language which clearly allows the agent in a passivized clause to be expressed obliquely using a prepositional phrase headed by the preposition av ‘of, from’.
Indeed, Swedish PPs headed by av in other contexts are best translated into \ as an NP in elative case, the same oblique case in which the agent NP in a passive \ sentence is found.

Some other examples of transitive verbs and their passivized equivalents using -duvv are shown in vblzDUVVex1 through vblzDUVVex3.

tjåvvde-tuntie- inftjåvde-duvva-tuntie- pass- infbe liberated3233

dahka-tmake- infdaga-duvva-tmake- pass- infbe made110331b069

There are not sufficient data in the corpus to state any more about passive derivation, particularly concerning morphophonological effects of passivization on verb stems, and this and other related topics must be left for future study. The reader is referred to for a more thorough morphological and semantic account of \ passives.
Inflectional aspects of passivized verbs are treated in passiveVinflection, while syntactic aspects of clauses with passive verbs are presented briefly in passiveVoice.

Note that the derivational suffix -duvv can have meanings other than passive when attached to a nominal or adjectival base. Typically it then expresses a change of state that is related to the referent of the root involved. A few examples are provided in vblzDUVVex5 through vblzDUVVex8.

summary: Transitive verbs can be passivized with the derivational suffix **-duvv**, which places the verb in inflectional Class IV and yields forms such as infinitive **-duvva-** and perfect **-duvvum**. The passive is valency-decreasing: the patient becomes the sole core argument in nominative case, while the agent may appear in an oblique case such as elative, unlike claims for North Saami that the agent cannot be expressed in passive clauses. The passage also notes that corpus data are too limited for further generalizations about morphophonological effects, and that **-duvv** can have non-passive change-of-state meanings with nominal or adjectival bases.

Only two derivational processes exist for adjectivals: the non-productive derivation of adjectives by suffix!derivational -s, and the productive derivation of ordinal numerals from cardinal ones.

These are described below.
summary: The passage states that there are only two derivational processes for adjectivals. These are the non-productive formation of adjectives with the derivational suffix **-s** and the productive formation of ordinal numerals from cardinal numerals.

text:
It seems conceivable that adjectives can be derived by the suffix -s (glossed as adjz).
For instance, bahá is a nominal meaning ‘evil’, as in derivADJex1, and bahás is the equivalent attributive adjective form, as in derivADJex2.

dat almatj lä bahá\\
d-a-t almatj lä bahá\\
dem- dist- nom.sg person nom.sg be 3sg.prs evil nom.sg \\
That person is evil. 09092613m36s

bahás almatj\\
bahá-s almatj\\
evil- adjz person nom.sg\\
evil person 09092613m40s

In addition, the nominalized form bahá-k ‘evil’ can be further derived into an adjective bahágis ‘painful’ as in derivADJex3.

bahá-kevil- nmlzbahá-gi-sevil- nmlz- adjzpainful0102

However, as pointed out in detail in adjectivesATTR through notePredNounsAdjs, not all adjectives follow this pattern. In fact, based on the current data, the -s suffix marks attributive adjectives (as in derivADJex2) and as well as predicative adjectives,
and, synchronically, it is not considered to be productive for either attributive or predicative forms at all.
summary: The passage suggests that adjectives may be derivable with the suffix **-s**: for example, *bahá* ‘evil’ becomes the attributive adjective *bahás* ‘evil’, and the nominalized form *bahá-k* can further yield *bahágis* ‘painful’. However, the text emphasizes that not all adjectives follow this pattern, and synchronically **-s** is not considered productive for either attributive or predicative adjectives.

text:
derivation!numeral
Numerals, a sub-category of adjectivals (cf. numerals ), are subject to derivation.

The basic ordinal numeral!ordinal numerals can be derived by applying the derivational suffix -át (or its allomorph -et)
to the respective cardinal numeral, although the forms vuostas ‘first’ and mubbe ‘second’ are suppletive. Ordinal derivation is discussed in ordinalNums in more detail, including a comparison of cardinal and ordinal numbers in Table basicNumsTable.
derivation!adjectival|)
summary: Numerals, treated as a subcategory of adjectivals, can undergo derivation. Basic ordinal numerals are generally formed from cardinal numerals by adding the suffix **-át** or its allomorph **-et**, though **vuostas** ‘first’ and **mubbe** ‘second’ are suppletive forms.

text:
derivation!adverbial
Adverbs are not common in the corpus (as opposed to other word classes and phrase types with adverbial functions), but do appear to be derivable from an adjective base using the suffix suffix!derivational -git. This is dealt with in more detail in derivedADVs.
summary: Adverbs are relatively rare in the corpus compared with other word classes and phrase types serving adverbial functions. When they do occur, they appear to be derivable from adjective bases by means of the derivational suffix **-git**; this is discussed further in the section on derived adverbs.

summary: The passage states that there are five types of phrases in the language, and that these phrases can form syntactic constituents of other phrases or of clauses. The five types listed are verb complex (VC), nominal phrase (NP), adjectival phrase (AP), adverbial phrase (AdvP), and postpositional phrase (PP), and the chapter includes a table summarizing their main syntactic functions and relevant sections.
