phrase!verb complex|( verb complex|see phrase

The \ verb complex (abbreviated ‘VC’) consists minimally of a finite verb, and maximally of a finite verb!finite verb and one or two non-finite verb forms verb!non-finite.
With the exception of the mood!imperativeimperative, the finite verb inflects for tense tense or mood mood, number number and person person, and agrees agreement with the subject.
The imperative only inflects for number.

In combination with non-finite verb forms, the verbal categories negation negation, mood mood, and aspect aspect can also be expressed.

To better describe the distribution of finite and non-finite verbs forms in VCs, verbs are divided into two groupings:
itemize
lexical verbs and the copular verb verb!copular årrot ‘be’
grammatical verbs (the negation verb, the aspectual auxiliary verb årrot ‘be’, and the verb!modalmodal verbs; cf. multiVdeclarativeClauses ).
itemize

In VCs featuring only one verb form, the finite verb is a lexical verb or the copular verb. In VCs with two or three verb forms, the finite verb is a grammatical verb, while
the selection of each non-finite form is determined by the type of verb governing it: the verb of negation triggers the connegative verb!non-finite!connegative form, the aspectual auxiliary verb triggers either the perfect or the progressive form, and the modal verbs trigger the infinitive form.
This is summarized in Table VCstructures.

The constituent order constituent order of the individual verbal components is not strictly set, although the ordering indicated in Table VCstructures is most common. Furthermore, other clause-level components may occur between these verb forms (cf. constituentOrderClauses and multiVdeclarativeClauses ).

For instance, the examples in VCex1 and VCex2 each feature a VC consisting solely of a finite verb. In VCex1 it is the singular mood!imperativeimperative form of the lexical verb vädtjat ‘fetch’, while in VCex2 it is the encliticized 3sg.prs form of the copular verb.

vietja pahparav!\\
[vietja] pahpara-v\\
fetch sg.imp paper- acc.sg\\
Get some paper! 090519316

dun váre namma'l Sállvo\\
d-u-n váre namma=[l] Sállvo\\
dem- rmt- gen.sg mountain gen.sg name nom.sg=be 3sg.prs Sállvo nom.sg\\
The name of that mountain is Sállvo. 100404005

In VCex3, there are two VCs. The first VC is ij…dága
The complete phrase ij aktagav dága is likely a calque of the Swedish language contact phrase det gör ingenting ‘that doesn’t matter’ (lit.: ‘that does nothing’).
and consists of the finite negation verb and the lexical verb dáhkat ‘make, do’ in its connegative form, but is split by the particle dä and the NP argument aktagav. The second VC is the verb vähtjat ‘fetch’, here in its 1sg.prs finite form.

ij dä aktagav dága, mån viehtjav dav maŋŋel\\
[i-j] 1 dä aktaga-v [dága] 1 mån [viehtja-v] 2 d-a-v maŋŋel\\
neg- 3sg.prs then nothing- acc.sg make conneg 1sg.nom fetch- 1sg.prs dem- dist- acc.sg after\\
It doesn’t matter, I’ll get that later. 100404157

The example in VCex4 consists of three VCs. The first, lin båhtam ‘had come’, is headed by the 3pl.pst form of the auxiliary verb årrot ‘be’ and combines with the perfect form of the main lexical verb båhtet ‘come’. The second and third VCs are both simple VCs consisting only of a finite verb form.

jus stalpe lin båhtam elo sissa, dä vuolgin ja vitjin davva\\
jus stalpe [li-n båhta-m] 1 elo sissa dä [vuolgi-n] 2 ja [vitji-n] 3 d-a-vva\\
if wolf nom.pl be- 3pl.pst come- prf reindeer.herd gen.sg into then drive- 3pl.pst and fetch- 3pl.pst dem- dist- acc.sg\\
If wolves had entered the reindeer herd, they went and got him. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a091

A modal verb
and a non-finite verb form are illustrated by the VC máhtta… båhtet ‘can come’ in VCex5. Here, the modal máhtta ‘can’ is the finite verb, and båhtet ‘come’ is in the infinitive form.

båtsoj máhtta duv nala båhtet\\
båtsoj [máhtta] duv nala [båhte-t] \\
reindeer nom.sg can 3sg.prs 2sg.gen upon come- inf\\
The reindeer can attack you.(lit: ‘come upon you’) 080909048

Similarly, in VCex5a, the VC virrten märrket ‘have to mark’ contains the finite verb virrten ‘must’ and the infinitive verb form märrket ‘mark’.

dä virrten märrket dajt miesijd dále tjaktjan\\
dä [virrte-n märrke-t] d-a-jt miesi-jd dále tjaktja-n\\
then must- 1du.prs mark- inf dem- dist- acc.pl calf- acc.pl now autumn- iness.sg\\
Then we have to mark those calves now in the autumn. 080909008

Note that, formally, clauses featuring a modal verb are identical to clause!complementcomplement clauses featuring an infinitival predicate; cf. infinitiveComplementClauses.

Finally, the clauses in VCex6 through VCex8 provide examples of VCs with three verb forms. In VCex6, the VC consists of the finite negation verb in 1sg.prs ( iv), the aspectual auxiliary årrot in connegative form ( lä), and the lexical verb gullat ‘hear’ in its perfect form ( gullam). The VC in example VCex7 contains the finite negation verb 3sg.prs ( ij), the modal verb máhttet in connegative form ( máhte), and the lexical verb adnet ‘have’, in its infinitive form. Finally, in VCex8, the finite aspectual auxiliary lev combined with the perfect form of the modal verb máhttet ‘can’ and the infinite complement ságastit ‘speak’ constitute the VC.

dä iv lä åbå gullam dav\\
dä [i-v lä] åbå [gulla-m] d-a-v\\
then neg- 1sg.prs be conneg at.all hear- prf dem- dist- acc.sg\\
I haven’t heard that at all. 090702203

ij vanj dä máhte ilá stuor dålåv adnet\\
[i-j] vanj dä [máhte] ilá stuor dålå-v [adne-t] \\
neg- 3sg.prs really then can conneg too big fire- acc.sg have- inf\\
One cannot really have too big of a fire. 090702176

mån lev máhttam sámev ságastit\\
mån [le-v máhtta-m] sáme-v [ságasti-t] \\
1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs can- prf Saami- acc.sg speak- inf\\
I have been able to speak Saami. 12100946m27s

The corpus does not provide any evidence for three-verb VCs with a modal verb as the finite verb, so whether this logically possible structures is acceptable
must be left to future research. However, it is clear that the negation verb is only attested as a finite verb, and can never occur as the second or third verb in a multi-verb VC.
phrase!verb complex|)
summary:
The passage describes the structure of the verb complex (VC), which minimally contains a finite verb and may include one or two non-finite verb forms. Finite verbs normally inflect for tense or mood, number, person, and agreement with the subject, while the imperative inflects only for number; with non-finite forms, negation, mood, and aspect can also be expressed.

It distinguishes lexical verbs and the copular verb from grammatical verbs such as the negation verb, the aspectual auxiliary årrot ‘be’, and modal verbs. In multi-verb VCs, the finite verb is grammatical and determines the form of the non-finite verb(s): negation takes the connegative, aspectual auxiliary takes perfect or progressive, and modals take the infinitive; the passage also notes that constituent order is flexible, the negation verb is only attested as finite, and no evidence was found for three-verb VCs with a modal as the finite verb

text:
phrase!nominal|( nominal phrase|see phrase
Nominal phrases (abbreviated ‘NP’) in \ are divided into two groups:
itemize
full NPs
pronouns pronoun

itemize
NPs can function as arguments, adjuncts, predicates, adverbials, dependents of postpositions and possessors or modifiers of other NPs.
They consist of at least one nominal component that inflects for case case and number number.
Note that NPs can also be modified by postpositional phrases and non-finite verb forms, but due to a lack of sufficient data, a description of these NP modifiers must be left for future study.
Finally, relative clauses also modify an NP; these are covered in relativeClauses.

NPs have the structure illustrated in NPstructures, with optional components in parentheses..99! 1mm[(demonstrative) \ (other modifier (s)) \ nominal \ (refl-intensifier) \ (rel-clause)]

Either a noun or a pronoun forms the head of an NP. The demonstrative demonstrative, the nominal and any attributive reflexive pronoun!reflexive pronoun always inflect for case and number, while generally the other modifiers do not. Other modifiers may be an adjectival phrase, a numeral or an NP in genitive case. An intensifier in the form of a reflexive pronoun (cf. reflexivePronouns )
can modify a noun phrase as well, and occurs after the head. Finally, the head can be modified by a relative clause, which also occurs after the head.
Some examples for possible NP structures are found below.

The only NP in NPstructureEx0 consists solely of the noun Tjeggelvasav ‘Lake Tjeggelvas’.

ja dä vuojnav Tjeggelvasav\\
ja dä vuojna-v [Tjeggelvasa-v] \\
and then see- 1sg.prs Lake.Tjeggelvas- acc.sg\\
And then I see Lake Tjeggelvas. 100404013

In the example in NPstructureEx1, the NP dat ello ‘that reindeer herd’ consists of a demonstrative and the head noun, and is the subject of the clause.
In NPstructureEx2, the subject NP consists of the head noun ello ‘reindeer herd’ and the genitive NP dáj Skailej ‘of these Skailes’ Skaile is a family name.
which modifies the head noun.

ja dä såkoj dat ello\\
ja dä såko-j [d-a-t ello] \\
and then drown- 3sg.pst dem- dist- nom.sg reindeer.herd nom.sg\\
And then that reindeer herd drowned. 0906_Ahkajavvre_b0906_Ahkajavvre_b010

dáj Skailej ello såkoj\\
[[d-á-j Skaile-j] 1 ello] 2 såko-j\\
dem- prox- gen.pl Skaile- gen.pl reindeer.herd nom.sg drown- 3sg.pst\\
These Skailes’ reindeer herd drowned. 0906_Ahkajavvre_b0906_Ahkajavvre_b002

An NP marked for genitive case can also function as a modifier that narrows the reference of the head noun by signifying some characteristic of the head noun’s referent, as in NPstructureEx2 above. Similarly, in NPstructureGenNPex1 the genitive NP mále ‘blood’ modifies the head noun gamsajd ‘dumplings’.

ja dágaj mále gamsajd\\
ja dága-j [[mále] 1 gamsa-jd] 2 \\
and make- 3sg.pst blood gen.sg dumpling- acc.pl\\
And one made blood dumplings. 080924253

In the example in NPstructureEx3, the NP nåv edna båtsoj ‘so many reindeer’ Note that the word båtsoj ‘reindeer’ is often marked for singular, even when referring to more than one reindeer.
consists of the AP nåv edna ‘so many’ and the head noun båtsoj ‘reindeer’.

dä lij nåv edna båtsoj\\
dä li-j [nåv edna båtsoj] \\
then be- 3sg.pst so much reindeer nom.sg\\
There were so many reindeer.(lit.: ‘so much reindeer’) 0906_Ahkajavvre_b0906_Ahkajavvre_b013

As the example in NPstructureEx4 illustrates, it is possible for more than one modifier to be included in an NP. Here, both APs guäkte ‘two’ and stuor ‘big’ modify the noun head, which is the derived compound guhkajuolgagijd ‘long-leggers’ (referring to moose).

dä inijmä guäkte stuora guhkajuolgagijd\\
dä ini-jmä [guäkte stuora guhka-juolga-gi-jd] \\
then have- 1pl.pst two big long-leg- nmlz- acc.pl\\
Then we had two big moose.(lit.: ‘long-leggers’) 090702331

If the context is sufficiently clear, it is possible that the head noun is not realized when a demonstrative and/or modifier is present; such cases are referred to as elliptical constructions.
Numerals numeral, for instance, can be in elliptical constructions,
as in NPstructureEx6, in which the noun referring to ‘nets’ is not realized, so gålmát ‘third’ composes the entire NP.

ja gålmát sjadda dä Stutjaj\\
ja [gålm-át] 1 sjadda dä [Stutja-j] 2\\
and three- ord become 3sg.prs then Stutja- ill.sg\\
And the third one is then placed at Stutja.(referring to ‘fishing net’) 090702026-027

With the exception of the. \ form of akta ‘one’, numerals do not inflect for case and number (cf. numerals ).

Less commonly, an adjectival phrase phrase!adjectival can be in an elliptical construction, either with or without a demonstrative (cf. ADJinHeadlessNPs ). In the absence of a head noun, the adjective in the AP is the host for case case and number number, and is morphologically a nominal.
In the example in adjNPheadEx3repeat includes a demonstrative; here, the head noun referring to a girl is not overt, and the NP only contains the demonstrative dat ‘that’ and the adjective tjábba ‘beautiful’.
The sentence in NPstructureEx8 illustrates a similar structure, but without a demonstrative. In this case, the head noun referring to a piece of candy is not realized, and the NP consists only of the adjective rupsisav ‘red’, which inflects for case and number. Cf. ADJinHeadlessNPs for more details about adjectives in elliptical structures.

dat tjábba máhtta sáme gielav\\
[d-a-t tjábba] 1 máhtta [sáme giela-v] 2\\
dem- dist- nom.sg beautiful nom.sg can 3sg.prs Saami gen.sg language- acc.sg\\
That beautiful one can speak the Saami language. 090930a148

bårov rupsisav\\
båro-v [rupsisa-v] \\
eat- 1sg.prs red- acc.sg\\
I eat the red one. 090930a119

There are many examples in the corpus of NPs consisting of a pronoun, such as the demonstrative pronoun pronoun!demonstrative dajd in NPstructureProEx1, or the personal pronoun pronoun!personal mån in NPstructureProEx2.

bisij dajd såbe nanne\\
bisi-j [d-a-jd] 1 [såbe] 2 nanne\\
fry- 3sg.pst dem- dist- acc.pl stick gen.sg on\\
He fried those on a stick. 100404125

mån mähttiv ráhpat uksav\\
[mån] 1 mähtti-v ráhpa-t [uksa-v] 2\\
1sg.nom can- 1sg.pst open- inf door- acc.sg\\
I could open the door. 100404347

The second NP in NPstructureProEx1, såbe ‘stick’, also illustrates a genitive NP functioning as the complement!phrasecomplement of a PP.
summary:
Nominal phrases (NPs) in the language may be full NPs or pronouns, and they can function as arguments, adjuncts, predicates, adverbials, and dependents or possessors/modifiers of other NPs. An NP normally contains a head noun or pronoun that inflects for case and number, optionally preceded by a demonstrative and other modifiers such as adjectival phrases, numerals, or genitive NPs, and optionally followed by a reflexive intensifier or relative clause.

The passage also notes that head nouns can be omitted in elliptical constructions when the context makes the reference clear, so a demonstrative, numeral, or adjective may alone form the NP. Examples show that genitive NPs can narrow the reference of a noun, and that pronouns can themselves constitute entire NPs.

text:
When the head of an NP is a personal pronoun, it is also possible to modify it. For instance, in NPstructureProEx3, the 1sg.nom reflexive pronoun etj modifies the 1sg.nom personal pronoun mån as an intensifier. Note that this ordering (modifier following the head) deviates from the general pattern, in which the modifier occurs before the head of the NP.

mån etj hålåv dále navte\\
[mån etj] hålå-v dále navte\\
1sg.nom refl 1sg.nom say- 1sg.prs now like.that\\
I myself say it like that. 09091029m05s

Finally, a relative clause clause!relative can also occur after the head as part of the NP. An example is provided in NPstructureRelClEx1; see relativeClauses for more on relative clauses.

dá lä jisse gistá mejd dálven gallga adnet\\
d-á lä jisse [gistá me-jd dálve-n gallga adne-t] \\
dem prox- nom.pl be 3pl.prs precisely glove nom.pl rel- acc.pl winter- iness.sg shall 3sg.prs have- inf\\
These are gloves which one has in winter. 080708_Session08006
summary:
A personal pronoun can be modified within an NP, as in the example where the 1sg.nom reflexive pronoun *etj* intensifies the pronoun *mån* (“I myself”). This ordering is unusual because the modifier follows the head, whereas modifiers normally precede the head in NP structure.  

The passage also notes that a relative clause can follow the head as part of the NP, illustrated by an example meaning “These are gloves which one has in winter.”

text:
Nominal phrases,
particularly when referring to time or place, and thus inflected for one of the locative cases (illative, inessive or elative), are often used as temporal or locational adverbials, as in giesen ‘in summer’ in ADVnounsEx1, and in hiejman ‘at home’ in ADVnounsEx2, respectively. Furthermore, the word vahkov ‘week’ in ADVnounsEx2 shows that an accusative NP can function as a temporal adverbial indicating a period of time.

men jáhkav minniv giesen\\
men jáhka-v minni-v [giese-n] \\
but believe- 1sg.prs go- 1sg.pst summer- iness.sg\\
I believe I went in the summer. 100404163

ja Henning lij jou hiejman urrum vahkov\\
ja [Henning] 1 li-j jou [hiejma-n] 2 urru-m [vahko-v] 3\\
and Henning nom.sg be- 3sg.pst well home- iness.sg be- prf week- acc.sg\\
And Henning had been home for a week. 090702285

Finally, the deverbal noun diedon literally translates as ‘in knowledge’, and can be used as a modal adverbial meaning ‘of course’, as in ADVnounsEx3.

etja diedon ednen mielkev ja vuostav\\
[etj-a] 1 [died-o-n] 2 edne-n [mielke-v] 3 ja [vuosta-v] 4\\
self- nom.pl know- nmlz1- iness.sg have- 3pl.pst milk- acc.sg and cheese- acc.sg\\
They themselves of course had milk and cheese. 080708_Session02080708_Session02034

phrase!nominal|)
summary: Nominal phrases inflected for locative cases, especially when referring to time or place, are often used as temporal or locational adverbials, as shown by forms meaning “in summer” and “at home.” The passage also notes that an accusative noun phrase can express a time span, as in “for a week,” and that the deverbal noun *diedon* can function as a modal adverbial meaning “of course.”

text:
phrase!adjectival|( adjectival phrase|see phrase
Adjectival phrases (abbreviated ‘AP’) in \ are divided into three groups based on the type of adjective required as head:
itemize
attributive APs (headed by attributive adjectives adjective!attributive)
predicate APs (headed by predicative adjectives adjective!predicative)
numeral APs (headed by numerals numeral)
itemize

In the first case, the attributive AP is syntactically embedded in an NP phrase!nominal whose head noun it modifies. In the second case, the predicative AP ascribes the property it concerns to the entire NP which is the subject of the copular clause which the AP is embedded in. Numeral APs can occur both attributively and predicatively.

The three possible constituent structures of APs are presented in APstructures.

The only difference in internal structure between the two adjective APs is the choice of adjective: attributive vs. predicative.
Numeral APs normally consist only of a numeral, but can be further modified by an adverbial.

Adverbial phrases phrase!adverbial are not common in APs.
The data are quite limited concerning which type of AdvPs are acceptable, and future study is needed in this respect. Examples from the corpus include
ilá ‘too’, nåv ‘so’, huj ‘really’, åbbå ‘completely’ and gajk ‘all’.

Several examples of APs are provided here. In APstructureEx1, the AP consists only of the attributive adjective njalga ‘tasty’ and modifies biebmov ‘food’, the head of the NP.

ja danna lip bårråm njalga biebmov\\
ja danna li-p bårrå-m [njalga] biebmo-v\\
and there be- 1pl.prs eat- prf tasty food- acc.sg\\
And we ate tasty food there. 110517b2005

The example in APstructureEx2 illustrates an attributive adjective modified by an AdvP.

ja dat lä urrum huj buorak giesse\\
ja d-a-t lä urru-m [huj buorak] giesse\\
and dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.prs be- prf really good summer nom.sg\\
And it has been a really good summer. 080909009

In APstructureEx3, the predicative adjective nuorra ‘young’ agrees with the subject NP mánná ‘child’ in number.

mánná lä nuorra\\
mánná lä [nuorra] \\
child nom.sg be 3sg.prs young sg\\
The child is young. 090930a310

As the example in APstructureEx4 shows, predicative adjectives are syntactically adjectives, as the predicate adjective buojde ‘fat’ is the head of an AP modified by an AdvP ( nåv ‘so’).

dä lä vuosjkuna nåv buojde\\
dä lä vuosjkun-a [nåv buojde] \\
then be 3pl.prs perch- nom.pl so fat pl\\
Then the perch are so fat. 090702080

Finally, examples of numeral APs are provided in APstructureEx5 through APstructureEx7. In the example in APstructureEx5, guäkte ‘two’ modifies the NP dåpe ‘houses’.

dä guäkte dåpe lä danne\\
dä [guäkte] dåpe lä danne \\
then two house nom.pl be 3pl.prs there\\
Then two houses are there. 080924385

The example in APstructureEx6
is noteworthy because it shows that the modifying numeral can be inflected as a superlative; here the ordinal numeral vuostas is in the superlative form vuostamos meaning ‘very first’, and modifies the NP guhkajuolgak ‘moose’.

dieda, mån vuotjev vuostamos guhkajuolgagav\\
dieda mån vuotje-v [vuosta-mos] guhka-juolga-ga-v\\
know 2sg.prs 1sg.nom shoot- 1sg.pst first- superl long-leg- nmlz- acc.sg\\
You know, I shot my very first long-legger. 080924079

Numeral APs can include an adverbial modifier. The adverb ber ‘only’ modifies the numeral akkta ‘one’ in APstructureEx7.

vuostak lij ber akkta rommå\\
vuostak li-j [ber akkta] råmmå\\
first be- 3sg.pst only one room nom.sg\\
Initially there was only one room. 100310b051
summary:
Adjectival phrases (APs) are divided into three types according to their head: attributive APs, predicative APs, and numeral APs. Attributive APs modify a noun inside an NP, predicative APs ascribe a property to the subject of a copular clause, and numeral APs can function either way; the main structural difference between the two adjective APs is the choice of attributive versus predicative adjective, while numeral APs usually consist of a numeral that may be modified by an adverbial.  

Adverbial phrases are uncommon in APs, and the text notes that only limited data are available on which types are acceptable, though examples include forms meaning ‘too,’ ‘so,’ ‘really,’ ‘completely,’ and ‘all.’ The passage illustrates these patterns with examples of attributive, predicative, and numeral APs, including cases where the AP is modified by an adverbial.

summary:
A postpositional phrase (PP) is headed by a postposition and always follows an NP complement, with any case-inflected parts of that NP appearing in the genitive as well as agreeing in number. The complement can be various kinds of nominal phrases, such as nouns, demonstratives, pronouns, or interrogative phrases.  

PPs can function as clause-level adverbials, especially to express location, and a few postpositions may also be used as prepositions, though the corpus evidence for this is too limited to support conclusions.

chapter: Overview of the syntax of sentences
text:
In describing \ clauses, it is useful to begin with basic clauses that contain a full predicate and its arguments, complements and/or adjuncts, before moving on to describe complex clauses which consist of two or more clauses linked to one another.
Therefore, basic clauses are described in Chapter basicClauses, including declarative, interrogative and imperative clauses. Chapter complexClauses then deals with complex clauses, covering coordination and subordination.

However, in order to better understand the syntax of sentences, it is sensible to begin with two general discussions that provide a framework for understanding the syntactic descriptions that follow. The first of these, in grammaticalRelations below, covers grammatical relations in Pite Saami. This leads to the second discussion in constituentOrderClauses, which concerns clause-level constituent ordering, and the likely role that information structure plays in determining this.
summary:
The passage says that the description of clauses begins with basic clauses containing a full predicate and its arguments, complements, and/or adjuncts, and then moves to complex clauses made up of two or more linked clauses. Basic clauses are covered in Chapter basicClauses, including declarative, interrogative, and imperative clauses, while Chapter complexClauses covers coordination and subordination.

It also explains that two general discussions come first to provide a framework for the syntax: grammatical relations in Pite Saami, and clause-level constituent order, including the likely influence of information structure.

chapter: Overview of the syntax of sentences
text:
grammatical relations|(
\ is an accusative language because
the only argument of an intransitive valency!intransitive verb (S) is marked in the same way as the most-agent-like argument of a transitive valency!transitive verb (A): by the nominative case!nominative case.
The most-patient-like argument of a transitive verb (P) is marked differently: by the accusative case!accusative case. This is illustrated by the following examples, with an intransitive verb in intrans1 and a (mono-)transitive verb in monotrans1.

så mån tjielka sinne vällahiv\\
så mån tjielka sinne vällahi-v\\
so 1sg.nom sled gen.sg in lie- 1sg.pst\\
So I lay in the sled. 100404303

dä almatj biejaj risev dále nåvte\\
dä almatj bieja-j rise-v dále nåvte\\
then person nom.sg put- 3sg.prs stick- acc.sg now so\\
Then one places the stick like this. 100404216

The direct object of a ditransitive valency!ditransitive verb is also in the case!accusativeaccusative case, while the indirect object
of a ditransitive verb is in an oblique case (usually in the illative case!illative case, which prototypically indicates that the noun refers to the goal of a movement), as illustrated in ditrans1.

mån vaddav suhta buhtsujda biebmov\\
mån vadda-v suhta buhtsu-jda biebmo-v\\
1sg.nom give- 1sg.prs several reindeer- ill.pl food- acc.sg\\
I give food to several reindeer. 110413b157

Grammatical relations in \ are thus marked by morphological means. Constituent ordering constituent order does not indicate grammatical relations in any way. For instance, in monotrans2 the object precedes the subject.

ja dáv aj mån vuojnav vinndegest muv dåbest\\
ja d-á-v aj mån vuojna-v vindege-st muv dåbe-st\\
and dem- prox- acc.sg also 1sg.nom see- 1sg.prs window- elat.sg 1sg.gen house- elat.sg\\
And I also see this from the window from my house. 100310b030

The following section
provides more examples illustrating the flexibility of constituent ordering.
grammatical relations|)
summary: The passage explains that this language is accusative: the sole argument of an intransitive verb and the agent-like argument of a transitive verb are both marked with nominative case, while the patient-like argument is marked with accusative case. In ditransitive constructions, the direct object also takes accusative, while the indirect object appears in an oblique case, usually illative. It also states that grammatical relations are expressed morphologically rather than by word order, since constituent order is flexible and does not signal subject or object status.

chapter: Overview of the syntax of sentences
text:
constituent order|(
Clause-level constituent ordering in \ is not determined syntactically.
That being said, in elicited clauses from the corpus, some ordering patterns do occur more frequently than others, and indicate that SVO ordering is preferred in context-free elicited clauses, everything else being equal.
This is illustrated by the examples in standardConstOrder1 through standardConstOrder3.

sån usjuda\\
sån usjuda\\
3sg.nom think 3sg.prs \\
He thinks. 081011154

mån vuojnav bierdnav\\
mån vuojna-v bierdna-v\\
1sg.nom see- 1sg.prs bear- acc.sg \\
I see a bear. 08092601m24s

ålmaj vaddá blåmåv kuijdnaj\\
ålmaj vaddá blåmå-v kuijdna-j\\
man nom.sg give 3sg.prs flower- acc.sg woman- ill.sg\\
The man gives the flower to the woman. 10032465m25s

It is possible that this ordering is triggered by typical Swedish language contact constituent ordering, which is generally SVO, as Swedish was often used as the meta-language in elicitation sessions.

More significantly, the part of the \ corpus consisting of natural language situations confirms the lack of any set constituent ordering based on syntactic criteria. Note that Sammallahti claims that at least for North Saami (although it is not entirely clear whether he means North Saami or is generalizing for all Saami languages here), the “order of the main constituents […] is largely free from formal restrictions and guided by pragmatic principles”, but then states that the “basic order is SVO”. This seems to reflect the data from the \ corpus to the extent that context-free elicited clauses tend to be SVO, while in fact no syntactic criteria for constituent ordering can be ascertained in natural language.
Lagercrantz takes several pages to describe a variety of tendencies in constituent ordering for \ declarative clauses, even after describing ordering preferences concerning topic information structure!topic and focus information structure!focus within a discourse and summarizing the actual situation by stating quite vaguely that the position of the subject in a clause has a ‘certain stylistic effect’ (“Die Stellung des Satzgegenstandes hat eine gewisse stilistische Wirkung”).
Perhaps current descriptions of the syntax of the Saami languages would be better served if linguists
would cease trying to force these languages into an inaccurate (but typologically neat) label such as SVO.
To illustrate this syntactic flexibility, examples of SOV and OSV
constituent ordering are provided in deviantConstituentOrder1 and deviantConstituentOrder2,
respectively.

mån vuostasj vierbmev biejav Áktjuotjålbmáj \\
mån vuostasj vierbme-v bieja-v Áktjuotjålbmá-j \\
1sg.nom first net- acc.sg put- 1sg.prs Áktjuotjålbme- ill.sg\\
First I’ll put out the net in Áktjuotjålbme. 090702024

sågijd mån anav\\
sågi-jd mån ana-v\\
birch- acc.pl 1sg.nom use- 1sg.prs \\
I use birchwood. 090702149

The example in deviantConstituentOrder4 has VSO constituent order, and additionally has the non-finite verb complement!phrasecomplement (with OV ordering) in clause-final position.

dä galgav mån gåvåjd vuosedit\\
dä galga-v mån gåvå-jd vuosedi-t\\
then will- 1sg.prs 1sg.nom picture- acc.pl show- inf \\
Then I will show some pictures. 080825036

Attempting to determine constituent order patterns is further complicated by the fact that it is sometimes impossible to tell what the constituent ordering is because NPs phrase!nominal referring to
information provided by context alone are frequently not realized overtly, as in deviantConstituentOrder4 above and missingNP1 through missingNP4 below.

ber aktak tjårvev adna \\
ber aktak tjårve-v adna \\
only one antler- acc.sg have 3sg.prs\\
(The reindeer) only has one antler. 100405b019

gallga giesset ulgus\\
gallga giesse-t ulgus\\
will 3sg.prs pull- inf out\\
(The reindeer herder) will pull (the reindeer buck) out. 080909017

mån biejav dut\\
mån bieja-v dut\\
1sg.nom put- 1sg.prs there\\
I’ll put (the pole) there. 100404218

ja vadde, Eva-Karin!\\
ja vadde Eva-Karin\\
and give 2sg.imp Eva-Karin\\
And give (me) (a sausage), Eva-Karin! 090519208

While person person and number number markers on the finite verb indicate grammatical information about the subject, there is no overt subject in missingNP1 or missingNP2. The clauses in missingNP2 through missingNP4 are lacking overt objects. The final example is also missing the indirect object.

Indeed, a complete clause can consist of nothing more than an inflected verb, as in the response
in missingNP5, which consists of nothing more than the copular verb verb!copular inflected for 3sg.prs.

A: ja tjábba dállke!\\
ja tjábba dállke\\
and beautiful weather nom.sg \\
and such beautiful weather!\\
B: lä.\\
lä\\
be 3sg.prs\\
yes, it is(lit.: ‘is’)

The source of the example in missingNP5 is a recording
collected by linguist Martin Hilpert Hilpert, Martin during a pilot project he completed on \ in 2005. I am very grateful to him for providing me with his recordings and annotations. Note that Martin’s recordings are not included in the \ documentation corpus.

However, there are no examples in the corpus of verb-initial clauses featuring both an overt subject and a VC with a single verb. While there are plenty of examples of the finite verb preceding the subject and most other clausal constituents, some constituent always precedes the verb. Frequently, it is the adverb dä, as in ConstOrderAdvVex1.

ja dä båhta reksak\\
ja dä båhta reksak\\
and then come 3sg.prs ptarmigan nom.sg \\
And then a ptarmigan comes. 100404241

If the subject is not realized overtly, or if the VC contains more than one verb form, then the finite verb can be clause initial, as in ConstOrderAdvVex2 and ConstOrderAdvVex3, respectively.

bisij dajd dä såbe nanne\\
bisi-j d-a-jd dä såbe nanne\\
grill- 3sg.pst dem- dist- acc.pl then stick gen.sg on\\
He grilled them then on a stick. 100404125

ittjiv mån mujte\\
ittji-v mån mujte\\
neg- 1sg.pst 1sg.nom remember conneg \\
I didn’t remember. 100404227
summary:
The passage argues that clause-level constituent order in the language is not fixed by syntactic rules, even though context-free elicited clauses often show a preference for SVO order. This apparent tendency may reflect Swedish influence during elicitation, while natural corpus data show that constituent order is flexible and guided by pragmatic factors rather than a rigid basic order.  

The text also notes that SOV, OSV, and VSO orders occur, and that many clauses lack overt subjects or objects, sometimes consisting of only an inflected verb. In clauses with an overt subject and a single verb, no examples were found where the finite verb is clause-initial; when verb-initial order does occur, some other constituent usually precedes the verb.

chapter: Overview of the syntax of sentences
text:
information structure|(
Considering the syntactic flexibility described above, it is only reasonable to consider information structure as a constituent ordering constituent order strategy.
While a thorough investigation of information structure in \ is beyond the scope of the present study
and must be left for more thorough future research, some preliminary observations can be made.

Specifically, declarative clause!declarative clauses typically begin with the topic information structure!topic (frequently the subject in the nominative case!nominative case) and end with a comment on that topic. If the comment involves a transitive valency!transitive verb, the object or clause!complementcomplement clause (the focus information structure!focus) normally follows the verb, as in standardConstOrder2 and standardConstOrder3 above. However, clausal elements in focus can be moved from their ‘default’ position, which results in significant deviations from the
preferred SVO constituent order. This is reflected in constituent interrogative clause!interrogative!constituent clauses; here, the interrogative pronoun is in focus and always in clause-initial position
(cf. constituentQs ).

The short example text presented in mouseText4 and mouseText5 below should serve to give an impression of how information structure may be the driving force behind constituent ordering at clause-level. Here, the speaker is talking about looking inside her mother’s shoes after discovering that a mouse had been in them.

ja danne vuojdniv unna jåŋåtjav.\\
ja danne vuojdni-v unna jåŋå-tja-v\\
and there see- 1sg.pst small lingonberry- dim- acc.sg\\
And there I saw a little lingonberry. 100404353

jahkav skafferijav lä danne adnam,\\
jahka-v skafferija-v lä danne adna-m\\
believe- 1sg.prs pantry- acc.sg be 3sg.prs there have- prf\\
I think (the mouse) had a pantry there. 100404354

In the first clause mouseText4, the topic information structure!topic is danne ‘there’, which refers to the shoes (the topic of the anecdote at this point) and is clause-initial. The constituent jåŋåtjav ‘lingonberry’ is the focus information structure!focus, but it is not particularly significant in the anecdote, and it follows the finite verb vuojdniv ‘I saw’.
However, when particular emphasis is placed on the focus, as in the following clause in mouseText5, the constituent in focus can be fronted. Here, skafferijav ‘pantry’ is in focus, and receives particular emphasis The NP skafferijav ‘pantry’ probably receives special emphasis because it personifies the behavior of the mouse in a light-hearted way by claiming that a mouse can have a pantry. by occurring before the verb complex lä danne adnam ‘has had there’, while the topic (the mouse) is not realized overtly at all, but implied by the context and by the finite verb form inflected for 3sg.
This fronting of a constituent is often accompanied by higher acoustic intensity, as is the case here.
information structure|) constituent order|)
summary: The passage argues that information structure is a key strategy shaping constituent order in clauses. In declarative clauses, topics typically come first and comments follow, while focused elements normally appear after the verb but can be fronted for emphasis, as shown in constituent questions and the example sentences. Fronting the focus can significantly disrupt the preferred SVO order and is often marked by greater acoustic intensity.

text:
A basic clause is a syntactic unit at text-level consisting minimally of a finite verb!finite verb. In declarative clauses and interrogative clauses, this finite verb is marked morphologically for person person, number number, tense tense and/or mood mood. Aspect aspect can be expressed analytically at the clause level using an auxiliary verb and a non-finite verb form verb!non-finite.
In all basic clauses, the finite verb agrees agreement in number and, with the exception of imperative mood!imperativemood, in person with the syntactic subject of the sentence, which is a nominal phrase in the nominative case.
NPs referring to information provided by context alone are not necessarily realized overtly. As a result, the syntactic subject and other verbal arguments are often not overtly present.

The following sections first present basic declarative clauses with intransitive and transitive verbs, existential clauses, copular clauses and complex verbal constructions consisting of more than one verb ( declClauses ). Then, interrogClauses deals with interrogative clauses,
before imperClauses and potClauses cover syntactic aspects of the imperative mood and the potential mood, respectively.
summary: A basic clause is a text-level syntactic unit that minimally consists of a finite verb, which in declarative and interrogative clauses is morphologically marked for person, number, tense, and/or mood. The finite verb agrees in number and usually person with the syntactic subject in the nominative case, while aspect may be expressed analytically with an auxiliary and a non-finite verb form. Because noun phrases recoverable from context need not be overtly expressed, subjects and other verbal arguments are often omitted.

text:
clause!declarative|(
Declarative clauses are the most common type of clause in the \ corpus. In the following, declarative clauses with a single verb are dealt with first, covering intransitive and transitive verbs, and two special cases (existential clauses and copular clauses). Then, declarative clauses featuring a modal or auxiliary verb in addition to the lexical head verb are described; because negation negation is expressed by an auxiliary verb, it is covered in the same section. While constituent ordering is mentioned in the following sections, it mostly refers to tendencies only, and the flexible nature of \ constituent ordering should always be kept in mind, as discussed in constituentOrderClauses.
summary: Declarative clauses are the most common clause type in the corpus. The passage says it will first describe declarative clauses with a single verb, including intransitive and transitive verbs as well as existential and copular clauses, and then clauses with modal or auxiliary verbs, including negation since it is expressed by an auxiliary. It also notes that constituent order is discussed only as a tendency, because clause constituent ordering is flexible.

text:
The subject of an intransitive declarative clause is in the nominative case,
as in basicIntransDeclaratives1 through basicIntransDeclaratives3.

almatj usjut ja...\\
almatj usjut ja\\
person nom.sg think 3sg.prs and \%odd-syllable verbs for ER have no -a in 3sg.prs, but do have -a for DS, IF
One thinks, and... 100404172

mån tjájmav\\
mån tjájma-v\\
1sg.nom laugh- 1sg.prs \\
I laugh. 100323a005

dáj Skaile ello såkoj\\
d-á-j Skaile ello såko-j\\
dem- prox- gen.pl Skaile gen.pl reindeer.herd nom.sg drown- 3sg.pst \\

text:
passive
When a transitive verb is passivized, Transitive verbs can be passivized using the derivational suffix suffix!derivational -duvv; cf. VdervPassives on derivational morphology and passiveVinflection on inflectional morphology for passives.
its valency is reduced, and it becomes intransitive. In this, the patient is the subject of the verb complex phrase!verb complex, and therefore marked by nominative case!nominative case; the agent may be left out. This is illustrated by the pair of elicited examples in passVoiceEx1 and passVoiceEx2, in which the former is a transitive clause in active voice, and the latter is an intransitive clause in passive voice.

máná lä tsiggim gådev\\
máná lä tsiggi-m gåde-v\\
child nom.pl be 3pl.prs build- prf hut- acc.sg\\
Children have built the hut. 110518a28m14s

dat lä tsiggiduvvum\\
d-a-t lä tsiggi-duvvu-m\\
dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.prs build- pass- prf\\
That (hut) was built. 110518a27m41s

Similarly, the example from a narrative in passVoiceEx2b presents an intransitive valency!intransitive passive construction.

dát lä vanj dä gajk vuorasumos dágaduvvum\\

dem- prox- nom.sg be 3sg.prs probably then all old- superl sg make- pass- prf\\
This was probably the absolute oldest made.\\ 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a120

The NP referring to the agent of an event can optionally occur obliquely in the elative case if the verb is passivized, as in passVoiceEx3.
gåhte lä tsiggiduvvum mánájst\\

text:
In declarative clauses featuring a monotransitive valency!transitive verb,
the subject is in nominative case!nominative and is typically the agent, while the object is in the accusative case!accusative case and is typically the patient of the predicate. Examples can be seen in basicMonotransDeclaratives1 through basicMonotransDeclaratives3.

ja mån vuojnav muähtagav danne\\
ja mån vuojna-v muähtaga-v danne\\
and 1sg.nom see- 1sg.prs snow- acc.sg here\\
And I see snow here. 100404020

danne sáme edne båhtsujd giesen\\
danne sáme edne båhtsu-jd giese-n\\
there Saami nom.pl have 3pl.prs reindeer- acc.pl summer- iness.sg \\
The Saami keep the reindeer there in the summer. 100404011

almatj bedja virbmijd ehket\\
almatj bedja virbmi-jd ehket\\
person nom.sg put 3sg.prs fishing.net- acc.pl evening\% nom.sg\\
One puts out fishing nets in the evening. 100310b020

In declarative clauses with a ditransitive valency!ditransitive verb, the direct object is also in the case!accusativeaccusative case and is typically theme, while the indirect object, typically recipient, is normally in the illative case!illative case. Examples can be seen in basicDitransDeclaratives1 and basicDitransDeclaratives2.

mån vaddav gålbmå buhtsujda biebmov\\
mån vadda-v gålbmå buhtsu-jda biebmo-v\\

summary: In declarative clauses with monotransitive verbs, the subject is nominative and typically functions as the agent, while the object is accusative and typically functions as the patient. In ditransitive clauses, the direct object is also accusative and usually the theme, whereas the indirect object is normally in the illative case and usually the recipient.

clause!existential|(
The verb gävdnut Much like its Swedish language contact counterpart finnas, which is a derivation of the verb finna ‘find’, the \ verb gävdnut is derived from the verb gávdnat ‘find’.
is used as an existential verb. Note that a clause!copularcopular clause containing an adjunct can also be used as an existential; cf. copulaClauses.
The item whose existence is posited is the syntactic subject of the sentence and thus in the nominative case!nominative case, which gävdnut agrees agreement in person and number with.
Examples can be found in existential1 and existential2.

váren gävdnu aj juomo\\
váre-n gävdnu aj juomo\\
mountain- iness.sg exist 3pl.prs also sorrel nom.pl\\
There is sorrel in the mountains, too.(lit.: there are sorrels…) 080924178

dal itjij gävndoj aktak tjårvebielle\\
dal itji-j gävndoj aktak tjårve-bielle\\
now neg- 3sg.pst exist conneg any horn-half nom.sg\\
There isn’t a single tjårvebielle \ now. 100405b021

A tjårvebielle (lit.: horn-half) is a term used to describe a reindeer with only one antler remaining after the other antler has broken off.

The subject frequently follows the verb because the subject is often the focus information structure!focus of the clause, but as the clause in existential3 shows, the subject may occur before the verb if it is the topic information structure!topic and/or is presupposed knowledge (cf. infoStructure on information structure).

motora vadnasij. “motora” ij gävdnu sáme gielan\\
motora vadnasi-j motora ij gävdnu sáme giela-n\\
motor gen.sg boat- com.pl “motor” neg 3sg.prs exist conneg Saami gen.sg language- iness.sg\\
…with motor boats. There is no (word for) “motor” in the Saami language. 080924482,484

clause!existential|)
summary:
The verb **gävdnut**, like Swedish **finnas**, is an existential verb derived from the verb **gávdnat** ‘find’. In existential clauses, the entity whose existence is asserted functions as the syntactic subject, appears in the nominative case, and agrees with **gävdnut** in person and number.  

The subject often follows the verb because it is typically focused, but it can also precede the verb when it is topical or presupposed. The passage also notes that a copular clause with an adjunct can sometimes serve the same existential function.

clause!copular|(
There are several types of copular clauses in Pite Saami. All of these feature the copular verb verb!copular årrot ‘be’
(see theCopulaVerb for more details).
Copular clauses can be used to express a variety of information about the subject referent, and these are discussed below.

When the complement of the copula is an NP phrase!nominal in nominative case!nominative case, it identifies or classifies the subject referent, as in copula1 and copula2, respectively.

Mattijá lij morbror munje\\
Mattijá li-j morbror munje\\
Matthias nom.sg be- 3sg.pst maternal.uncle nom.sg 1sg.ill\\
Matthias was my maternal uncle. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a007

mån lev sábme\\
mån le-v sábme\\
1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs Saami nom.sg\\
I am a Saami. 08081300m35s

Note that morbror is a nonce borrowing from language contactSwedish. Cf. Swedish morbror ‘maternal uncle’.

The complement of a copular clause can be one or more phrase!adjectivaladjectival phrases headed by a predicative adjective which ascribes properties to the subject referent, as in copula3.

buhtsoj lä nav buojde ja tjábbe\\
buhtsoj lä nav buojde ja tjábbe\\
reindeer nom.pl be 3pl.prs so fat pl and beautiful pl\\
The reindeer are so fat and beautiful. 080703014

The complement of a copular clause can be an NP in the inessive case!inessive case in which case it describes the location of the subject referent, as in copula4.

måj lijmen Fuordnagin\\
måj lij-men Fuordnagi-n\\
1du.nom be- 1du.pst Fuordnak- iness.sg\\
We two were in Fuordnak. 080924590

The complement of a copular clause can be an NP in the elative case!elative case in which case it describes the material which the subject referent is made of, as in copula5.

ja dát lä aj struvdast\\
ja d-á-t lä aj struvda-st\\
and dem- prox- nom.sg be 3sg.prs also cloth- elat.sg\\
And this is also (made) of cloth. 080708_Session08080708_Session08015

A copular clause can also function as an clause!existentialexistential clause when it includes a temporal adjunct. In such cases, the existence of the subject referent is posited at that particular time indicated by the adjunct. Pragmatically, this usually announces an event connected to the subject referent. Typically, the temporal referent occurs first constituent order in the sentence, then the copular verb, and the subject is last (just as with the existential verb gädvnut; cf. existentialClauses ), as it is usually the information structure!focusfocus.
This is illustrated by the example in copulaNr.

ja dále'l káffa\\
ja dále=l káffa\\
and now=be 3sg.prs coffee nom.sg\\
And now it’s coffee (time). 090519313

Possession possession can also be expressed by a copular construction. In such a construction, the possessed NP is the subject of the clause in the nominative case!nominative case, which the finite verb agrees agreement with in person and number. The possessor NP is in the inessive case!inessive case. Such a construction is illustrated by the example in copula6.

muvne lä akta mánná\\
muvne lä akta mánná\\
1sg.iness be 3sg.prs one child nom.sg\\
I have one child. 08062130m54s

In the corpus, such possessive constructions always have the constituent order
possessor copula possessed.

While this type of possessive construction is the native Saamic structure, it is very uncommon in the \ corpus, and almost exclusively limited to elicitation sessions. The elicitation scenario may have had an effect on the constituent order, The equivalent language contactSwedish structure is also normally possessor \ verb \ possessed.
but it is more likely the case that the constituent order reflects information structure preferences, specifically the tendency for the topic information structure!topic (more often the possessor, which is animate) to come before the information structure!focusfocus Cf. infoStructure on information structure.
(more often the possessed, which is inanimate).

In any case, a clause-level construction using the monotransitive valency!transitive verb adnet ‘have’ Historically, adnet meant ‘use’ or ‘keep’, but synchronically it is most frequently used to indicate possession in a transitive verb construction which is essentially identical to the equivalent language contactSwedish verb ha or the English verb have.
expressing possession, as in copula7, is now the standard in Pite Saami. While this construction using the transitive verb adnet ‘have’ is clearly not a copular clause, it is worth pointing this out here, particularly for any readers from Uralic studies, because the copular construction (as in the example in copula6) is no longer the true standard for expressing possession at clause level in.

ja dä inijmä gusajd \\
ja dä ini-jmä gusa-jd \\
and then have- 1pl.pst cow- acc.pl\\
And then we had cows. 080924091

clause!copular|)
summary: Pite Saami copular clauses use the verb *årrot* ‘be’ and can express identification, classification, adjectival properties, location, or material composition, depending on the type of complement. They can also function as existential clauses with temporal adjuncts and as possessive constructions, where the possessor is in the inessive and the possessed NP is the nominative subject. Although this possessive copular pattern is native, it is rare in the corpus and has largely been replaced by the transitive verb *adnet* ‘have’ for possession at clause level.

Verbs which govern non-finite verb!non-finite verbal complements clause!complement can be classified into three groups based on the type of non-finite complement verb form they co-occur with, as illustrated in Table auxVerbTable.

The finite verb occurs before the non-finite lexical complement verb, unless the complement is in information structure!focusfocus, in which case it can occur before the finite verb.
These verb types are dealt with in modalVs, auxV and negation, respectively.
summary: Verbs that take non-finite verbal complements are grouped into three classes according to the type of non-finite complement verb form they combine with. In these constructions, the finite verb normally precedes the non-finite lexical complement verb, but if the complement is in focus it may come before the finite verb.

verb!modal|(
Modal verbs are used to express modality for the event denoted by the verbal complement. The complement!phrasecomplementing verb is in the infinitive (marked by the suffix -t). Modal verbs include máhttat ‘can, be able to’,
ådtjot The modal verb ådtjot ‘be allowed to’ is homophonous with the full verb ådtjot ‘get, receive’. This pattern is found in language contactSwedish, as well, with the verb få ‘be allowed to’ and ‘receive’, and in English, e.g.: ‘I get to go to the movies’.
‘may, be allowed to’,
virrtit ‘must’, hähttut The word hähttut ‘must’ is likely limited to northern dialects of Pite Saami.
‘must’, sihtat ‘want’ and gallgat ‘will/shall’.
Some examples are provided in modalVerbs1 through modalVerbs3.

tjátsev ådtjobihtet juhgat dasste\\
tjátse-v ådtjo-bihtet juhga-t d-a-sste\\
water- acc.sg may- 2pl.prs drink- inf dem- dist- iness.sg\\
You all may drink water from that. 090519022

ja dä del virrtin allget bäbbmat\\
ja dä del virrti-n allge-t bäbbma-t\\
and then well must- 3pl.pst begin- inf feed- inf\\

mij máhttep ságastit Bidumsáme gielav\\
mij máhtte-p ságasti-t Bidum-sáme giela-v\\
1pl.nom can- 1pl.prs speak- inf Pite-Saami gen.sg language- acc.sg\\
We can speak the Pite Saami language. 110517b2022

The modal verb sihtat ‘want’ behaves the same when the subject of the complementing verb complex is coreferential with the subject of the matrix clause, as in modalVerbs4.

mån sidav gulijd adnet\\
mån sida-v guli-jd adne-t\\
1sg.nom want- 1sg.prs fish- acc.pl have- inf\\
I want to have fish. 090702012

However, when the subject of the modal verb sihtat is not coreferential with the subject of the complement!phrasecomplementing verb complex phrase!verb complex, then a finite verb clause
is the complement to the modal verb, as in the negated clause in modalVerbs5. Note that, here, sihtat is in the connegative non-finite form sida.

dä ij del almatj sida nagin sadjáj vuällget\\
dä i-j del almatj sida nagin sadjá-j vuällge-t\\
then neg- 3sg.prs obviously person nom.sg want conneg some place- ill.sg go- inf\\
Then one obviously doesn’t want to go anywhere. 080924052

The modal verb gallgat ‘will’ can also be used to locate events in the future tense!future, as in future1 through future3 below.

dä galgav såmes mujjtemuv ságastit\\
dä galga-v såmes mujjtemu-v ságasti-t\\
then will- 1sg.prs some memory- acc.sg say- inf\\
Then I will tell (you) a memory. 100703a001

jo, da lä akta vuoberis, gallga giesset ulgus\\
jo da lä akta vuoberis gallga giesse-t ulgus\\
yes then be 3sg.prs one buck nom.sg will 3sg.prs pull- inf out\\
Yes, it’s a 3-year old reindeer buck, (he) will pull (it) out. 080909016-017
Specifically, a vuoberis is a three-year-old reindeer buck, but the gloss has been shortened to save space.

gallgap dav girjev ådtjot\\
gallga-p d-a-v girje-v ådtjo-t\\
will- 1pl.prs dem- dist- acc.sg book- acc.sg get- inf\\
We will get that book. 110517b2022

The modal verb gallgat ‘will’ is often used in conditional mood!conditional clauses, as in condClause1.

jus galga sáme viesov valldet, dä galga mielagav dal navt rutastit\\
jus galga sáme vieso-v vallde-t dä galga mielaga-v dal navt rutasti-t\\
if will 3sg.prs Saami gen.sg life- acc.sg take- inf then will 3sg.prs sternum- acc.sg then so pull- inf\\
If I choose Saami style, then I will pull the sternum like this. 080909097

verb!modal|)
summary:
Modal verbs in Pite Saami express modality for the event in the infinitival complement, which is marked with the suffix -t. The modal verbs listed include máhttat ‘can’, ådtjot ‘be allowed to’, virrtit/hähttut ‘must’, sihtat ‘want’, and gallgat ‘will/shall’; ådtjot is homophonous with the full verb meaning ‘get, receive’.  

The passage shows that sihtat takes an infinitival complement when its subject is coreferential with the matrix subject, but a finite clause when the subjects differ. It also notes that gallgat can mark future reference and is often used in conditional clauses.

verb!negation verb|(
\ clause negation is expressed by a special finite negation negation verb. Unlike other verbs, the negation verb does not have an infinitive or any other non-finite form verb!non-finite, but is always a finite verb (cf. theNegationVerb ). As such, it always agrees agreement in person and number with the subject of the clause, and inflects for tense and mood as well. In this respect, \ differs significantly from for instance North Saami negative clauses in which the main verb and not the finite negation verb inflects for tense.
The complement!phrasecomplement verb occurs in a special non-finite form called the connegative.
Examples for the negative verb can be found in negation1 through negation3.

iv jáhke\\
i-v jáhke\\
neg-1sg.prs believe conneg \\
I don’t believe so. 090702411

ittjij åbbå gävdno vuodja åsstet\\
ittji-j åbbå gävdno vuodja åsste-t\\
neg-3sg.pst at.all exist conneg butter nom.sg buy- inf\\
There wasn’t any butter to buy at all. 080708_Session03080708_Session03006

men ijtjin del bårå dan sisste \\
men ijtji-n del bårå d-a-n sisste \\
but neg-3pl.pst then eat conneg dem- dist- gen.sg out\\
But they didn’t eat out of this. 080708_Session03080708_Session03019

In the examples above, the non-finite complement!phrasecomplement to the connegative verb!non-finite!connegative verb is a lexical verb. In the following examples in negation4 through negation6, the complement connegative verb is a verb!modalmodal or verb!auxiliaryauxiliary verb whose own complement then follows in the appropriate non-finite form.

ij vanj dä máhte ilá stuor dålåv adnet\\

While \ constituent order constituent order is generally flexible (cf. constituentOrderClauses ), there are no examples in the corpus of the verb of negation occurring after the negated complement, but instead the connegative complement verb always follows the finite negation verb in a clause.

summary: Clause negation is expressed by a special finite negation verb, which always inflects for person, number, tense, and mood and has no non-finite forms. The main complement verb appears in a special non-finite connegative form; if the complement is a modal or auxiliary, its own complement then follows in the appropriate non-finite form. In the corpus, the connegative verb always follows the finite negation verb, and there are no examples of the negation verb occurring after its complement.

text: Constituent interrogative clauses in \ are consistently marked as such syntactically, and thus are distinct from declarative clauses. Polar interrogative clauses, on the other hand, do not differ significantly from declarative clauses, although some syntactic constructions are more common than others. The following sections deal first with constituent interrogative clauses, then polar interrogative clauses in more detail.
summary: Constituent interrogative clauses are consistently marked syntactically and are therefore distinct from declarative clauses. Polar interrogative clauses show little syntactic difference from declaratives, though some constructions are more frequent than others. The discussion first addresses constituent interrogatives and then turns to polar interrogatives in more detail.

text:
clause!interrogative!constituent|(
Constituent interrogative clauses are the only type of independent clause in \ which is consistently marked syntactically as a clause type. Specifically, every constituent interrogative clause is marked as such by having an interrogative word or phrase in clause-initial position. When it is an interrogative pronoun, it inflects for case and number consistent with its grammatical role in the clause (as with any pronoun), while the humanness of its (expected) referent determines the choice of the root. Interrogative pronouns referring to non-human NPs all feature a ma- root, while those referring to human NPs have a ge- root. Interrogative adverbs also begin with g-. Cf. interrogativePronouns.
Some examples can be found in questionWordQ1 through questionWordQ4.

mav dån hålå?\\
ma-v dån hålå\\
what- acc.sg 2sg.nom say 2sg.prs\\
What are you saying? 090519329

majd dä viehkedi?\\
ma-jd dä viehkedi\\
what- acc.pl then help 2sg.pst\\
What then did you help (with)? 080924615

gejna dä tjuovvo\\
ge-jna dä tjuovvo\\
who- com.sg then accompany 2sg.pst\\
Who did you go with? 080924071

man mällgadav ana dajd riehpenen\\
man mällgada-v ana d-a-jd riehpene-n\\
how long- acc.sg have 2sg.prs dem- dist- acc.pl smoke.hole- iness.sg\\
How long do you have those in the smoke hole for? 090702168

Alternatively, the interrogative can be an adverb adverb, as in questionWordQ6 through questionWordQ8.

gukt lä dát\\
gukte lä d-á-t\\
how be 3sg.prs dem- prox- nom.sg\\
How is it? 080924130

guste dån bådá\\
guste dån bådá\\
from.where 2sg.nom come 2sg.prs\\
Where are you coming from? 080924003

gånne dajt tjogidä\\
gånne d-a-jt tjogi-dä\\
where dem- dist- acc.pl pick- 2pl.pst\\
Where did you pick those? 080924168

Assuming that any constituent which is the pragmatic focus information structure!focus can be marked by fronting, as preliminarily asserted in infoStructure, then the fronting of the interrogative word is consistent with focus-marking. However, for constituent interrogative clauses, fronting is then obligatory.
The rest of the clause is constructed syntactically just as freely as any declarative clause!declarative clause would be. While subject-verb inversion can occur, the flexible nature of \ constituent ordering prevents this from necessarily marking a clause as interrogative.

It is worth noting that the discourse marker nå, which can be translated as ‘well’ or sometimes ‘yes’, frequently precedes constituent interrogative clauses, as in nåQ1. However, it is not obligatory, nor is it restricted to interrogative clauses. It is likely a discourse marker, perhaps simply indicating the speaker’s active interest in the conversation.

nå gukte lij Áhkabákten gu dånnå lidje mánná?\\
nå gukte li-j Áhkabákte-n gu dånnå lidje mánná\\

Well what was Áhkkabákkte like when you were a child? 080924063

clause!interrogative!constituent|)
summary: Constituent interrogative clauses are the only independent clause type that is consistently marked syntactically, by placing an interrogative word or phrase in clause-initial position. Interrogative pronouns agree in case and number with their grammatical role, with ma- roots used for non-human referents, ge- roots for human referents, and interrogative adverbs beginning with g-; the rest of the clause is otherwise built like a declarative clause, though subject-verb inversion may occur but is not diagnostic. The discourse marker nå often precedes these clauses, but it is optional and not specific to interrogatives.

text:
clause!interrogative!polar|(
Because of flexible constituent ordering in Pite Saami, there is no reliable syntactic test for whether a clause is a polar interrogative. The intonation intonation of polar questions does not seem to differ significantly from any other types of clauses, either.
However, polar interrogative clauses frequently have a constituent order constituent order in which the finite verb!finite verb occurs before the subject.
Furthermore, this finite verb is generally the first element in a clause. The examples in polarQinversion1 through polarQinversion3 illustrate this.

galga dån ságastit enabuv?\\
galga dån ságasti-t ena-bu-v\\
will 2sg.prs 2sg.nom say- inf much- comp- acc.sg\\
Are you going to say more? 0906_Ahkajavvre_b0906_Ahkajavvre_b041

suovade dån?\\
suovade dån\\
smoke 2sg.prs 2sg.nom\\
Do you smoke? 080702b073

lij sån uktu jala lij Halvar aj maŋŋen\\
li-j sån uktu jala li-j Halvar aj maŋŋen\\
be- 3sg.pst 3sg.nom alone or be- 3sg.pst Halvar nom.sg also along\\
Was he alone or was Halvar also along? 080924308

As with any \ clause, the syntactic subject does not have to be realized overtly. In such cases, the finite verb is also usually word initial, as in polarQinversion4.

udtju sáme gielav danne sagastit?\\
udtju sáme giela-v danne sagasti-t\\
may 2sg.pst Saami gen.sg language- acc.sg there speak- inf\\
Were you allowed to speak Saami there? 080924351

However, it is also possible to front other elements which normally occur after the finite verb, as in polarQinversion5 and polarQinversion6. Here, the non-finite verb!non-finite perfect form of the complement!phrasecomplement verb immediately precedes the aspect-marking aspect auxiliary verb.

juhkum lä gajtsa mielkev?\\
juhku-m lä gajtsa mielke-v\\
drink- prf be 2sg.prs goat gen.sg milk- acc.sg\\
Have you ever drunk goat’s milk? 080924128

bårråm lä dån biergov danne?\\
bårrå-m lä dån biergo-v danne\\
eat- prf be 2sg.prs 2sg.nom meat- acc.sg there\\
Have you eaten meat there? 090519130
summary:
In Pite Saami, there is no reliable syntactic or intonational test for identifying polar interrogative clauses because constituent order is flexible and question intonation is not clearly distinct. However, polar questions frequently show inversion, with the finite verb occurring before the subject and often as the first element in the clause.

When the subject is omitted, the finite verb is usually clause-initial as well. The passage also shows that other elements can be fronted before the finite verb, including a non-finite perfect verb form before the aspect auxiliary.

subsubsection: Polar interrogatives and the question marker
text:
interrogative!question marker
It is possible for polar interrogative clauses to be identified as such by a question marker gu gus following the finite verb. However, the use of the question marker in polar interrogatives is exceptionally uncommon and can hardly be considered obligatory in current \ usage; this is reflected in the data from the corpus, which contain only three tokens. See QpartWordform for a preliminary discussion of the question marker, including the three tokens from the corpus.
clause!interrogative!polar|)
summary: Polar interrogative clauses can be marked by the question marker **gu/gus** following the finite verb, but this marking is exceptionally uncommon and not obligatory in current usage. The corpus evidence is very limited, with only three tokens of the marker found.

text:
mood!imperative
Clauses in the imperative mood stand out syntactically by lacking an overt subject NP. Furthermore, they are marked by special portmanteau morphemes
on the finite verb which express imperative mood as well as the number of the implied subject of the clause, which is always 2 nd person.
The finite verb tends to be in clause-initial position, as shown by the examples in impClause1 Låddávvre is the name of a lake.
and impClause2.

giehto naginav dan Låddávre birra\\
giehto nagina-v d-a-n Låddávre birra\\
tell sg.imp something- acc.sg dem- dist- gen.sg Låddávvre gen.sg about\\
Say something about this Låddávvre! 080924314

bieja pirunav bävvdaj\\
bieja piruna-v bävvda-j\\
put sg.imp potato- acc.sg table- ill.sg\\
Put the potato on the table! 101208478

Nonetheless, the standard phrase for ‘thank you’, shown in impClause3 in dual person, indicates that a constituent other than the finite verb may occur before a finite verb in imperative mood.

gijtov adnen\\
gijto-v adne-n\\
thank- acc.sg have- du.imp\\
Thank you (two)!(lit.: have thanks!) 101208292

However, no other examples of such constructions are found in the corpus, and this constituent ordering may be due to this phrase being a common expression and non-productive lexicalized structure calqued from the language contactSwedish expression tack ska du ha! (literally ‘thanks you shall have!’).

The adverb dále ‘now’ is common in imperative mood!imperative clauses, and is frequently abbreviated to dál, as in impClause5.

årren dál\\
årre-n dál\\
sleep- du.imp now\\
Go to sleep now! 110518a06m55s
summary: Imperative clauses lack an overt subject NP and are marked on the finite verb by special portmanteau morphemes that indicate both imperative mood and the number of the implied second-person subject. The finite verb is usually clause-initial, though a few exceptions occur, such as the fixed expression for “thank you,” which may reflect a lexicalized calque from Swedish rather than a productive pattern. The adverb dále/dál ‘now’ is common in imperative clauses.

potSyntaxEx2 and potSyntaxEx3.

nå hålåv, vuolgetjip del\\

mood!potential|)
summary:
Clauses in the potential mood are finite, marked by the suffix **-tj**, and generally lack an overt subject, though an overt subject is still possible. Because of this, they do not differ syntactically from declarative clauses.

The potential mood can also express a milder command, similar to the imperative mood, and in this use it likewise does not take an overt subject.

Two or more clauses can be conjoined by coordination or subordination.
After coordination is covered in clausalCoordination, complement clauses are presented in complementClauses and adverbial clauses are dealt with in adverbialClauses.
Finally, relative clauses which do not form a constituent of a matrix clause, but are instead part of a nominal phrase, are described in detail in this chapter as well (in relativeClauses ).
summary: Two or more clauses can be linked either by coordination or by subordination. Coordination is discussed elsewhere, while complement clauses and adverbial clauses are treated in separate sections; relative clauses are also covered here, since they belong to nominal phrases rather than forming a constituent of the matrix clause.

coordination|(
There are several coordinating conjunctions that are used to syntactically join the basic clauses described in Chapter basicClauses. In such cases, a coordinating conjunction occurs between the two clauses it connects. The clauses themselves are otherwise not marked in any way for coordination. The coordinating conjunctions are ja ‘and’, vala ‘but’, men Note that men is a borrowing from language contactSwedish (< men ‘but’) and is used almost exclusively in the corpus, while the native Saamic word vala is only found in a \ reading based on a Lule Saami translation of the New Testament (recording pit100403pit100403). Several examples in include men (e.g. on p. 20), so it has been part of \ for at least a century.
‘but’, jala ‘or’ and eller Just as with men, eller is a borrowing from language contactSwedish (< eller ‘or’); however, the native Saamic word jala is rather common as well in the corpus. Furthermore, unlike men, eller is not mentioned in, so it seems that eller is likely a more recent word-choice development, perhaps due to increased dominance of the Swedish language over the last century.
‘or’. The examples in coordination1 and coordination2 illustrate clausal coordination using the coordinators ja and men, respectively.

mån anav Árjepluove gaptev nanne, ja Ivan adna Arrvehavre gaptev\\
mån ana-v Árjepluove gapte-v nanne ja Ivan adna Arrvehavre gapte-v\\
1sg.nom have- 1sg.prs Arjeplog gen.sg frock- acc.sg on and Ivan have- 3sg.prs Arvidsjaur gen.sg frock- acc.sg\\
I have an Arjeplog frock on, and Ivan has an Arvidsjaur frock. 080825047

men ijtjin del bårå dan siste, men ednen biebmojd biergojd ja dále návte deggara sinne\\
men ijtji-n del bårå d-a-n siste men edne-n biebmo-jd biergo-jd ja dále návte deggara sinne\\
but neg- 3pl.pst obviously eat conneg dem- dist- gen.sg out but have- 3pl.pst food- acc.pl meat- acc.pl and now like.this such gen.pl in\\
But they obviously didn't eat out of that, but they had food, meat and so on in such things. 080708_Session03080708_Session03019

When jala and eller function as clausal coordinators in the corpus,
they are mostly used to indicate meta-language commentary showing that the second clause is an alternate or amended version of the first clause, as in ORcoordination1, rather than to provide clause-level alternatives.

dále’l gámbal dåhpe, jala almatj hållå “unna dåbátj”\\
dále=l gámbal dåhpe jala almatj hållå unna dåbá-tj\\
now=be 3sg.prs old house nom.sg or person nom.sg say 3sg.prs small house- dim nom.sg\\
Now this is the old house, or one says “the little house”. 100310b047-049

coordination|)
summary: The passage explains that several coordinating conjunctions join basic clauses syntactically by appearing between them, without any other special marking on the clauses. It notes that **ja** ‘and’, **men** ‘but’, **jala** ‘or’, and **eller** ‘or’ are used, with **men** and **eller** borrowed from Swedish; **men** is the dominant form in the corpus while **vala** is rare, and **eller** may be a more recent development than native **jala**. It also observes that when **jala** and **eller** coordinate clauses, they usually introduce metalinguistic commentary in which the second clause restates or amends the first rather than expressing a true alternative.
