subordination|(
Certain types of \ clauses can be subordinate to another clause or to a nominal phrase phrase!nominal.
When embedded at clause-level, a subordinate clause can be either a complement clause or an adverbial clause, depending on whether it fills an argument or an adverbial role.
These two types of subordinate clause are described in complementClauses and adverbialClauses, respectively.
Subordinate clauses featuring non-finite verb forms verb!non-finite are likely also found in, a possibility which is dealt with briefly in otherSubclauses.
Finally, relative clauses are covered in relativeClauses.
summary: Certain clauses can be subordinate either to another clause or to a nominal phrase. At the clause level, subordinate clauses may function as complement clauses or adverbial clauses, depending on whether they fill an argument or an adverbial role; non-finite subordinate clauses are also possible. Relative clauses are treated separately.

text:
clause!complement|( complement!clause|see clause
A complement clause fills an argument slot of the verbal predicate in the matrix clause it belongs to.
There are a variety of complement clause constructions, and both finite and infinitive predicates are possible. Complement clause!complement clauses can be marked by a complementizer
or can stand in juxtaposition to the matrix clause.
The different complement clause marking strategies are summarized in Table complementClauseSummary and described in the following sections.
summary: A complement clause fills an argument slot of the verbal predicate in its matrix clause. Complement clauses can be finite or infinitival, and they may be marked by a complementizer or simply placed in juxtaposition with the matrix clause. The different marking strategies are summarized in the table and discussed in the following sections.

subsubsection: Complement clauses with a finite predicate
text:
Complement clauses with a fully inflected finite verb!finite predicate are attested using one of two strategies.
First, the borrowed complementizer complementizer att Cf. the language contactSwedish marker att, which is also a complementizer.
can mark a complement clause. In such cases, the complement clause typically follows the matrix clause.

The complementizer is in clause-initial position in the complement clause.
Examples can be found in complementizer1 and complementizer2.

ja dä mån hålåv att sidav bajket\\
ja dä mån hålå-v att sida-v bajke-t\\
and then 1sg.nom say- 1sg.prs subord want- 1sg.prs poop- inf\\
And then I say that I want to poop. 080924591

men mån diedav att háre lä jávren\\
men mån dieda-v att háre lä jávre-n\\
but 1sg.nom know- 1sg.prs subord greyling nom.pl be 3pl.prs lake- iness.sg\\
But I know that there are greyling in the lake. 100404052

Secondly, complement clauses with a finite predicate may be juxtaposed to the matrix clause they belong to. The complement clause typically follows the matrix clause.
Verbs hosting such complements include jáhkket ‘believe’, diehtet ‘know’, hållåt ‘say’ and tuhtjet ‘like’.
Examples can be found in complClauseJuxFin1 through complClauseJuxFin3.

mån jáhkav stuor tjuovtja lä danne\\
mån jáhka-v stuor tjuovtj-a lä danne\\
1sg.nom believe- 1sg.prs big whitefish- nom.pl be 3pl.prs there\\
I believe there are big whitefish there. 090702123

men mån tuhtjiv dat lij nav suohtas tieltajn viessot\\
men mån tuhtji-v d-a-t lij nav suohtas tielta-jn viesso-t\\
but 1sg.nom think- 1sg.prs dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.pst so nice tent- iness.pl live- inf\\
But I think it was so nice to stay in tents. 080924644

men hålåv, vuhtjijmä mija sárvav\\
men hålå-v vuhtji-jmä mija sárva-v\\
but say- 1sg.prs shoot- 1pl.pst 1pl.nom moose- acc.sg\\
But then I say we shot a moose. 090702404

Constituent interrogative clauses clause!interrogative!constituent can also be juxtaposed complement clauses. As with any such interrogative clause, an interrogative pronoun pronoun!interrogative or other question word occurs as the initial element of the complement clause.
This strategy typically coincides with complements of epistemic verbs such as diehtet ‘know’ or skenit ‘understand’.
Some examples are provided in Qsubordination1 through Qsubordination3.

mån iv diede gåsse gillgin gávnadit maŋep bále\\
mån i-v diede gåsse gillgi-n gávnadi-t maŋe-p bále\\
1sg.nom neg-1sg.prs know conneg when will- 1du.prs meet- inf after- comp time gen.sg\\
I don’t know when we’ll meet next time. 081011183

mån iv skene mav dån hålå\\
mån i-v skene ma-v dån hålå\\
1sg.nom neg-1sg.prs understand conneg what- acc.sg 2sg.nom say 2sg.prs\\
I don’t understand what you’re saying. 08092605m14s

mån diedav gie lä\\
mån dieda-v gie lä\\
1sg.nom know- 1sg.prs who nom.sg be 3sg.prs\\
I know who she is. 090702460

While the complement clause typically follows the matrix clause, this does not necessarily have to be the case, as illustrated by Qsubordination4.

man mälgat lij gu lij hiejman, iv mån diede\\
man mälgat li-j gu li-j hiejma-n i-v mån diede\\
how far be- 3sg.pst when be- 3sg.pst home- iness.sg neg-1sg.prs 1sg.nom know conneg\\
I don’t know how far it was to get home. 100404317
summary: Finite complement clauses are attested in two main ways: either they are introduced by the borrowed complementizer *att*, which appears clause-initially in the complement clause, or they are simply juxtaposed with the matrix clause. The second strategy is used with verbs such as *jáhkket* ‘believe’, *diehtet* ‘know’, *hállåt* ‘say’, and *tuhtjet* ‘like’, and constituent interrogative clauses can also serve as juxtaposed complements, typically after epistemic verbs. Although complement clauses usually follow the matrix clause, this order is not obligatory.

subsubsection: Complement clauses with an infinitive predicate
text:
Complement clauses with an infinitive verb!non-finite predicate can be juxtaposed to the matrix clause they belong to. The complement clause typically follows the matrix clause.
While not particularly common in the corpus, verbs such as állget ‘begin’ and vajáldahtet/ åjaldahtet The word vajáldahtet ‘forget’ is likely limited to the northern dialects of, while åjaldahtet is preferred in the south.
‘forget’
are accompanied by complement clauses headed by an infinitive verb, as in complClauseJuxInf1 through complClauseJuxInf4.

nå gosse dijá älgijdä Örnvikast vuodjet vadnásav?\\
nå gosse dijá älgi-jdä Örnvika-st vuodje-t vadnása-v\\
well when 2pl.nom begin- 2pl.pst Örnvik- elat.sg drive- inf boat- acc.sg\\
Well when did you start to take the boat from Örnvik? 080924563

ja dä del virrtin allget biebmat, fodderijd vuodjet\\
ja dä del virrti-n allge-t biebma-t fodderi-jd vuodje-t\\
and then obviously must- 3pl.pst begin- inf feed- inf feed- acc.pl drive- inf\\
And so they obviously had to start to feed, to transport the feed. 100405a029

nä, mån liv åjaldahtam valldet maŋen\\
nä mån li-v åjaldahta-m vallde-t maŋen\\
no 1sg.nom be- 1sg.prs forget- prf take- inf with\\
No, I forgot to take it along. 090519322

vajálduhtiv hållåt, gu vusjkonijd dihkiv...\\
vajálduhti-v hållå-t gu vusjkoni-jd dihki-v\\
forget- 1sg.prs say- inf when perch- acc.pl do- 1sg.pst\\
I am forgetting to say, when I did the perch... 090702079

clause!complement|)
summary: Complement clauses with an infinitive non-finite verb can be juxtaposed directly to the matrix clause, and they usually follow it. This pattern is not very common in the corpus, but it occurs with verbs such as *állget* ‘begin’ and *vajáldat* / *åjaldahtet* ‘forget’ (with *vajáldahtet* likely northern and *åjaldahtet* southern), as shown in examples like “begin to feed” and “forget to take.”

text:
clause!adverbial|(
An adverbial clause is a subordinate clause that fills an adverbial function in the matrix clause.
Adverbial clauses begin with a subordinating element such as gu ‘when, once’, jus ‘if’, maŋŋel ‘after’, åvdål ‘before’, innan Note that the conjunction innan is a borrowing from Swedish language contact and is only attested once in the corpus. ‘before’
or gukte ‘how’,
but otherwise are not marked syntactically as subordinate clauses. The adverbial clause itself is headed by a fully inflected finite verb verb!finite.

For instance, the example in adverbialClause1 shows that the adverbial clause can follow the matrix clause.

hihtu vanj dä baktjat innan mån stärtiv motorav\\
hihtu vanj dä baktja-t innan mån stärti-v motora-v\\
must 2sg.prs well then back- inf before 1sg.nom start- 1sg.prs motor- acc.sg\\
Well you have to back up then before I start the motor. 090702018-019

In the example in adverbialClause2, the dependent clause!complementcomplement clause gu lidjin sladjim ‘once they had harvested’ precedes the matrix clause dä båhtin da bajás ‘then they came up’.

gu lidjin sladjim, dä båhtin da bajás\\
gu lidji-n sladji-m dä båhti-n d-a bajás\\
when be- 3pl.pst harvest- prf then come- 3pl.pst dem- dist sg.nom up\\
Once (the farmers) had harvested, then they (the plants) came up. 080924173

Adverbial clauses introduced by the subordinator jus ‘if’ set a condition for the matrix sentence. Other than this conjunction, there is no special marking for the mood!conditionalconditional.

The conditional clause can occur before or after the matrix clause, as shown in conditionalClause1 through conditionalClause3.

jus gussa dajd ulli, dä bårre dajd, dija gamasuijnijd\\
jus gussa d-a-jd ulli dä bårre d-a-jd dija gama-suijni-jd\\
if cow nom.pl dem- dist- acc.pl reach- 3pl.prs then eat 3pl.prs dem- dist- acc.pl 2pl.gen shoe-hay- acc.pl\\
If the cows reach up to it, then they eat it, your shoe hay. 080924221 Note that in example conditionalClause1, ‘hay’ and both pronouns referring to ‘hay’ are plural; however, for ease of reading, these are singular in the English translation. Gamasuäjdne ‘shoe-hay’ refers to a special type of grass placed inside shoes to insulate one’s feet from cold and moisture.

ja dat lij samma, jus del lij guallbana vaj bijjadaga vaj smav biehtsasdaga\\
ja d-a-t li-j samma jus del lij guallban-a vaj bijjadag-a vaj smav biehtsasdag-a\\
and dem- dist- nom.sg be- 3sg.pst same if then be- 3sg.pst flat.pine.heath- nom.pl or high.ground- nom.pl or small pine.forest- nom.pl\\
And that was the same whether it was flat-pine-heath or higher-ground or small pine-forests. 100405a009

jus galga njuallga dajd njuovvat dä galga dajd valdet olgus åvdål gádsastam\\
jus galga njuallga d-a-jd njuovva-t dä galga d-a-jd valde-t olgus åvdål gádsasta-m\\
if will 2sg.prs correct dem- dist- acc.pl slaughter- inf then will- 2sg.prs dem- dist- acc.pl take- inf out before hang- prf\\
If you slaughter them correctly, then you take them out before hanging (them) up. 080909105

clause!adverbial|)
summary:
Adverbial clauses are subordinate clauses that function adverbially in the matrix clause and are introduced by elements such as *gu* ‘when, once’, *jus* ‘if’, *maŋŋel* ‘after’, *åvdål* ‘before’, *innan* ‘before’, and *gukte* ‘how’. They are otherwise not specially marked as subordinate and are headed by a fully inflected finite verb.  

Conditional clauses introduced by *jus* express a condition for the main clause and do not have special conditional mood marking apart from the conjunction; they may appear before or after the matrix clause.

subsection: Other subordinate clauses with non-finite verb forms
text:
verb!non-finite
The literature on Saami languages often mentions other non-finite verb forms in addition to those mentioned above, which can be considered part of non-finite subordinate clauses often in adverbial function. These include the verb genitive, verb abessive or gerunds, for instance (cf. and for North Saami, or for Lule Saami).
For, describes the morphological form for a number of such non-finite forms, The non-finite forms are also included in the verb paradigms in.
but does not go into how these are used syntactically, and only one or two example clauses are provided at all. does not describe such verb forms.

With this in mind, it is certainly plausible that \ can make use of non-finite verb forms other than those mentioned above. However, there is little evidence of such forms in the corpus, and even this is limited to progressive forms in elicitation sessions. For instance, as mentioned in ADVverbs, the progressive non-finite verb form can be used adverbially. One example featuring the progressive form gullamin ‘listening’ is repeated here in ADVverbsEx2repeat. Even here, it is not clear whether such non-finite forms can include arguments or adjuncts.

gullamin mån tjálav\\
gulla-min mån tjála-v\\
listen- prog 1sg.nom write- 1sg.prs\\
I write while listening. 110404089

Ultimately, the syntactic behavior of such non-finite verbs, and whether these can be part of subordinate clauses, must be left for future study.
summary: The passage notes that Saami grammars sometimes mention additional non-finite verb forms, such as verb genitive, abessive, and gerunds, but these are usually described only morphologically and with little discussion of their syntax. In the corpus, there is little evidence for such forms beyond progressive forms used adverbially in elicitation data, and even then it remains unclear whether they can take arguments or adjuncts. The syntactic status of these non-finite verbs, including whether they form subordinate clauses, is left for future study.

text:
clause!relative|(
\ relative clauses are marked by a clause-initial relative pronoun pronoun!relative. The fact that this relative pronoun

is always the initial constituent constituent order in the relative clause is the only internal syntactic marking for relative clauses; otherwise, relative clauses are ordinary clauses with a fully inflected finite verb verb!finite.
The relative pronoun
inflects for case according to the syntactic function it fills within the relative clause, and for the number of the NP phrase!nominal that it modifies, as illustrated by relClause1 through relClause3.

dä inijmä aktav vuoksav majna vuojadijmä muorajd\\
dä ini-jmä akta-v vuoksa-v ma-jna vuojadi-jmä muora-jd\\
then have- 1pl.pst one- acc.sg bull- acc.sg rel- com.sg drive- 1pl.pst wood- acc.pl\\
We had one bull with which we transported firewood. 0906_Ahkajavvre_a0906_Ahkajavvre_a020

ja dä maŋŋemus skoterijd majd iniga\\
ja dä maŋŋe-mus skoteri-jd ma-jd ini-ga\\
and then after- superl snowmobile- acc.pl rel- acc.pl have- 3du.pst\\
…and the last snowmobiles which they had. 100404281

dä lä ájge ma lä urrum\\
dä lä ájge ma lä urru-m \\
then be 3pl.prs time nom.pl rel nom.pl be 3pl.prs be- prf\\
Those are times which have been.(i.e.: ‘those were the good old days’) 090702409

Just as demonstrative pronoun!demonstrative and interrogative pronoun!interrogative pronouns, relative pronouns only inflect for singular and plural, but not for dual number!dual number, as illustrated by the example in relClause4.

måj ma lin båhtam\\
måj ma li-n båhta-m\\
1du.nom rel nom.pl be- 3pl.pst come- prf\\
We two who had come. 11032932m45s

Note that the relative pronouns are homophonous with the
set of interrogative pronouns referring to non-human NPs. Cf. interrogativePronouns and relativePronouns for more on interrogative and relative pronouns, respectively.
However, not only do relative pronouns have a different syntactic function than interrogative pronouns in general, they are not sensitive to the humanness of the referent, unlike interrogative pronouns. For instance, the relative pronoun ma is the same in both relClause3 above and relClause5 below, although the former has ‘times’ as an antecedent and the latter refers to ‘young people’.

dä lin nuora álmatja ma lin riejdnohimen\\
dä li-n nuora álmatj-a ma li-n riejdnohi-men\\
then be- 3pl.pst young pred.pl people- nom.pl rel nom.pl be- 3pl.pst herd- prog\\
They were young people who were herding. 0906_Ahkajavvre_b0906_Ahkajavvre_b017

In the previous examples, relative clauses immediately follow the head of the noun phrase they modify. However, it is possible for a postposition adposition!postposition to occur between the modified NP and the relative clause, as illustrated by relClause6.

dat lij duv gugu masa båhten\\
d-a-t li-j duv gugu ma-sa båhte-n\\
dem- dist- nom.sg be- 3sg.pst 2sg.gen to rel- ill.sg come- 3pl.pst\\
It was to you they came. 11032937m04s

This shows that it is possible, in this case, for a relative clause to not be embedded syntactically in the modified NP, as the relative clause can occur outside the postpositional phrase phrase!postpositional which the modified NP is a constituent of. It should be emphasized that only a postposition can split a relative clause from the matrix NP it modifies.

There does not appear to be any restriction on the syntactic function that a relative pronoun can fill within the relative clause. With the exception of abessive case!abessive and essive case!essive, which are rare in the corpus for all nominals, relative pronouns are attested for all grammatical cases, as well as being the dependent NP in a postpositional phrase (in genitive case!genitive case), as in relClause7, or similarly as the possessor NP (also in genitive case) modifying a noun, as in relClause8.

dat lä náhppe man sisa båhtjen buhtsujd\\
d-a-t lä náhppe ma-n sisa båhtje-n buhtsu-jd\\
dem- dist- nom.sg be 3sg.prs milking.bowl nom.sg rel- gen.sg into milk- 3pl.pst reindeer- acc.pl\\
This is a milking bowl into which they milked reindeer. 080708_Session02080708_Session02003

men dä lä danne urrum dat pluovve man namma lä, mij lä namma dan, dáv mijá Árjepluovev\\
men dä lä danne urru-m d-a-t pluovve ma-n namma lä mij lä namma d-a-n d-á-v mijá Árjepluove-v\\
but then be 3sg.prs there be- prf dem- dist- nom.sg pond nom.sg rel- gen.sg name nom.sg be 3sg.prs rel nom.sg be 3sg.prs name nom.sg dem- dist- gen.sg dem- prox- acc.sg 1pl.gen Arjeplog- acc.sg\\
But here was the pond whose name was, which was the name of that, this, our Arjeplog. 090915013

This latter example is clear evidence for such a structure, but it is part of a false-start, as it also contains a semantically-driven self-correction just after the targeted example; however, as the single instance in the corpus for a relative pronoun modifying a noun, it must suffice as evidence at this point.

In summary, relative pronouns can fulfill a variety of syntactic functions in a relative clause. Specifically, relative pronouns can be
an argument NP,
an adjunct NP,
a dependent of a PP, or
a possessor of an NP.
clause!relative|)
subordination|)
summary:
Relative clauses are introduced by a clause-initial relative pronoun, and this initial position is the only special syntactic marking; otherwise, they are ordinary finite clauses. The relative pronoun agrees in case with its function in the relative clause and in number with the modified noun phrase, but it does not show dual number and is not sensitive to humanness, unlike interrogative pronouns.

Relative clauses normally follow the noun phrase they modify, though a postposition can intervene between the noun phrase and the relative clause. The relative pronoun can serve in many syntactic roles inside the clause, including as an argument, adjunct, dependent of a postposition, or possessor.
